claim_source_map.locator: Section 3(a)–(b): trigger, principal/relative scope and exact immigration sanctions
claim_source_map.passage: SEC. 3. SANCTIONS WITH RESPECT TO THE INTERNATIONAL CRIMINAL COURT. (a) In General.--Not later than 60 days after the date of enactment of this Act, and on an ongoing basis thereafter, if the International Criminal Court is engaging in any attempt to investigate, arrest, detain, or prosecute any protected person, the President shall impose-- (1) the sanctions described in subsection (b) with respect to any foreign person the President determines-- (A) has directly engaged in or otherwise aided any effort by the International Criminal Court to investigate, arrest, detain, or prosecute a protected person; (B) has materially assisted, sponsored, or provided financial, material, or technological support for, or goods or services to or in support of any effort by the International Criminal Court to investigate, arrest, detain, or prosecute a protected person; or (C) is owned or controlled by, or is currently acting or purports to have acted, directly or indirectly, for or on behalf of any person that directly engages in any effort by the International Criminal Court to investigate, arrest, detain, or prosecute a protected person; and (2) the sanctions described in subsection (b)(2) with respect to the immediate family members of each foreign person who is subject to sanctions pursuant to paragraph (1). (b) Sanctions Described.--The sanctions described in this subsection with respect to a foreign person described in subsection (a) are the following: (1) Property blocking.--The President shall exercise all of the powers granted by the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (50 U.S.C. 1701 et seq.) to the extent necessary to block and prohibit all transactions in all property and interests in property of any foreign person described in subsection (a)(1) if such property and interests in property are in the United States, come within the United States, or are or come within the possession or control of a United States person. (2) Aliens inadmissible for visas, admission, or parole.-- (A) Visas, admission, or parole.--In the case of an alien described in subsection (a), the alien is-- (i) inadmissible to the United States; (ii) ineligible to receive a visa or other documentation to enter the United States; and (iii) otherwise ineligible to be admitted or paroled into the United States or to receive any other benefit under the Immigration and Nationality Act (8 U.S.C. 1101 et seq.). (B) Current visas revoked.-- (i) In general.--The visa or other entry documentation of an alien described in subparagraph (A) shall be revoked, regardless of when such visa or other entry documentation was issued. (ii) Immediate effect.--A revocation under clause (i) shall-- (I) take effect immediately; and (II) automatically cancel any other valid visa or entry documentation that is in the alien's possession.

claim_source_map.locator: Section 3(c)–(f): implementation, notification, waiver and termination
claim_source_map.passage: (c) Implementation; Penalties.-- (1) Implementation.--The President may exercise all authorities provided under sections 203 and 205 of the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (50 U.S.C. 1702 and 1704) to carry out this section. (2) Penalties.--A person that violates, attempts to violate, conspires to violate, or causes a violation of this section or any regulation, license, or order issued to carry out this section shall be subject to the penalties set forth in subsections (b) and (c) of section 206 of the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (50 U.S.C. 1705) to the same extent as a person that commits an unlawful act described in subsection (a) of that section. (d) Notification to Congress.--Not later than 10 days after any imposition of sanctions pursuant to subsection (a), the President shall brief and provide written notification to the appropriate congressional committees regarding the imposition of sanctions that shall include-- (1) a description of the foreign person or persons subject to the imposition of such sanctions, including the foreign person's role at or relation to the International Criminal Court; (2) a description of any activity undertaken by such foreign person or persons in support of efforts to investigate, arrest, detain, or prosecute any protected person; and (3) the specific sanctions imposed on such foreign person or persons. (e) Waiver.-- (1) In general.--The President may, on a case-by-case basis and for periods not to exceed 90 days each, waive the application of sanctions imposed or maintained with respect to a foreign person under this section if the President submits to the appropriate congressional committees before the waiver is to take effect a report that contains a determination of the President that the waiver is vital to the national security interests of the United States. (2) Contents.--Each report required by paragraph (1) with respect to a waiver of the application of sanctions imposed or maintained with respect to a foreign person under this section, or the renewal of such a waiver, shall include-- (A) a specific and detailed rationale for the determination that the waiver is vital to the national security interests of the United States; (B) a description of the activity that resulted in the foreign person being subject to sanctions; (C) a detailed description and list of actions the United States has taken to stop the International Criminal Court from engaging in any effort to investigate, arrest, detain, or prosecute all protected persons; and (D) a detailed description and list of actions the International Criminal Court has taken to permanently close, withdraw, end, or otherwise terminate any preliminary examination, investigation, or any other effort to investigate, arrest, detain, or prosecute all protected persons. (3) Form.--Each report required by paragraph by paragraph (1) shall be submitted in unclassified form but may include a classified annex. (f) Special Rule.--The President may terminate the sanctions with respect to the foreign persons described in subsection (a) if the President certifies in writing to the appropriate congressional committees that the International Criminal Court-- (1) has ceased engaging in any effort to investigate, arrest, detain, or prosecute all protected persons; and (2) has permanently closed, withdrawn, ended, and otherwise terminated any preliminary examination, investigation, or any other effort by the International Criminal Court to investigate, arrest, detain, or prosecute all protected persons.

claim_source_map.passage: SEC. 4. RESCISSION OF FUNDS FOR INTERNATIONAL CRIMINAL COURT. (a) In General.--Effective on the date of the enactment of this Act, any amounts appropriated for the International Criminal Court and available for obligation as of such date of enactment are hereby rescinded. (b) Prohibition on Future Appropriations.--On and after the date of the enactment of this Act, no appropriated funds may be used for the International Criminal Court. SEC. 5. DEFINITIONS. In this Act: (1) Admitted alien.--The terms ``admitted'' and ``alien'' have the meanings given those terms in section 101 of the Immigration and Nationality Act (8 U.S.C. 1101). (2) Ally of the united states.--The term ``ally of the United States'' means-- (A) a government of a member country of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization; or (B) a government of a major non-NATO ally, as that term is defined by section 2013(7) of the American Service-Members' Protection Act (22 U.S.C. 7432(7)). (3) Appropriate congressional committees defined.--The term ``appropriate congressional committees'' means-- (A) the Committee on Foreign Affairs, the Committee on Financial Services, and the Committee on the Judiciary of the House of Representatives; and (B) the Committee on Foreign Relations the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs, and the Committee on the Judiciary of the Senate. (4) Foreign person.--The term ``foreign person'' means a person that is not a United States person. (5) Immediate family member.--The term ``immediate family member'', with respect to a foreign person, means the spouse, parent, sibling, or adult child of the person. (6) International criminal court; rome statute.--The terms ``International Criminal Court'' and ``Rome Statute'' have the meaning given those terms in section 2013 of the American Service-Members' Protection Act (22 U.S.C. 7432). (7) Protected person.--The term ``protected person'' means-- (A) any United States person, unless the United States provides formal consent to International Criminal Court jurisdiction and is a state party to the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court, including-- (i) current or former members of the Armed Forces of the United States; (ii) current or former elected or appointed officials of the United States Government; and (iii) any other person currently or formerly employed by or working on behalf of the United States Government; (B) any foreign person that is a citizen or lawful resident of an ally of the United States that has not consented to International Criminal Court jurisdiction or is not a state party to the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court, including-- (i) current or former members of the Armed Forces of such ally of the United States; (ii) current or former elected or appointed government officials of such ally of the United States; and (iii) any other person currently or formerly employed by or working on behalf of such a government. findings.headline: H.R. 5103 DC commission immigration recommendations and monitoring
findings.compact: Foushee opposed passage of the complete H.R. 5103 EH proposal; no preferred alternative is established. H.R. 5103 would establish a DC commission to recommend and review immigration-enforcement policies and monitor sanctuary-city compliance, alongside broader policing and beautification work, through January 2, 2029.
detail: Foushee opposed passage of the complete H.R. 5103 EH proposal; no preferred alternative is established.

The complete H.R. 5103 EH establishes a statutory District of Columbia Safe and Beautiful Commission in the executive branch. Its section 3(d)(1) functions are to RECOMMEND ACTIONS and REVIEW THEIR EFFECTIVENESS with respect to the listed tasks, including developing and encouraging policies directing maximum Federal immigration-law enforcement within DC and encouraging redirection of available Federal, State or local law-enforcement resources to apprehend/deport the aliens described in the printed provision; and monitoring DC sanctuary-city status and Federal immigration-law enforcement compliance. These are express operative immigration-specific recommendation/monitoring functions, not only findings or the fact DHS is a member. The proposal does not itself order a named person removed, adjudicate unlawful status, redefine sanctuary city, create a new admission/removal ground, directly repeal DC sanctuary legislation or newly grant the Commission the underlying agencies arrest, detention or deportation powers. Its operational-assistance/coordination permission is expressly TO THE EXTENT PERMITTED BY LAW. Commission membership includes nine specified Federal departments/components or U.S. Attorney offices, the DC Executive Office of the Mayor AS DEFINED in 1-315.02(3), and additional Federal entities chosen by the chair. That DC definition covers specified managerial/budget/personnel/secretarial/planning/information/special-support offices and excludes the named Office of Personnel; it is not every DC agency or a requirement for the Mayor personally to serve. Heads designate representatives within 45 days, including 45 days after later chair designations for added Federal entities. The President designates a SENIOR EOP official as chair within 45 days, with meeting scheduling/entity selection and a consultatively developed charter submitted within 7 days of completion. The Commission reports its carried-out functions/authorities and appropriate legislative recommendations to the specified House Oversight and Senate Homeland Security committees, without an invented periodic reporting deadline. Its other tasks concern forensic-lab accreditation, police staffing/capabilities, concealed-carry-license processing, qualified pretrial policies, transit crime and law-enforcement presence; they are whole-package context, not independently attributed Immigration component choices. The separate Interior program is developed within 30 days with specified Federal/DC consultation, coordinates cleanliness/graffiti, qualified monument restoration and private participation, and reports after 1 year and annually. Both statutory sections/program/Commission end January 2,2029. This is not the first related federal initiative: original EO 14252 of March 27,2025 independently established a RELATED Safe and Beautiful Task Force with immigration-enforcement coordination/monitoring, related agencies, executive reporting and Interior beautification directives. The bill establishes its own statutory Commission, chair/designation/charter/report/sunset framework, including the DC Executive Office representative, and recommendation/review wording. The earlier EO language expressly directs Task Force coordination on specified enforcement tasks in the Washington metropolitan area, whereas the bill immigration-policy clause specifies DC; do not equate their geographic wording or legal objects. Original EO 14252 is a dated baseline witness, not an exhaustive assertion about every later executive change or actual implementation. Its law/appropriation and no-private-enforceable-benefit limits are preserved. The bill does not say it repeals that Task Force, first creates all existing agency enforcement power or appropriates a specified new enforcement amount. The whole final-passage choice encompasses Commission and beautification work, not a separate vote on deportation, sanctuary status or a particular police operation. One H.R. 5103 episode. No actual deportation, safety improvement, compliance, spending or enactment follows from the House vote.
The Clerk recorded the House result as 'Passed' on 2026-03-25. This does not establish enactment.
qualifications_on_both_levels: The Commission recommendation, review and sanctuary-compliance monitoring functions are operative. They do not establish an actual deportation, individual unlawful status, new removal ground or repeal of every DC sanctuary rule.

Operational assistance and coordination remain limited by existing law. The Commission does not receive an unrestricted independent arrest/detention/deportation power or a specified new enforcement appropriation.

The bill statutory Commission, chair/member/charter/report duties and January 2,2029 sunset differ from the related original 2025 executive Task Force. Do not claim first enforcement authority or identity of every executive/bill scope.

This is the whole Commission-plus-beautification proposal, including broader police and civic work. No immigration-component-only preference, periodic Commission-report clock, automatic benefit or observed implementation is inferred.

claim_source_map.passage: [Congressional Bills 119th Congress] [From the U.S. Government Publishing Office] [H.R. 5103 Engrossed in House (EH)] <DOC> 119th CONGRESS 2d Session H. R. 5103 _______________________________________________________________________ AN ACT To establish a program to Beautify the District of Columbia and establish the District of Columbia Safe and Beautiful Commission. Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the United States of America in Congress assembled, SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE. This Act may be cited as the ``Make the District of Columbia Safe and Beautiful Act of 2025''. SEC. 2. PROGRAM TO BEAUTIFY DISTRICT OF COLUMBIA. (a) Establishment.-- (1) In general.--Not later than 30 days after the date of the enactment of this section, the Secretary of the Interior (hereinafter the ``Secretary'') shall develop a program to beautify the District of Columbia (hereinafter the ``Program''). (2) Consultation.--The Secretary, when establishing the Program, shall consult with each of the following: (A) The Attorney General. (B) The Secretary of Transportation. (C) The Mayor of the District of Columbia. (D) The United States Attorney for the District of Columbia. (E) The Administrator of General Services. (F) The heads of such other Federal departments and agencies and District of Columbia officials as the Secretary deems appropriate. (b) Purpose.--The purpose of the Program is to establish and implement a plan for Federal and local officials to-- (1) coordinate, and maintain, the cleanliness, of Federal and District of Columbia facilities, monuments, land, public spaces, sidewalks, parks, highways, roads, transit systems, and other commonly visited areas within the District of Columbia, including through the removal of graffiti; (2) restore, to the extent practicable, District of Columbia and Federal public monuments, memorials, statues, markers, and similar properties that have been damaged or defaced or inappropriately removed or changed; and (3) encourage private-sector participation in the efforts of the Program. (c) Report.--Not later than 1 year after the date of the enactment of this section, and annually thereafter, the Secretary shall submit a report to the Committees on Oversight and Government Reform and on Natural Resources of the House of Representatives and the Committees on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs and on Energy and Natural Resources of the Senate that includes a summary of the progress of the Program and the plan as described in subsection (b). (d) Sunset.--This section, and the Program established by this section, shall terminate on January 2, 2029. SEC. 3. DISTRICT OF COLUMBIA SAFE AND BEAUTIFUL COMMISSION. (a) Establishment.--There is established in the executive branch a District of Columbia Safe and Beautiful Commission (hereafter the ``Commission''). (b) Membership.-- (1) In general.--The Commission shall be comprised of representatives of each of the following entities: (A) The Department of the Interior. (B) The Department of Transportation. (C) The Department of Homeland Security. (D) The Federal Bureau of Investigation. (E) The United States Marshals Service. (F) The Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives. (G) The United States Attorney's Office for the District of Columbia. (H) The United States Attorney's Office for the District of Maryland. (I) The United States Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of Virginia. (J) The Executive Office of the Mayor of the District of Columbia (as defined in section 3(3) of the Governmental Reorganization Procedures Act of 1981; sec. 1-315.02(3), D.C. Official Code). (K) Such other entities of the Federal government as may be determined by the Chair of the Commission. (2) Designation of members.--Not later than 45 days after the date of the enactment of this section (or, in the case of an entity described in subsection (b)(1)(K), not later than 45 days after the Chair of the Commission designates the entity), the head of each entity described in subsection (b)(1) shall designate a representative of that entity to serve as the representative of the entity on the Commission. (c) Chair.-- (1) Designation.--Not later than 45 days after the date of the enactment of this section, the President shall designate a senior level official from the Executive Office of the President to serve as the Chair of the Commission. (2) Functions.--The Chair shall perform functions that include the following: (A) Developing a schedule of meetings for the Commission. (B) Designating entities who shall be represented on the Commission under subsection (b)(1)(K). (C) In consultation with the members of the Commission, developing a charter for the Commission and, not later than 7 days after the date on which the charter is completed, submitting the charter to the appropriate committees of Congress. (d) Functions and Authorities.-- (1) Functions.--The functions of the Commission are to recommend actions, and review the effectiveness of such actions, with respect to, but not limited to, the following: (A) Developing and encouraging the implementation of polices which will direct the maximum enforcement of Federal immigration law within the District of Columbia, including policies to encourage the redirection of available Federal, State, or local law enforcement resources to apprehend and deport illegal aliens. (B) Monitoring the District of Columbia's sanctuary-city status and compliance with the enforcement of Federal immigration law. (C) Facilitating the prompt and complete accreditation of the District of Columbia's forensic crime laboratory. (D) In collaboration with its leadership and union, ensuring that the Metropolitan Police Department of the District of Columbia is provided with assistance to facilitate the recruitment, retention, and capabilities of its officers and facilitating the provision of Federal personnel, resources, and expertise to reduce crime. (E) Collaborating with appropriate local government entities to provide assistance to increase the speed and lower the cost of processing concealed carry license requests in the District of Columbia. (F) Reviewing and, as appropriate, recommending revisions to Federal prosecutorial policies on pretrial detention of criminal defendants to ensure that individuals who pose a genuine threat to public safety are detained to the maximum extent permitted by law. (G) Collaborating with appropriate local government entities to provide assistance to end fare evasion and other crime within the Washington Metropolitan Area Transit Authority system. (H) Facilitating the deployment of a more robust Federal law enforcement presence, and in coordination with local law enforcement agencies, facilitating the deployment of a more robust local law enforcement presence (as appropriate) within the District of Columbia, including the National Mall and Memorial Parks, museums, monuments, Lafayette Park, Union Station, Rock Creek Park, Anacostia Park, the George Washington Memorial Parkway, the Suitland Parkway, and the Baltimore-Washington Parkway. (2) Coordination with other authorities.--The Commission may, to the extent permitted by law, request operational assistance from and coordinate with Federal and local officials as appropriate, including the Metropolitan Police Department of the District of Columbia, the Washington Metropolitan Area Transit Authority, and the Amtrak Police. (e) Report.--The Commission shall submit a report to the appropriate committees of Congress which includes a summary of the functions and authorities carried out pursuant to subsection (d), and shall include in the report such recommendations for legislation as the Commission considers appropriate. (f) Appropriate Committees of Congress Defined.--In this section, the term ``appropriate committees of Congress'' means-- (1) the Committee on Oversight and Government Reform of the House of Representatives; and (2) the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs of the Senate. (g) Sunset.--This section, and the Commission established by this section, shall terminate on January 2, 2029. Passed the House of Representatives March 25, 2026. claim_source_map.locator: Complete exact House EH, complete original dated executive baseline or complete incorporated DC Executive Office definition
claim_source_map.passage: Federal Register, Volume 90 Issue 63 (Thursday, April 3, 2025) [Federal Register Volume 90, Number 63 (Thursday, April 3, 2025)] [Presidential Documents] [Pages 14559-14561] From the Federal Register Online via the Government Publishing Office [ www.gpo.gov ] [FR Doc No: 2025-05837] � � � Presidential Documents � � ��Federal Register / Vol. 90, No. 63 / Thursday, April 3, 2025 / Presidential Documents�� [[Page 14559]] Executive Order 14252 of March 27, 2025 Making the District of Columbia Safe and Beautiful By the authority vested in me as President by the Constitution and the laws of the United States of America, it is hereby ordered: Section 1. Purpose. As the Federal capital city, Washington, D.C., is the only city that belongs to all Americans and that all Americans can claim as theirs. As the capital city of the greatest Nation in the history of the world, it should showcase beautiful, clean, and safe public spaces. America's capital must be a place in which residents, commuters, and tourists feel safe at all hours, including on public transit. Its highways, boulevards, and parks should be clean, well-kept, and pleasant. Its monuments, museums, and buildings should reflect and inspire awe and appreciation for our Nation's strength, greatness, and heritage. Our citizens deserve nothing less. Sec. 2. Policy. It is the policy of the United States to make the District of Columbia safe, beautiful, and prosperous by preventing crime, punishing criminals, preserving order, protecting our revered American monuments, and promoting beautification and the preservation of our history and heritage. Sec. 3. Making the District of Columbia Safe by Fighting Crime. (a) My Administration shall work closely with local officials to share information, develop joint priorities, and maximize resources to make the District of Columbia safe. Such coordination shall occur through the D.C. Safe and Beautiful Task Force (Task Force), which is hereby established by this order. The Task Force shall be chaired by the Assistant to the President and Homeland Security Advisor or his designee, and shall otherwise include representatives from the following departments, agencies, or components, selected as such department, agency, or component determines: (i) the Department of the Interior; (ii) the Department of Transportation; (iii) the Department of Homeland Security; (iv) the Federal Bureau of Investigation; (v) the United States Marshals Service; (vi) the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives; (vii) the United States Attorney's Office for the District of Columbia; (viii) the United States Attorney's Office for the District of Maryland; and (ix) the United States Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of Virginia. The Chairman of the Task Force may also select other departments, agencies, or components to participate as he deems necessary. Representatives of such other departments, agencies, or components shall be selected as such department, agency, or component determines. (b) The Task Force may, to the extent permitted by law, request operational assistance from and coordinate with the Metropolitan Police Department of the District of Columbia (MPD), Washington Metropolitan Area Transit Authority, United States Park Police, Amtrak Police, and other Federal and local officials as appropriate. (c) The Task Force shall coordinate to ensure effective Federal participation in the following tasks: [[Page 14560]] (i) directing maximum enforcement of Federal immigration law and redirecting available Federal, State, or local law enforcement resources to apprehend and deport illegal aliens in the Washington, D.C. metropolitan area; (ii) monitoring the District of Columbia's sanctuary-city status and compliance with the enforcement of Federal immigration law; (iii) providing assistance to facilitate the prompt and complete accreditation of the District of Columbia's forensic crime laboratory; (iv) in collaboration with its leadership and union, providing MPD with assistance to facilitate the recruitment, retention, and capabilities of its police officers and to facilitate work with Federal personnel, resources, and expertise to reduce crime; (v) collaborating with appropriate local government entities to provide assistance to increase the speed and lower the cost of processing concealed carry license requests in the District of Columbia; (vi) reviewing and, as appropriate, revising Federal prosecutorial policies on seeking pretrial detention of criminal defendants to ensure that individuals who pose a genuine threat to public safety are detained to the maximum extent permitted by law; (vii) collaborating with appropriate local government entities to provide assistance to end fare evasion and other crime within the Washington Metropolitan Area Transit Authority system; and (viii) deploying a more robust Federal law enforcement presence and coordinating with local law enforcement to facilitate the deployment of a more robust local law enforcement presence as appropriate in areas in or about the District of Columbia, including in such areas as the National Mall and Memorial Parks, museums, monuments, Lafayette Park, Union Station, Rock Creek Park, Anacostia Park, the George Washington Memorial Parkway, the Suitland Parkway, and the Baltimore-Washington Parkway, and ensuring that all applicable quality of life, nuisance, and public-safety laws are strictly enforced, such as those prohibiting assault, battery, larceny, graffiti and other vandalism, unpermitted disturbances and demonstrations, noise, trespassing, public intoxication, drug possession, sale, and use, and traffic violations, including as prescribed by Executive Order 13933 of June 26, 2020 (Protecting American Monuments, Memorials, and Statues and Combating Recent Criminal Violence), which was reinstated by Executive Order 14189 of January 29, 2025 (Celebrating America's 250th Birthday). (d) The Task Force shall report to me as necessary through the Assistant to the President and Homeland Security Advisor regarding safety in the District of Columbia, and the tasks set forth in subsection (c) of this section. As part of this reporting, the Attorney General, in consultation with the Task Force, shall assess whether public-safety circumstances in the District of Columbia require additional executive action. Sec. 4. Making the District of Columbia Beautiful. (a) The Secretary of the Interior, in consultation with the Attorney General, the Secretary of Transportation, the United States Attorney for the District of Columbia, the Administrator of General Services, the National Capital Planning Commission, and the heads of such other executive departments or agencies and local officials as the Secretary of the Interior deems appropriate, shall develop and implement a program to beautify and make safe and prosperous the District of Columbia. (b) The program under subsection (a) of this section shall include, at a minimum, the following elements as appropriate and consistent with applicable law: (i) a coordinated beautification plan for Federal and local facilities, monuments, land, parks, and roadways in and around the District of Columbia; [[Page 14561]] (ii) restoration of Federal public monuments, memorials, statues, markers, or similar properties that have been damaged or defaced, or inappropriately removed or changed, in recent years; (iii) removal of graffiti from commonly visited areas, with local assistance; (iv) proposals to ensure Federal buildings or lands adequately uplift and beautify public spaces and generate in the citizenry pride in and respect for our Nation; (v) a coordinated Federal and local approach to ensure the cleanliness of public spaces, sidewalks, parks, highways, roads, and transit systems in and around the District of Columbia; and (vi) the encouragement of private-sector participation in coordinated beautification and clean-up efforts in the District of Columbia. (c) The Secretary of the Interior shall immediately issue a directive to the National Park Service requiring prompt removal and cleanup of all homeless or vagrant encampments and graffiti on Federal land within the District of Columbia subject to the National Park Service's jurisdiction, to the maximum extent permitted by law. Sec. 5. General Provisions. (a) Nothing in this order shall be construed to impair or otherwise affect: (i) the authority granted by law to an executive department or agency, or the head thereof; or (ii) the functions of the Director of the Office of Management and Budget relating to budgetary, administrative, or legislative proposals. (b) This order shall be implemented consistent with applicable law and subject to the availability of appropriations. (c) This order is not intended to, and does not, create any right or benefit, substantive or procedural, enforceable at law or in equity by any party against the United States, its departments, agencies, or entities, its officers, employees, or agents, or any other person. (Presidential Sig.) THE WHITE HOUSE, March 27, 2025. [FR Doc. 2025-05837 Filed 4-2-25; 8:45 am] Billing code 3395-F4-P

findings.headline: H.R. 8029 exact annual DHS funding and immigration conditions
findings.compact: Foushee opposed passage of the whole exact H.R. 8029 annual DHS funding proposal; no preferred funding or immigration alternative is established. H.R. 8029 would fund FY 2026 border, ICE and USCIS operations within the whole DHS package, retaining qualified sponsor, custody, contracting and oversight limits and adding surveillance, camera and budget-reporting provisions. It also carries qualified lapse-pay and obligation provisions.
detail: Foushee opposed passage of the whole exact H.R. 8029 annual DHS funding proposal; no preferred funding or immigration alternative is established.

The complete H.R. 8029 EH is the whole March 26 House annual DHS proposal with division A annual appropriations and division B lapse-pay/qualified obligation-ratification provisions. Its own sections 3-5 define thisAct references in division A as that DIVISION except where express, explicitly incorporate the January 22 H.R. 7147 explanatory statement for allocation/implementation, and appropriate FY 2026 sums.230(b) uses the corrected DHS-funds-in-this-or-prior-Act scope, not the earlier January as-voted any-other-Act wording. The complete body independently compared to 7147 EH retains the annual DHS package, makes technical 237 enumeration changes, and omits 554 Senate-datarepeal (already 119-75 H 105), rather than silently adding a new removal or sanctions policy. The parallel 7744/8029 bodies were independently compared: distinct exact bills/dates/short titles, with otherwise matching operative annual/lapse-pay bodies. Each remains its own bill episode; no cross-bill analytical relation or unique-concept-breadth claim is invented. DivisionB 1001 covers the lapse ON OR ABOUT February 13, 2026 (not the February 14 date in the March 27 CRreplacement);1002 directs available 119-37 A/newdivision A personnel pay/allowance/benefit payments under existing 31 US 1341(c);1003 ratifies essential-life/property/orderly-shutdown/otherwise-authorized obligations only IF OTHERWISE IN ACCORD with the referenced Acts. Existing 1341(c) already supplies qualified furloughed/excepted standard-pay/leave compensation after a covered lapse ends subject to ending appropriations; this is not first-ever backpay or actual payment, and division B does not substitute a new 106(3)CRouterdate. The annual DHS titles would fund existing border processing/security, immigration enforcement, custody and removal, citizenship-services processing and verification, and associated oversight for FY 2026 within a wider DHS package. CBP Operations and Support is $17.727974 billion, with $550 million available through September 30, 2027, mixed customs/trade/travel, UAC transport, air/marine and law-enforcement functions, Harbor Maintenance and user-fee components, and qualified informant, preclearance and Tribal-road uses. CBP procurement/construction is $222.886 million with distinct September 2028 asset and September 2030 construction availability. The final table allocates CBP Ops across Border Security $6.644912 billion, Trade/Travel $6.610801 billion, Integrated Operations $1.730551 billion and Mission Support $2.741710 billion; these are not four independently voted immigration policies or all-person-removal spending. The earlier $650 million CBP-to-FEMA shelter-transfer row has no new Final Bill amount. ICE Ops is $10.036362 billion, including $46.696 million through September 2027, no-year forced-labor funds, qualified HERO/IP-rights/informant/special-operations uses and up to $11.216 million for care, maintenance and repatriation of smuggled aliens UNLAWFULLY PRESENT. The final allocations are HSI $2.591251 billion, ERO $5.453706 billion, Mission Support $1.543711 billion and OPLA $447.694 million. ERO includes Custody $3.838340 billion, Fugitive $165.016 million, Criminal Alien Program $312.835 million, ATD $393.647 million and Transport/Removal $743.868 million. HSI includes many non-immigration investigations; detention and ATD are different uses. These table amounts do not themselves establish actual beds, removals or expenditure. ICE procurement is $5 million through September 2028. USCIS Ops is $122.941 million: $112.566 million Employment Status Verification and $10.375 million Application Processing/backlog reduction in the Final Bill table, not exclusively E-Verify. USCIS has no new Federal Assistance/Citizenship and Integration Grant amount in the final table; previously funded grants and termination-justification reporting are distinct. Existing adjudication-fee authority 1356(m)/(n) and the bill no-required-fee-reduction proviso remain; the separate fee-funded-program table is not an extra new discretionary appropriation. OSEM Ops $316.295 million includes $10 million CRCL, $5 million Citizenship/Immigration Services Ombudsman, no new Immigration Detention Ombudsman allocation, and no new $15 million ATD Case Management Grant allocation; the last two do not abolish their statutory offices or all ATD. OBIM receives $271 million and IDENT/HART procurement $25 million. OIG Ops $257.599 million includes $20 million additional detention inspections through September 2027 and $12.814 million reconciliation-fund oversight. Section 109 adds $20 million for body-worn cameras for agents/officers enforcing INA authorities plus a 30 day spending plan. FEMA includes $85.5 million Operation Stonegarden within $494 million State Homeland grants. The wider TSA, Coast Guard, Secret Service, disaster, cyber, training, research, Supreme Court-security and air-traffic provisions remain whole-package context; membership in DHS does not make all their spending Immigration evidence.

The statutory restrictions preserve their exact funding and trigger scopes. Section 207 bars a NEW defined land-border crossing fee and a related study, beginning enactment, for pedestrians/cyclists/private-vehicle drivers/passengers at northern/southern LPOEs; it does not abolish all existing immigration or inspection fees.208 requires a 90 day CBP procurement plan before this Act's funds are obligated;209 permits altering National Targeting Center operations but protects planned vetting at existing locations across specified current/prior/fee funds unless later statute authorizes a reduction.210 bars funds for Border Security Assets/Infrastructure in this or prior Acts from procuring/deploying NONAUTONOMOUS surveillance SYSTEMS, using 119-21 section 90004(c)'s definition; the older 90004(b) restriction separately concerns tested/accepted autonomous TOWERS using that section's funds.211 requires the November 30, 2021 CBP pregnant/postpartum/nursing/infant custody policy OR substantively similar standards developed with maternal/pediatric experts to be in effect and fully implemented. The original covered populations include pregnancy with medical concerns OR third trimester/active labor, nursing individuals, postpartum within six months or recent pregnancy loss, and infants under one year. Health interviews/assessment/referral retain resource/operational and offered-assessment/acceptance qualifications; documented fifteen-minute welfare checks, nutrition/breastfeeding/infant supplies, facility/operational qualifications and incident records remain; it is not first-ever care, an automatic 72 hour release rule, or identical unqualified entitlements for every person.212 prohibits using ICE Ops to CONTINUE 287(g) delegations when the DHS IG determines a MATERIAL agreement violation.213 prohibits continuing a detention-services contract if its TWO most recent OVERALL performance evaluations are BELOW adequate/equivalent median, with ICE OPR conducting the evaluations. Neither trigger is every complaint or one failed component score.214 permits necessary ICE Ops reprogramming/transfers for detention of aliens prioritized for removal without 503(d)'s time/condition limit; it is not an unrestricted waiver of every appropriation or statutory restriction.

215 continues semimonthly 2021 detention-data reporting, including the original 2020 operational/ATD/facility/detention/release/removal data and 2021 additions such as solitary-confinement use/duration and length-of-stay bins.216 reapplies complete 2020 sections 216/217: no covered detention/removal/referral/initiation-of-proceeding of a UAC sponsor, potential sponsor or household member BASED ON HHS-shared information, EXCEPT the specified background-check findings of an aggravated-felony/child-abuse/sexual-violence/child-porn felony conviction OR pending related FELONY charge, business association involving unrelated minors below legal wage or denied school, or prostitution participation/implementation. It is neither an absolute sponsor exemption nor an exception for every conviction or illegal-entry suspicion. The accompanying IG 287(g) report covers participation, training, criminality/nationality, removals, outreach and future plans.217 replaces the earlier 45 day current-Act plan with a 30 day Director briefing/written plan covering ALL available current/prior/carryover/fee funds, monthly PPA/pay/nonpay projections and unchanged initial comparison; monthly updates are due within 15 days after the following month begins. Conditional $100,000 Executive Leadership/Oversight amounts become available on the 16 th of each month, at most $700,000 for the fiscal year, subject to timely reporting beginning 30 days after enactment.218 requires a 90 day plan for 119-21 detention-facility funding, locations/beds/cost/transport/removal-flight/end-state capacity, with quarterly updates within 30 days; reporting projections are not observed immigration outcomes.219 protects ICE attaché/liaison presence at foreign embassies/consulates using this or other Act funds, except the joint DHS/State foreign-policy explanation or a host-country cessation request.238 reapplies the 2021 fencing restriction WITH RESPECT TO THIS ACT's funds in the same manner: Santa Ana, Bentsen-Rio Grande Valley State Park, La Lomita, National Butterfly Center, within OR EAST of Vista del Mar Ranch, and historic cemeteries. Do not infer an unrestricted prohibition on every separate reconciliation-fund use.

USCIS 401 permits only five replacement vehicles where GSA does not lease, with authorized home/work use;402 restricts A-76 competition for five named USCIS employee classes, including temporary/term staff;403 permits collection/use of biometrics at Application Support Centers overseen VIRTUALLY by USCIS personnel using appropriate technology. This repeats existing 2024 authority, rather than first authorizing biometrics, universal remote adjudication or unrestricted searches.512 continues the THIS ACT funding restriction on amending the INA 337 naturalization oath, preserving 1448's existing qualifying modified oaths and disability/qualifying-child waivers;517 uses 1324 a(h)(3)'s employment-at-the-particular-time definition, excluding LPRs and law-authorized workers from unauthorized alien, not all noncitizens.514 restricts this Act's funds for national-ID planning/testing/piloting/development, not every immigration identity document.527 continues the funding restriction on restraints for pregnant or post-delivery women in DHS custody/transport/outside treatment, with individualized unavoidable serious flight risk/immediate harm or therapeutic-medical exceptions for a pregnant woman, safest/least-restrictive provider-determined restraints, an ABSOLUTE active-labor/delivery ban, barred pregnant positions/belts and feasible left-side positioning.528 protects covered death/possible-sexual-assault/abuse records and allegations of abuse/crime/disruption BY detainees from destruction, with disclosure on an affected punished individual's request under applicable law/litigation rules. It is not unrestricted public access to all detainee or staff records.536 repeats a this/other-Act funding bar on transferring/releasing/assisting transfer to or within the United States/territories/possessions of the specified Guantanamo DOD-held-on-or-after-June 24, 2009 NONcitizen/NONmilitary detainees, not a general new INA inadmissibility ground for all people held elsewhere.547 bars THIS ACT DHS funds from blocking Members or designated House/Senate employees conducting oversight of DHS-operated/contracted ALIEN detention/housing facilities or restaging conditions: Members need no prior notice; staff may be required 24 hours. It is not an unrestricted public-visitor right or a blanket rule for all HHS facilities/funding sources.

General appropriation controls remain:501 current-fiscal-year obligation limit unless express longer/no-year availability;502 merges prior balances for the original purposes/availability;503 advance reprogramming notices and 5 percent transfers/no more than 10 percent augmentation, June 15 initial-notification limit with imminent-life/property exception, grant/new-unapproved-PPA restrictions and deobligated-balance procedures.503(f) permits UP TO $20 million transferred into the EXISTING Immigration Emergency Fund with five-day notice. The old 404 note separately authorizes a $35 million BALANCE and qualified immigration-emergency withdrawals needing Presidential determination/certification, plus capped State/local reimbursements under 404(b)(2) for which that emergency determination is not needed. A transfer here is not a new emergency declaration, unrestricted withdrawal or actual reimbursement.505 carries up to 50 percent unobligated FY 2026 Ops balances through September 2027 with the printed June 15, 2027 recording deadline and 503 notification.524's qualified report publication retains national-interest determination, security/proprietary exceptions and 45 day committee availability unless otherwise specified, now with 503 suspension for failure;525 permits minor Ops procurement/construction with unit caps $250,000 personal/$4 million real property.537/538 require monthly independently validated arrival and detention/removal estimates, demographic separation, common planning/budget assumptions and agency/committee sharing; failure suspends 503 authority.539 requires alternatives/cost-benefit analysis BEFORE requesting DoD border support and post-request/grant/quarterly reports.541 transfers AT LEAST $5 million to ICE Blue Campaign with pre-obligation notice.546 requires seven-day and quarterly 119-21 obligations/fee-retention/remittance/planned-use reports.551-553 rescind only identified UNOBLIGATED account balances, with the printed emergency-designation exception in 551 and defined 2024 carryover balances in 552; this is not cancellation of every outstanding obligation or all reconciliation funds.107's I&A covered-activity funding restriction incorporates 6303: specified charged/custodial unadjudicated criminal interviews need consent AFTER counsel consultation, targeting journalists in their functions is covered, and U. S.-person interviews require factual reasonable belief in significant foreign intelligence; the definition includes known LPRs and qualified associations/corporations, with foreign-controlled-corporation exception. Legal/privacy/civic oversight and specified lawful information sharing are expressly preserved. It is not a general no-intelligence rule or new immigration status ground.

The January 22 explanatory narrative and visually checked FINAL BILL tables govern the named allocations; earlier House Report 119-173 PROPOSAL amounts and numbered proposed riders are not substituted for this actual text. The narrative says House report LANGUAGE has equal weight unless noted or addressed to the contrary, and repetition does not negate it unless expressly provided. Its operative directions include 287(g) cost-benefit/training/agreement evaluations and reports; border/credible-fear/parole/UAC/parent/veteran/tribal/arrest/removal/wrongful-return data; warrants/probable-cause/flight-risk reports; HART/IDENT oversight and qualified child-separation notifications; medical/water/food/shelter/TEDS and continued migrant-care requirements; free confidential ICE counsel communication/document/VAV access and legal-orientation continuation TO THE MAXIMUM EXTENT POSSIBLE; qualified family-unity/separation, pregnant-custody redeterminations and sensitive-location directions; facilities/segregation/inspections/PREA oversight; ATD metrics/consequence reporting, monitoring-feasibility and procurement directions; and USCIS processing dashboards/backlogs, fees/waivers, asylum/refugee/EAD/SIJ/H-2 A/H-2 B/R-1 processing/abuse and policy-change reporting. The separately incorporated 118-85,116-458 and 118-553 directions are source-bound, retaining their population/exception/scheduling/privacy/feasibility wording and distinguishing requested reports, encouraged actions, directives and statutory rights. For example, the port-of-entry counsel paragraph requests a 90 day briefing on requirements for a meaningful one-hour consultation for U. S. nationals, LPRs returning from a temporary foreign visit, valid unexpired immigrant/nonimmigrant visa holders, refugees, returning asylees or approved parole applicants, with greatest-practicable in-person advocacy, not an unconditional new lawyer entitlement for every border entrant. The related ICE counsel direction concerns free confidential unmonitored 60 minute calls/video with 24 hour scheduling, document exchange/delivery and facility access, not government-paid representation. Continued family reunification is qualified by best interests/possibility; the pregnancy-custody direction preserves required-law/exceptional-circumstance grounds and monthly review. The House TPS-Venezuela direction calls for reconsideration/analysis and a 30 day briefing, while the Ukraine program language urges continuation; neither itself grants a named person TPS/parole or first changes individual eligibility. The final fee-waiver language supersedes the House cost-recovery restriction while mandatory statutory fees and their own waiver limits are not silently repealed. The Housereport 50,000-bed proposal, earlier PPA figures and former numbered proposed sanctuary/rhetoric riders are not treated as actual present statutory conditions merely because the report is referenced. Conflicting or uncertain application of retained report language versus the final allocation/statutory scope remains a candidate-review question, not an accepted adjudication.

Baseline: 119-4 incorporated FY 2024 DHS 118-47 division C with specified exceptions/anomalies, including ICE's $9.986542 billion FY 2025 Ops level;119-37 division A carried relevant FY 2025 rates/conditions with its own exceptions, and 119-75 division H changed the residualCR date to February 13. The annual proposal replaces the relevant continuation with full FY 2026 DHS appropriations; many sponsor/contract/287(g)/fencing/oath/employment/restraint/oversight/biometric controls already existed and are not first-ever rights or powers. The separate 119-21 reconciliation appropriations and fees are not all repealed/replaced by these annual totals. Whole passage includes enforcement funds, services, protective limits, oversight and other DHS/non-DHS provisions together. No component-only preference, motive, actual detention/deportation/care improvement, pay/spending, later enactment or individual legal outcome is inferred.
The Clerk recorded the House result as 'Passed' on 2026-03-26. This does not establish enactment.
qualifications_on_both_levels: This is the whole exact annual DHS package, mixing enforcement, processing, custody protections, oversight and other spending. No component-only preference or actual removal/bed/care/spending outcome is inferred.

The FINAL BILL allocation columns control: CBP/ICE contain non-immigration uses; USCIS includes verification AND application processing. Fee-funded figures and separate reconciliation appropriations are not added as new discretionary funding here.

Existing sponsor restrictions retain specified background exceptions;287(g) and detention-contract bars require material IG findings or two below-adequate overall OPR evaluations. They are not absolute sponsor immunity or a bar triggered by any complaint.

Pregnant/postpartum custody policy may be replaced by substantively similar expert-developed standards. Restraint exceptions, absolute labor/delivery protections and retained law/exceptional-circumstance custody boundaries are not flattened into universal release or no-restraint claims.

Counsel/family/medical/report directions retain population, timing, privacy, legal and feasibility qualifications. POE counsel assessment is distinct from ICE confidential-access directives and government-paid representation; proposed report riders/amounts do not silently become actual statute.

Congressional oversight access applies to named Members/designated staff at DHS alien facilities with the printed notice and funding scopes; record disclosure, fee, fence and intelligence limits retain their own exceptions and scopes.

Some controls are continued; others add reporting, camera, surveillance or budget conditions. No new general INA admission/removal power, wholesale fee abolition, every visa-program sunset extension or unqualified expenditure authority is established.

The exact legislative version and bill episode control. Later engrossment corrections, the March continuing-resolution replacement and parallel bills do not retrospectively change this member choice. Ambiguous report/incorporation application remains candidate review, with no acceptance or public authorization.

OSEM Ops $316.295 million includes $10 million CRCL, $5 million Citizenship/Immigration Services Ombudsman, no new Immigration Detention Ombudsman allocation, and no new $15 million ATD Case Management Grant allocation; the last two do not abolish their statutory offices or all ATD. OBIM receives $271 million and IDENT/HART procurement $25 million. OIG Ops $257.599 million includes $20 million additional detention inspections through September 2027 and $12.814 million reconciliation-fund oversight. Section 109 adds $20 million for body-worn cameras for agents/officers enforcing INA authorities plus a 30 day spending plan. FEMA includes $85.5 million Operation Stonegarden within $494 million State Homeland grants. The wider TSA, Coast Guard, Secret Service, disaster, cyber, training, research, Supreme Court-security and air-traffic provisions remain whole-package context; membership in DHS does not make all their spending Immigration evidence.

The statutory restrictions preserve their exact funding and trigger scopes. Section 207 bars a NEW defined land-border crossing fee and a related study, beginning enactment, for pedestrians/cyclists/private-vehicle drivers/passengers at northern/southern LPOEs; it does not abolish all existing immigration or inspection fees.208 requires a 90 day CBP procurement plan before this Act's funds are obligated;209 permits altering National Targeting Center operations but protects planned vetting at existing locations across specified current/prior/fee funds unless later statute authorizes a reduction.210 bars funds for Border Security Assets/Infrastructure in this or prior Acts from procuring/deploying NONAUTONOMOUS surveillance SYSTEMS, using 119-21 section 90004(c)'s definition; the older 90004(b) restriction separately concerns tested/accepted autonomous TOWERS using that section's funds.211 requires the November 30, 2021 CBP pregnant/postpartum/nursing/infant custody policy OR substantively similar standards developed with maternal/pediatric experts to be in effect and fully implemented. The original covered populations include pregnancy with medical concerns OR third trimester/active labor, nursing individuals, postpartum within six months or recent pregnancy loss, and infants under one year. Health interviews/assessment/referral retain resource/operational and offered-assessment/acceptance qualifications; documented fifteen-minute welfare checks, nutrition/breastfeeding/infant supplies, facility/operational qualifications and incident records remain; it is not first-ever care, an automatic 72 hour release rule, or identical unqualified entitlements for every person.212 prohibits using ICE Ops to CONTINUE 287(g) delegations when the DHS IG determines a MATERIAL agreement violation.213 prohibits continuing a detention-services contract if its TWO most recent OVERALL performance evaluations are BELOW adequate/equivalent median, with ICE OPR conducting the evaluations. Neither trigger is every complaint or one failed component score.214 permits necessary ICE Ops reprogramming/transfers for detention of aliens prioritized for removal without 503(d)'s time/condition limit; it is not an unrestricted waiver of every appropriation or statutory restriction.

215 continues semimonthly 2021 detention-data reporting, including the original 2020 operational/ATD/facility/detention/release/removal data and 2021 additions such as solitary-confinement use/duration and length-of-stay bins.216 reapplies complete 2020 sections 216/217: no covered detention/removal/referral/initiation-of-proceeding of a UAC sponsor, potential sponsor or household member BASED ON HHS-shared information, EXCEPT the specified background-check findings of an aggravated-felony/child-abuse/sexual-violence/child-porn felony conviction OR pending related FELONY charge, business association involving unrelated minors below legal wage or denied school, or prostitution participation/implementation. It is neither an absolute sponsor exemption nor an exception for every conviction or illegal-entry suspicion. The accompanying IG 287(g) report covers participation, training, criminality/nationality, removals, outreach and future plans.217 replaces the earlier 45 day current-Act plan with a 30 day Director briefing/written plan covering ALL available current/prior/carryover/fee funds, monthly PPA/pay/nonpay projections and unchanged initial comparison; monthly updates are due within 15 days after the following month begins. Conditional $100,000 Executive Leadership/Oversight amounts become available on the 16 th of each month, at most $700,000 for the fiscal year, subject to timely reporting beginning 30 days after enactment.218 requires a 90 day plan for 119-21 detention-facility funding, locations/beds/cost/transport/removal-flight/end-state capacity, with quarterly updates within 30 days; reporting projections are not observed immigration outcomes.219 protects ICE attaché/liaison presence at foreign embassies/consulates using this or other Act funds, except the joint DHS/State foreign-policy explanation or a host-country cessation request.238 reapplies the 2021 fencing restriction WITH RESPECT TO THIS ACT's funds in the same manner: Santa Ana, Bentsen-Rio Grande Valley State Park, La Lomita, National Butterfly Center, within OR EAST of Vista del Mar Ranch, and historic cemeteries. Do not infer an unrestricted prohibition on every separate reconciliation-fund use.

USCIS 401 permits only five replacement vehicles where GSA does not lease, with authorized home/work use;402 restricts A-76 competition for five named USCIS employee classes, including temporary/term staff;403 permits collection/use of biometrics at Application Support Centers overseen VIRTUALLY by USCIS personnel using appropriate technology. This repeats existing 2024 authority, rather than first authorizing biometrics, universal remote adjudication or unrestricted searches.512 continues the THIS ACT funding restriction on amending the INA 337 naturalization oath, preserving 1448's existing qualifying modified oaths and disability/qualifying-child waivers;517 uses 1324 a(h)(3)'s employment-at-the-particular-time definition, excluding LPRs and law-authorized workers from unauthorized alien, not all noncitizens.514 restricts this Act's funds for national-ID planning/testing/piloting/development, not every immigration identity document.527 continues the funding restriction on restraints for pregnant or post-delivery women in DHS custody/transport/outside treatment, with individualized unavoidable serious flight risk/immediate harm or therapeutic-medical exceptions for a pregnant woman, safest/least-restrictive provider-determined restraints, an ABSOLUTE active-labor/delivery ban, barred pregnant positions/belts and feasible left-side positioning.528 protects covered death/possible-sexual-assault/abuse records and allegations of abuse/crime/disruption BY detainees from destruction, with disclosure on an affected punished individual's request under applicable law/litigation rules. It is not unrestricted public access to all detainee or staff records.536 repeats a this/other-Act funding bar on transferring/releasing/assisting transfer to or within the United States/territories/possessions of the specified Guantanamo DOD-held-on-or-after-June 24, 2009 NONcitizen/NONmilitary detainees, not a general new INA inadmissibility ground for all people held elsewhere.547 bars THIS ACT DHS funds from blocking Members or designated House/Senate employees conducting oversight of DHS-operated/contracted ALIEN detention/housing facilities or restaging conditions: Members need no prior notice; staff may be required 24 hours. It is not an unrestricted public-visitor right or a blanket rule for all HHS facilities/funding sources.

General appropriation controls remain:501 current-fiscal-year obligation limit unless express longer/no-year availability;502 merges prior balances for the original purposes/availability;503 advance reprogramming notices and 5 percent transfers/no more than 10 percent augmentation, June 15 initial-notification limit with imminent-life/property exception, grant/new-unapproved-PPA restrictions and deobligated-balance procedures.503(f) permits UP TO $20 million transferred into the EXISTING Immigration Emergency Fund with five-day notice. The old 404 note separately authorizes a $35 million BALANCE and qualified immigration-emergency withdrawals needing Presidential determination/certification, plus capped State/local reimbursements under 404(b)(2) for which that emergency determination is not needed. A transfer here is not a new emergency declaration, unrestricted withdrawal or actual reimbursement.505 carries up to 50 percent unobligated FY 2026 Ops balances through September 2027 with the printed June 15, 2027 recording deadline and 503 notification.524's qualified report publication retains national-interest determination, security/proprietary exceptions and 45 day committee availability unless otherwise specified, now with 503 suspension for failure;525 permits minor Ops procurement/construction with unit caps $250,000 personal/$4 million real property.537/538 require monthly independently validated arrival and detention/removal estimates, demographic separation, common planning/budget assumptions and agency/committee sharing; failure suspends 503 authority.539 requires alternatives/cost-benefit analysis BEFORE requesting DoD border support and post-request/grant/quarterly reports.541 transfers AT LEAST $5 million to ICE Blue Campaign with pre-obligation notice.546 requires seven-day and quarterly 119-21 obligations/fee-retention/remittance/planned-use reports.551-553 rescind only identified UNOBLIGATED account balances, with the printed emergency-designation exception in 551 and defined 2024 carryover balances in 552; this is not cancellation of every outstanding obligation or all reconciliation funds.107's I&A covered-activity funding restriction incorporates 6303: specified charged/custodial unadjudicated criminal interviews need consent AFTER counsel consultation, targeting journalists in their functions is covered, and U. S.-person interviews require factual reasonable belief in significant foreign intelligence; the definition includes known LPRs and qualified associations/corporations, with foreign-controlled-corporation exception. Legal/privacy/civic oversight and specified lawful information sharing are expressly preserved. It is not a general no-intelligence rule or new immigration status ground.

The January 22 explanatory narrative and visually checked FINAL BILL tables govern the named allocations; earlier House Report 119-173 PROPOSAL amounts and numbered proposed riders are not substituted for this actual text. The narrative says House report LANGUAGE has equal weight unless noted or addressed to the contrary, and repetition does not negate it unless expressly provided. Its operative directions include 287(g) cost-benefit/training/agreement evaluations and reports; border/credible-fear/parole/UAC/parent/veteran/tribal/arrest/removal/wrongful-return data; warrants/probable-cause/flight-risk reports; HART/IDENT oversight and qualified child-separation notifications; medical/water/food/shelter/TEDS and continued migrant-care requirements; free confidential ICE counsel communication/document/VAV access and legal-orientation continuation TO THE MAXIMUM EXTENT POSSIBLE; qualified family-unity/separation, pregnant-custody redeterminations and sensitive-location directions; facilities/segregation/inspections/PREA oversight; ATD metrics/consequence reporting, monitoring-feasibility and procurement directions; and USCIS processing dashboards/backlogs, fees/waivers, asylum/refugee/EAD/SIJ/H-2 A/H-2 B/R-1 processing/abuse and policy-change reporting. The separately incorporated 118-85,116-458 and 118-553 directions are source-bound, retaining their population/exception/scheduling/privacy/feasibility wording and distinguishing requested reports, encouraged actions, directives and statutory rights. For example, the port-of-entry counsel paragraph requests a 90 day briefing on requirements for a meaningful one-hour consultation for U. S. nationals, LPRs returning from a temporary foreign visit, valid unexpired immigrant/nonimmigrant visa holders, refugees, returning asylees or approved parole applicants, with greatest-practicable in-person advocacy, not an unconditional new lawyer entitlement for every border entrant. The related ICE counsel direction concerns free confidential unmonitored 60 minute calls/video with 24 hour scheduling, document exchange/delivery and facility access, not government-paid representation. Continued family reunification is qualified by best interests/possibility; the pregnancy-custody direction preserves required-law/exceptional-circumstance grounds and monthly review. The House TPS-Venezuela direction calls for reconsideration/analysis and a 30 day briefing, while the Ukraine program language urges continuation; neither itself grants a named person TPS/parole or first changes individual eligibility. The final fee-waiver language supersedes the House cost-recovery restriction while mandatory statutory fees and their own waiver limits are not silently repealed. The Housereport 50,000-bed proposal, earlier PPA figures and former numbered proposed sanctuary/rhetoric riders are not treated as actual present statutory conditions merely because the report is referenced. Conflicting or uncertain application of retained report language versus the final allocation/statutory scope remains a candidate-review question, not an accepted adjudication.

Baseline: 119-4 incorporated FY 2024 DHS 118-47 division C with specified exceptions/anomalies, including ICE's $9.986542 billion FY 2025 Ops level;119-37 division A carried relevant FY 2025 rates/conditions with its own exceptions, and 119-75 division H changed the residualCR date to February 13. The annual proposal replaces the relevant continuation with full FY 2026 DHS appropriations; many sponsor/contract/287(g)/fencing/oath/employment/restraint/oversight/biometric controls already existed and are not first-ever rights or powers. The separate 119-21 reconciliation appropriations and fees are not all repealed/replaced by these annual totals. Whole passage includes enforcement funds, services, protective limits, oversight and other DHS/non-DHS provisions together. No component-only preference, motive, actual detention/deportation/care improvement, pay/spending, later enactment or individual legal outcome is inferred.
The Clerk recorded the House result as 'Passed' on 2026-03-26. This does not establish enactment.
qualifications: This is the whole exact annual DHS package, mixing enforcement, processing, custody protections, oversight and other spending. No component-only preference or actual removal/bed/care/spending outcome is inferred.

The FINAL BILL allocation columns control: CBP/ICE contain non-immigration uses; USCIS includes verification AND application processing. Fee-funded figures and separate reconciliation appropriations are not added as new discretionary funding here.

Existing sponsor restrictions retain specified background exceptions;287(g) and detention-contract bars require material IG findings or two below-adequate overall OPR evaluations. They are not absolute sponsor immunity or a bar triggered by any complaint.

Pregnant/postpartum custody policy may be replaced by substantively similar expert-developed standards. Restraint exceptions, absolute labor/delivery protections and retained law/exceptional-circumstance custody boundaries are not flattened into universal release or no-restraint claims.

Counsel/family/medical/report directions retain population, timing, privacy, legal and feasibility qualifications. POE counsel assessment is distinct from ICE confidential-access directives and government-paid representation; proposed report riders/amounts do not silently become actual statute.

Congressional oversight access applies to named Members/designated staff at DHS alien facilities with the printed notice and funding scopes; record disclosure, fee, fence and intelligence limits retain their own exceptions and scopes.

Some controls are continued; others add reporting, camera, surveillance or budget conditions. No new general INA admission/removal power, wholesale fee abolition, every visa-program sunset extension or unqualified expenditure authority is established.

The exact legislative version and bill episode control. Later engrossment corrections, the March continuing-resolution replacement and parallel bills do not retrospectively change this member choice. Ambiguous report/incorporation application remains candidate review, with no acceptance or public authorization.
