"In this title, the following definitions apply: "(1) Driver's license .—The term 'driver's license'— "(A) means a motor vehicle operator's license, as defined in section 30301 of title 49, United States Code; and "(B) includes driver's licenses stored or accessed via electronic means, such as mobile or digital driver's licenses, which have been issued in accordance with regulations prescribed by the Secretary. "(2) Identification card .—The term 'identification card'— "(A) means a personal identification card, as defined in section 1028(d) of title 18, United States Code, issued by a State; and "(B) includes identification cards stored or accessed via electronic means, such as mobile or digital identification cards, which have been issued in accordance with regulations prescribed by the Secretary. "(3) Official purpose .—The term 'official purpose' includes but is not limited to accessing Federal facilities, boarding federally regulated commercial aircraft, entering nuclear power plants, and any other purposes that the Secretary shall determine. "(4) Secretary .—The term 'Secretary' means the Secretary of Homeland Security. "(5) State .—The term 'State' means a State of the United States, the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico, the Virgin Islands, Guam, American Samoa, the Northern Mariana Islands, and any other territory or possession of the United States. "SEC. 202. MINIMUM REQUIREMENTS AND ISSUANCE STANDARDS FOR FEDERAL RECOGNITION. "(a) Minimum Standards for Federal Use.— "(1) In general .—Beginning 3 years after the date of the enactment of this division [May 11, 2005], a Federal agency may not accept, for any official purpose, a driver's license or identification card issued by a State to any person unless the State is meeting the requirements of this section. "(2) State certifications .—The Secretary shall determine whether a State is meeting the requirements of this section based on certifications made by the State to the Secretary. Such certifications shall be made at such times and in such manner as the Secretary may prescribe by regulation. "(3) Limitation .—The presentation of digital information from a mobile or digital driver's license or identification card to an official of a Federal agency for an official purpose may not be construed to grant consent for such Federal agency to seize the electronic device on which the license or card is stored or to examine any other information contained on such device. "(b) Minimum Driver's License and Identification Card Requirements .—To meet the requirements of this section, a State shall include, at a minimum, the following information and features on, or as part of, each driver's license and identification card issued to a person by the State: "(1) The person's full legal name. "(2) The person's date of birth. "(3) The person's gender. "(4) The person's driver's license or identification card number. "(5) A digital photograph of the person, which may be the photograph taken by the State at the time the person applies for a driver's license or identification card or may be a digital photograph of the person that is already on file with the State. "(6) The person's address of principal residence. "(7) The person's signature. "(8) Security features designed to prevent tampering, counterfeiting, or duplication of the driver's license or identification card for fraudulent purposes. "(9) A common machine-readable technology, with defined minimum data elements. "(c) Minimum Issuance Standards.— "(1) In general .—To meet the requirements of this section, a State shall require, at a minimum, presentation and verification of the following information before issuing a driver's license or identification card to a person: "(A) A photo identity document, except that a non-photo identity document is acceptable if it includes both the person's full legal name and date of birth. "(B) Documentation showing the person's date of birth. "(C) The person's social security account number or verification that the person is not eligible for a social security account number. "(D) Documentation showing the person's name and address of principal residence. "(2) Special requirements.— "(A) In general .—To meet the requirements of this section, a State shall comply with the minimum standards of this paragraph. "(B) Evidence of lawful status .—A State shall require, before issuing a driver's license or identification card to a person, valid documentary evidence that the person— "(i) is a citizen or national of the United States; "(ii) is an alien lawfully admitted for permanent or temporary residence in the United States; "(iii) has conditional permanent resident status in the United States; "(iv) has an approved application for asylum in the United States or has entered into the United States in refugee status; "(v) has a valid, unexpired nonimmigrant visa or nonimmigrant visa status for entry into the United States; "(vi) has a pending application for asylum in the United States; "(vii) has a pending or approved application for temporary protected status in the United States; "(viii) has approved deferred action status; "(ix) has a pending application for adjustment of status to that of an alien lawfully admitted for permanent residence in the United States or conditional permanent resident status in the United States; or "(x) is a citizen of the Republic of the Marshall Islands, the Federated States of Micronesia, or the Republic of Palau who has been admitted to the United States as a nonimmigrant pursuant to a Compact of Free Association between the United States and the Republic or Federated States. "(C) Temporary drivers' licenses and identification cards.— "(i) In general .—If a person presents evidence under any of clauses (v) through (ix) of subparagraph (B), the State may only issue a temporary driver's license or temporary identification card to the person. "(ii) Expiration date .—A temporary driver's license or temporary identification card issued pursuant to this subparagraph shall be valid only during the period of time of the applicant's authorized stay in the United States or, if there is no definite end to the period of authorized stay, a period of one year. "(iii) Display of expiration date .—A temporary driver's license or temporary identifica tion card issued pursuant to this subparagraph shall clearly indicate that it is temporary and shall state the date on which it expires. "(iv) Renewal .—A temporary driver's license or temporary identification card issued pursuant to this subparagraph may be renewed only upon presentation of valid documentary evidence that the status by which the applicant qualified for the temporary driver's license or temporary identification card has been extended by the Secretary of Homeland Security. "(3) Electronic presentation of identity and lawful status information .—A State may accept information required under paragraphs (1) and (2) through the use of electronic transmission methods if— "(A) the Secretary issues regulations regarding such electronic transmission that— "(i) describe the categories of information eligible for electronic transmission; and "(ii) include measures— "(I) to ensure the authenticity of the information transmitted; "(II) to protect personally identifiable information; and "(III) to detect and prevent identity fraud; and "(B) the State certifies to the Department of Homeland Security that its use of such electronic methods complies with regulations issued by the Secretary. "(4) Verification of documents .—To meet the requirements of this section, a State shall implement the following procedures: "(A) Before issuing a driver's license or identification card to a person, the State shall verify, with the issuing agency, the issuance, validity, and completeness of the information and documentation required to be presented by the person under paragraph (1) or (2). "(B) The State shall not accept any foreign document, other than an official passport, to satisfy a requirement of paragraph (1) or (2). "(C) Not later than September 11, 2005, the State shall enter into a memorandum of understanding with the Secretary of Homeland Security to routinely utilize the automated system known as Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements, as provided for by section 404 of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996 [Pub. L. 104–208, div. C, 8 U.S.C. 1324a note] (110 Stat. 3009–664), to verify the legal presence status of a person, other than a United States citizen, applying for a driver's license or identification card. "(d) Other Requirements .—To meet the requirements of this section, a State shall adopt the following practices in the issuance of drivers' licenses and identification cards: "(1) Employ technology to capture digital images of identity source documents so that the images can be retained in electronic storage in a transferable format. "(2) Retain paper copies of source documents for a minimum of 7 years or images of source documents presented for a minimum of 10 years. "(3) Subject each person applying for a driver's license or identification card to mandatory facial image capture. "(4) Establish an effective procedure to confirm or verify a renewing applicant's information. "(5) Confirm with the Social Security Administration a social security account number presented by a person using the full social security account number. In the event that a social security account number is already registered to or associated with another person to which any State has issued a driver's license or identification card, the State shall resolve the discrepancy and take appropriate action. "(6) Refuse to issue a driver's license or identification card to a person holding a driver's license issued by another State without confirmation that the person is terminating or has terminated the driver's license. "(7) Ensure the physical security of locations where drivers' licenses and identification cards are produced and the security of materials, records, and data from which drivers' licenses and identification cards are produced. "(8) Subject all persons authorized to manufacture or produce drivers' licenses and identification cards to appropriate background checks. "(9) Establish fraud detection and prevention training programs for appropriate employees engaged in the issuance of drivers' licenses and identification cards. "(10) Limit the period of validity of all driver's licenses and identification cards that are not temporary to a period that does not exceed 8 years. "(11) In any case in which the State issues a driver's license or identification card that does not satisfy the requirements of this section, ensure that such license or identification card— "(A) clearly states on its face that it may not be accepted by any Federal agency for federal identification or any other official purpose; and "(B) uses a unique design or color indicator to alert Federal agency and other law enforcement personnel that it may not be accepted for any such purpose. "(12) Provide electronic access to all other States to information contained in the motor vehicle database of the State. "(13) Maintain a State motor vehicle database that contains, at a minimum— "(A) all data fields printed on drivers' licenses and identification cards issued by the State; and "(B) motor vehicle drivers' histories, including motor vehicle violations, suspensions, and points on licenses.

Nationals but not citizens of the United States at birth Unless otherwise provided in section 1401 of this title, the following shall be nationals, but not citizens, of the United States at birth: (1) A person born in an outlying possession of the United States on or after the date of formal acquisition of such possession; (2) A person born outside the United States and its outlying possessions of parents both of whom are nationals, but not citizens, of the United States, and have had a residence in the United States, or one of its outlying possessions prior to the birth of such person; (3) A person of unknown parentage found in an outlying possession of the United States while under the age of five years, until shown, prior to his attaining the age of twenty-one years, not to have been born in such outlying possession; and (4) A person born outside the United States and its outlying possessions of parents one of whom is an alien, and the other a national, but not a citizen, of the United States who, prior to the birth of such person, was physically present in the United States or its outlying possessions for a period or periods totaling not less than seven years in any continuous period of ten years— (A) during which the national parent was not outside the United States or its outlying possessions for a continuous period of more than one year, and (B) at least five years of which were after attaining the age of fourteen years. Voting by aliens (a) It shall be unlawful for any alien to vote in any election held solely or in part for the purpose of electing a candidate for the office of President, Vice President, Presidential elector, Member of the Senate, Member of the House of Representatives, Delegate from the District of Columbia, or Resident Commissioner, unless— (1) the election is held partly for some other purpose; (2) aliens are authorized to vote for such other purpose under a State constitution or statute or a local ordinance; and (3) voting for such other purpose is conducted independently of voting for a candidate for such Federal offices, in such a manner that an alien has the opportunity to vote for such other purpose, but not an opportunity to vote for a candidate for any one or more of such Federal offices. (b) Any person who violates this section shall be fined under this title, imprisoned not more than one year, or both. (c) Subsection (a) does not apply to an alien if— (1) each natural parent of the alien (or, in the case of an adopted alien, each adoptive parent of the alien) is or was a citizen (whether by birth or naturalization); (2) the alien permanently resided in the United States prior to attaining the age of 16; and (3) the alien reasonably believed at the time of voting in violation of such subsection that he or she was a citizen of the United States.

This Act may be cited as the ``Confirmation Of Congressional Observer Access Act of 2024'' or the ``COCOA Act of 2024''. SEC. 2. ACCESS FOR CONGRESSIONAL ELECTION OBSERVERS. (a) Access Required.--Title III of the Help America Vote Act of 2002 (52 U.S.C. 21081 et seq.) is amended-- (1) by redesignating section 304 and 305 <<NOTE: 52 USC 21084, 21085.>> as sections 305 and 306; and (2) by inserting after section 303 the following new section: ``SEC. 304. <<NOTE: 52 USC 21083a note.>> ACCESS FOR CONGRESSIONAL ELECTION OBSERVERS. ``(a) Finding of Constitutional Authority.--Congress finds that, regardless of legislative action, it has the authority to send congressional election observers to observe polling locations, any location where processing, scanning, tabulating, canvassing, recounting, auditing, or certifying voting results is occurring, or any other part of the process associated with elections for Federal office under the authorities granted under article 1, section 5, clause 1 and article 1, section 4, clause 1 of the Constitution of the United States. Procedures described herein do not establish any new authorities or procedures with respect to Congress' constitutional authority to observe congressional elections but are provided simply to permit a convenient statutory reference for existing congressional authority and activity. ``(b) Requiring States To Provide Access for Observers.-- ``(1) Requirement.--A State shall provide each individual who is acting as a designated congressional election observer for an election for Federal office with full access to clearly observe all elements of election administration procedures, including, but not limited to, access to any area in which a ballot is cast, processed, scanned, tabulated, canvassed, recounted, audited, or certified, including during pre- and post-election procedures. ``(2) Restrictions on activities of observers.--No designated congressional election observer may handle a ballot or election equipment (whether voting or nonvoting or whether [[Page 138 STAT. 1592]] tabulating or nontabulating), advocate for any position or candidate, take any action to reduce ballot secrecy or voter privacy, take any action to interfere with the ability of a voter to cast a ballot or an election administrator to carry the administrator's duties, or otherwise interfere with the election administration process. ``(3) Rule of construction.--Nothing in this section shall prohibit a designated congressional election observer from asking questions of an election administrator, election official, or election worker, or any other State or local official. ``(c) Conduct of Observers.-- ``(1) Removal.-- ``(A) Authorization removal by election official.-- If a State or local election official has a reasonable basis to believe that a designated congressional election observer has engaged in or imminently will engage in intimidation or deceptive practices prohibited by Federal law, or in the disruption of voting, processing, scanning, tabulating, canvassing, or recounting of ballots, or the certification of results, a State or local election official may remove that observer from the area involved. ``(B) <<NOTE: Deadline.>> Notice to committee.--If a designated congressional election observer is removed from an area under subparagraph (A), the election official shall, within 24 hours of the observer's removal-- ``(i) inform the chair and ranking minority member of the Committee on House Administration of the House of Representatives or the Committee on Rules and Administration of the Senate, as applicable; and ``(ii) provide written notice detailing the reason or reasons the designated congressional election observer was removed. ``(2) Rule of construction.--For purposes of this subsection, the mere presence of a designated congressional election observer during an observation of election administration procedures, without any additional indicia supporting a reasonable basis for removal, is not a sufficient reason for removal under paragraph (1)(A). ``(3) Right to replace observer.--If a designated congressional election observer is properly removed under paragraph (1)(A), the chair or ranking minority member of the Committee on House Administration of the House of Representatives or the Committee on Rules and Administration of the Senate, as appropriate, may send another designated congressional election observer as a replacement for the remaining duration of the observation of election administration procedures. ``(d) Designated Congressional Election Observer Described.--In this section, a `designated congressional election observer' is a House or Senate employee who is designated in writing by the chair or ranking minority member of the Committee on House Administration of the House of Representatives or the Committee on Rules and Administration of the Senate, or a successor committee, to gather information with respect to an election, including in the event that the election is contested in the House of Representatives or the Senate and for other purposes permitted by article 1, section 5, clause 1 and article 1, section 4, clause 1 of the Constitution of the United States. [[Page 138 STAT. 1593]] ``(e) State Defined.--In this section, the term `State' means each of the 50 States, the District of Columbia, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, the United States Virgin Islands, Guam, American Samoa, and the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands.''. (b) Conforming Amendment Relating to Enforcement.--Section 401 of such Act (52 U.S.C. 21111) is amended by striking ``and 303'' and inserting ``303, and 304''. (c) Clerical Amendment.--The table of contents of such Act is amended-- (1) by redesignating the items relating to sections 304 and 305 as relating to sections 305 and 306; and (2) by inserting after the item relating to section 303 the following: ``Sec. 304. Confirming access for congressional election observers.''. Approved October 4, 2024. findings.headline: H.R. 2189 qualified device classification and incorporated firearm-removal ground
findings.compact: Foushee opposed passage of the complete H.R. 2189 EH package; no preferred alternative is established. H.R. 2189 would exclude narrowly defined less-than-lethal devices from the federal firearm definition incorporated by a conviction-based immigration removal ground, while retaining its separate destructive-device route, as part of a broader classification and tax package.
detail: Foushee opposed passage of the complete H.R. 2189 EH package; no preferred alternative is established.

The complete H.R. 2189 EH adds a narrowly defined less-than-lethal projectile-device exception to the second sentence of 18 USC 921(a)(3), alongside its pre-existing antique-firearm exception, and adds paragraph (39). This is not solely a label for general criminal enforcement: existing INA 237(a)(2)(C) expressly incorporates FIREARM OR DESTRUCTIVE DEVICE as defined in 921(a), and existing 922(g)(5) regulates firearms/ammunition using illegal or unlawful presence or admission under a nonimmigrant visa. The candidate domain connection is those express definition/status links, not presumed immigration consequences from a crime. The firearm branch of the incorporated definition would acquire the new exception. The separate 921(a)(4) destructive-device definition is NOT amended by TitleI, and the INA ground separately includes destructive devices; a qualifying-device label therefore does not establish exemption from every branch or every other immigration ground. Existing 237(a)applies to an alien IN AND ADMITTED TO the United States, with removal upon the specified order, and 237(a)(2)(C)requires an after-admission CONVICTION under any law of the specified purchase/sale/exchange/use/ownership/possession/carrying or attempt/conspiracy conduct involving a qualifying weapon, part or accessory in violation of law. Arrest, allegation or a conduct admission alone is not this conviction predicate. No individual device classification, state-conviction comparison, adjudication, cancellation of an existing order or actual avoidance of removal is inferred. The new device must satisfy ALL printed criteria: not designed/intended to expel, nor readily convertible to accept/discharge, common handgun/rifle/shotgun ammunition or any other projectile above 500 feet/second; designed/intended use not likely to cause death or serious bodily injury; and unable to accept or be readily modified to accept a feeding device loaded through a pistol grip or commonly used in semiautomatic firearms. It is not every less-lethal weapon, every projectile device or a universal harmlessness finding. The AG must make a requested device determination within 90 days AFTER RECEIVING THE DEVICE; the deadline is not automatic approval or compulsory classification of every product. Existing 922(g)(5) and (y) status predicates, hunting/sport/license, foreign-official and friendly-government law-enforcement exceptions and qualified AG waiver remain baseline; not all noncitizens are prohibited. Existing ammunition is separately defined by 921(a)(17), so the proposal is not a blanket permission to possess otherwise regulated ammunition or ordinary firearms. It confers no nationality, visa, lawful presence, admission, work authorization or unrestricted weapons right. TitleII separately adds 4181 excise-tax exemptions for the defined devices, devices on the Secretary annual list meeting the criteria except the above 500 velocity criterion, and specified shells/cartridges with the printed design/use conditions; adds 90 day classification duties, annual lists/reports, and expands the distinct 5845(a)NFA definition exclusions to those device categories. The TAX listed-above 500 category is not inserted into TitleI 921(a)(39) and cannot be imported into the INA firearm-definition exception. Section 202 sales apply after enactment; qualifying requests in the first 180 days are treated as received at the close of that period for the 90 day rule. No special retroactive immigration/conviction rule is printed. Existing 4182 military, small-manufacturer and paid-NFA exemptions, existing 5845 antique/qualified collector-device exclusions, and enacted 119-21 section 70436 zero transfer/making-tax and 4182(a)conforming provisions are retained context, so this is not the first federal device exemption or tax relief and not a claim every affected product previously paid the same tax. These are distinct criminal, immigration-incorporation and tax objects. The exact whole-bill final-passage choice includes BOTH titles, not a separate vote on the removal ground, noncitizen possession or an individual device. One H.R. 2189 episode; the failed 1042 and adopted 1057 rules only established proposed/pending consideration and do not add independent policy findings. No actual sales, tax savings, public-safety effect or enactment is inferred.
The Clerk recorded the House result as 'Passed' on 2026-02-12. This does not establish enactment.
qualifications_on_both_levels: The domain link is the express INA firearm/destructive-device incorporation and retained alien-status firearm restrictions. No arrest-only removal predicate, universal noncitizen prohibition or actual removal result is established.

The new firearm exception requires all device design, conversion, velocity, intended-use and feeding-device conditions. The separate destructive-device route and other grounds remain; no individual conviction or device is adjudicated here.
The Secretary tax list can include otherwise qualifying above500feet/second devices. That tax category does not expand the TitleI federal-firearm exception incorporated by the INA ground.

This is the whole two-title classification/tax package. Existing exceptions, alien-status qualifications/waivers and prior119-21tax changes remain context; no component preference, automatic classification approval, retroactive relief or actual savings is inferred.

The complete H.R. 2189 EH adds a narrowly defined less-than-lethal projectile-device exception to the second sentence of 18 USC 921(a)(3), alongside its pre-existing antique-firearm exception, and adds paragraph (39). This is not solely a label for general criminal enforcement: existing INA 237(a)(2)(C) expressly incorporates FIREARM OR DESTRUCTIVE DEVICE as defined in 921(a), and existing 922(g)(5) regulates firearms/ammunition using illegal or unlawful presence or admission under a nonimmigrant visa. The candidate domain connection is those express definition/status links, not presumed immigration consequences from a crime. The firearm branch of the incorporated definition would acquire the new exception. The separate 921(a)(4) destructive-device definition is NOT amended by TitleI, and the INA ground separately includes destructive devices; a qualifying-device label therefore does not establish exemption from every branch or every other immigration ground. Existing 237(a)applies to an alien IN AND ADMITTED TO the United States, with removal upon the specified order, and 237(a)(2)(C)requires an after-admission CONVICTION under any law of the specified purchase/sale/exchange/use/ownership/possession/carrying or attempt/conspiracy conduct involving a qualifying weapon, part or accessory in violation of law. Arrest, allegation or a conduct admission alone is not this conviction predicate. No individual device classification, state-conviction comparison, adjudication, cancellation of an existing order or actual avoidance of removal is inferred. The new device must satisfy ALL printed criteria: not designed/intended to expel, nor readily convertible to accept/discharge, common handgun/rifle/shotgun ammunition or any other projectile above 500 feet/second; designed/intended use not likely to cause death or serious bodily injury; and unable to accept or be readily modified to accept a feeding device loaded through a pistol grip or commonly used in semiautomatic firearms. It is not every less-lethal weapon, every projectile device or a universal harmlessness finding. The AG must make a requested device determination within 90 days AFTER RECEIVING THE DEVICE; the deadline is not automatic approval or compulsory classification of every product. Existing 922(g)(5) and (y) status predicates, hunting/sport/license, foreign-official and friendly-government law-enforcement exceptions and qualified AG waiver remain baseline; not all noncitizens are prohibited. Existing ammunition is separately defined by 921(a)(17), so the proposal is not a blanket permission to possess otherwise regulated ammunition or ordinary firearms. It confers no nationality, visa, lawful presence, admission, work authorization or unrestricted weapons right. TitleII separately adds 4181 excise-tax exemptions for the defined devices, devices on the Secretary annual list meeting the criteria except the above 500 velocity criterion, and specified shells/cartridges with the printed design/use conditions; adds 90 day classification duties, annual lists/reports, and expands the distinct 5845(a)NFA definition exclusions to those device categories. The TAX listed-above 500 category is not inserted into TitleI 921(a)(39) and cannot be imported into the INA firearm-definition exception. Section 202 sales apply after enactment; qualifying requests in the first 180 days are treated as received at the close of that period for the 90 day rule. No special retroactive immigration/conviction rule is printed. Existing 4182 military, small-manufacturer and paid-NFA exemptions, existing 5845 antique/qualified collector-device exclusions, and enacted 119-21 section 70436 zero transfer/making-tax and 4182(a)conforming provisions are retained context, so this is not the first federal device exemption or tax relief and not a claim every affected product previously paid the same tax. These are distinct criminal, immigration-incorporation and tax objects. The exact whole-bill final-passage choice includes BOTH titles, not a separate vote on the removal ground, noncitizen possession or an individual device. One H.R. 2189 episode; the failed 1042 and adopted 1057 rules only established proposed/pending consideration and do not add independent policy findings. No actual sales, tax savings, public-safety effect or enactment is inferred.
The Clerk recorded the House result as 'Passed' on 2026-02-12. This does not establish enactment.
qualifications: The domain link is the express INA firearm/destructive-device incorporation and retained alien-status firearm restrictions. No arrest-only removal predicate, universal noncitizen prohibition or actual removal result is established.

The new firearm exception requires all device design, conversion, velocity, intended-use and feeding-device conditions. The separate destructive-device route and other grounds remain; no individual conviction or device is adjudicated here.
The Secretary tax list can include otherwise qualifying above500feet/second devices. That tax category does not expand the TitleI federal-firearm exception incorporated by the INA ground.

This is the whole two-title classification/tax package. Existing exceptions, alien-status qualifications/waivers and prior119-21tax changes remain context; no component preference, automatic classification approval, retroactive relief or actual savings is inferred.

R. 2189 _______________________________________________________________________ AN ACT To modernize Federal firearms laws to account for advancements in technology and less-than-lethal weapons, and for other purposes. Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the United States of America in Congress assembled, TITLE I--LAW-ENFORCEMENT INNOVATE TO DE-ESCALATE SECTION 101. SHORT TITLE. This title may be cited as the ``Law-Enforcement Innovate to De- Escalate Act''. SEC. 102. EXEMPTION OF CERTAIN LESS-THAN-LETHAL PROJECTILE DEVICES FROM RESTRICTIONS UNDER TITLE 18, UNITED STATES CODE. Section 921(a) of title 18, United States Code, is amended-- (1) in the second sentence of paragraph (3), by inserting ``or a less-than-lethal projectile device'' before the period; and (2) by adding at the end the following: ``(39)(A) The term `less-than-lethal projectile device' means a device that-- ``(i) is not designed or intended to expel and may not be readily converted to accept and discharge-- ``(I) ammunition commonly used in handguns, rifles, or shotguns; or ``(II) any other projectile at a velocity exceeding 500 feet per second; ``(ii) is designed and intended to be used in a manner that is not likely to cause death or serious bodily injury; and ``(iii) does not accept, and is not able to be readily modified to accept, an ammunition feeding device-- ``(I) loaded through the inside of a pistol grip; or ``(II) commonly used in semiautomatic firearms. ``(B) If a person requests that the Attorney General determine whether a device satisfies the definition of `less-than-lethal projectile device' under subparagraph (A), the Attorney General shall make the determination not later than 90 days after the date on which the Attorney General receives the device pursuant to the request.''. TITLE II--INNOVATE LESS LETHAL TO DE-ESCALATE TAX MODERNIZATION SEC. 201. SHORT TITLE. This title may be cited as the ``Innovate Less Lethal to De- Escalate Tax Modernization Act''. SEC. 202. EXEMPTION OF CERTAIN LESS-THAN-LETHAL PROJECTILE DEVICES FROM FIREARMS AND AMMUNITION TAX. (a) In General.--Section 4182 of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 is amended-- (1) by redesignating subsection (d) as subsection (e), and (2) by inserting after subsection (c) the following new subsection: ``(d) Less-than-Lethal Projectile Devices.-- ``(1) In general.--The tax imposed by section 4181 shall not apply to-- ``(A) any less-than-lethal projectile device, ``(B) any device contained on the most recent list made available by the Secretary under paragraph (4)(B), and ``(C) any shell or cartridge that meets the requirement of paragraph (2)(B) and is designed for use in a device referred to in subparagraph (A) or (B). ``(2) Less-than-lethal projectile device.--The term `less- than-lethal projectile device' means a device that-- ``(A) is not designed or intended to expel, and may not be readily converted to accept and discharge-- ``(i) ammunition commonly used in handguns, rifles, or shotguns, or ``(ii) any other projectile at a velocity exceeding 500 feet per second, ``(B) is designed and intended to be used in a manner that is not likely to cause death or serious bodily injury, and ``(C) does not accept, and is not able to be readily modified to accept, ammunition feeding devices-- ``(i) loaded through the inside of a pistol grip, or ``(ii) commonly used in semiautomatic firearms. ``(3) Request for classification.--Pursuant to a request made by the manufacturer, producer, or importer of a device for a determination as to whether such device satisfies the requirements under paragraph (2), the Secretary shall make such determination not later than 90 days after the date of receipt of such request. ``(4) Annual review of new and emerging technologies.-- ``(A) List of less-than-lethal projectile devices.--The Secretary shall make publicly available a list of devices that the Secretary has determined are described in paragraph (2) and shall update such list annually to take into account new devices. ``(B) List of non-lethal devices the projectiles of which exceed 500 feet per second.-- ``(i) In general.--The Secretary shall-- ``(I) make publicly available a list of devices that the Secretary has determined are not described in paragraph (2) but would be so described if such paragraph were applied without regard to subparagraph (A)(ii) thereof, and ``(II) update such list annually to take into account new devices. ``(ii) Report to congress.--The Secretary shall annually submit a written report to the Committee on Ways and Means of the House of Representatives and the Committee on Finance of the Senate regarding the annual list of devices described in clause (i), including a copy of such list, a description of the devices that were considered for inclusion on such list, and the reasons for including or excluding such devices from such list.''. (b) Effective Date.-- (1) In general.--Except as otherwise provided in this subsection, the amendments made by this section shall apply to articles sold by the manufacturer, producer, or importer after the date of the enactment of this Act. (2) Requests for determinations.--Section 4182(d)(3) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 (as added by this section) shall apply to requests received after the date of the enactment of this Act, except that any request under such section which is received during the 180-day period beginning on the date of the enactment of this Act shall be treated for purposes of such section as received as of the close of such period. SEC. 203. EXEMPTION OF CERTAIN LESS-THAN-LETHAL PROJECTILE DEVICES FROM NATIONAL FIREARMS ACT. Section 5845(a) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 is amended by striking ``an antique firearm or'' and inserting ``any antique firearm, any less-than-lethal projectile device (as defined in section 4182(d)(2)), any device referred to in section 4182(d)(1)(B), or''. findings.headline: H.R. 6472 territorial U.S.-national tuition protection
findings.compact: Foushee supported passage of the complete H.R. 6472 EH territorial-national tuition and fee protection proposal. H.R. 6472 would cap tuition and fees at resident rates for U.S. nationals residing in four named territories at qualifying public higher-education institutions.
detail: Foushee supported passage of the complete H.R. 6472 EH territorial-national tuition and fee protection proposal.

The complete H.R. 6472 EH proposal adds HEA section 135A. A PUBLIC institution of higher education RECEIVING ASSISTANCE under the HEA must not charge a covered individual tuition OR fees above the rate charged for residents of the State WHERE THE INSTITUTION IS LOCATED. Covered individuals must satisfy BOTH residence in Guam, the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, American Samoa or the U.S. Virgin Islands AND U.S. nationality as defined by INA 101(a)(22). That definition includes U.S. citizens and noncitizens owing permanent allegiance to the United States. Residence alone, lawful permanent residence alone or a visa alone does not establish the required nationality; this proposal does not confer nationality, citizenship, immigration status or naturalization. The four covered-residence jurisdictions are a specific list; Puerto Rico, the District of Columbia and the Freely Associated States are not added to that beneficiary-residence list. The HEA institution-location definition of State is broader: it includes the several States, Puerto Rico, DC, the four named territories and the Freely Associated States (Marshall Islands, Federated States of Micronesia and Palau). That institutional definition must not expand the covered-residence list or be collapsed to only the fifty States. Existing HEA section 101 contains the general institutional education, authorization, public/nonprofit and accreditation framework plus specified additional institutions; the proposal requires a PUBLIC institution and HEA assistance, not every private school or any business offering courses. It does not waive the retained educational-admission qualifications, require admission, provide free tuition, grant an individual federal aid award, or alter visa/admission/removal/work-authorization law. The new section 487(a)(30) requires institutional program participation agreements to comply with section 135A AS APPLICABLE. Existing 487(a) is an institutional initial-and-continuing program-eligibility agreement framework with its subpart-4 exception; this compliance clause is not a replacement of every individual aid-eligibility condition. Existing section 135 already protects resident tuition rates for qualified Federal-service members with the required domicile or permanent duty station, spouses and dependent children, including continued enrollment after duty relocation. Its service categories and effective enrollment dates are retained baseline protections, not proof that this is the first federal resident-rate protection and not deadlines imported into new section 135A. The exact EH prints no special implementation deadline, proof-document procedure or retroactive-refund rule for the new category. This is a whole-bill suspension-and-passage choice and a separate H.R. 6472 episode. No actual institutional compliance, savings, admission or individual nationality determination is established.
The Clerk recorded the House result as 'Passed' on 2026-03-04. This does not establish enactment.
qualifications_on_both_levels: The new coverage requires BOTH residence in one of four named territories AND U.S. nationality; U.S. nationals include citizens and certain noncitizens. Residence, LPR status or visa status alone is insufficient.

Only qualifying public institutions receiving HEA assistance are covered. Tuition AND fees are capped at the resident rate for the institution-location State; this does not provide free college, admission or an individual aid award.
The HEA State definition for institution location includes Puerto Rico, DC and the Freely Associated States. The beneficiary-residence list remains only Guam, NMI, American Samoa and USVI.

Existing Federal-service tuition protections and institutional/individual eligibility rules are retained context. No new nationality/status award, passport requirement, special deadline, retroactive refund or actual savings is inferred.

Its service categories and effective enrollment dates are retained baseline protections, not proof that this is the first federal resident-rate protection and not deadlines imported into new section 135A. The exact EH prints no special implementation deadline, proof-document procedure or retroactive-refund rule for the new category. This is a whole-bill suspension-and-passage choice and a separate H.R. 6472 episode. No actual institutional compliance, savings, admission or individual nationality determination is established.
The Clerk recorded the House result as 'Passed' on 2026-03-04. This does not establish enactment.
qualifications: The new coverage requires BOTH residence in one of four named territories AND U.S. nationality; U.S. nationals include citizens and certain noncitizens. Residence, LPR status or visa status alone is insufficient.

Only qualifying public institutions receiving HEA assistance are covered. Tuition AND fees are capped at the resident rate for the institution-location State; this does not provide free college, admission or an individual aid award.
The HEA State definition for institution location includes Puerto Rico, DC and the Freely Associated States. The beneficiary-residence list remains only Guam, NMI, American Samoa and USVI.

Existing Federal-service tuition protections and institutional/individual eligibility rules are retained context. No new nationality/status award, passport requirement, special deadline, retroactive refund or actual savings is inferred.

findings.headline: H.R. 7744 exact annual DHS funding and immigration conditions
findings.compact: Foushee opposed passage of the whole exact H.R. 7744 annual DHS funding proposal; no preferred funding or immigration alternative is established. H.R. 7744 would fund FY 2026 border, ICE and USCIS operations within the whole DHS package, retaining qualified sponsor, custody, contracting and oversight limits and adding surveillance, camera and budget-reporting provisions. It also carries qualified lapse-pay and obligation provisions.
detail: Foushee opposed passage of the whole exact H.R. 7744 annual DHS funding proposal; no preferred funding or immigration alternative is established.

The complete H.R. 7744 EH is the whole March 5 House annual DHS proposal with division A annual appropriations and division B lapse-pay/qualified obligation-ratification provisions. Its own sections 3-5 define thisAct references in division A as that DIVISION except where express, explicitly incorporate the January 22 H.R. 7147 explanatory statement for allocation/implementation, and appropriate FY 2026 sums.230(b) uses the corrected DHS-funds-in-this-or-prior-Act scope, not the earlier January as-voted any-other-Act wording. The complete body independently compared to 7147 EH retains the annual DHS package, makes technical 237 enumeration changes, and omits 554 Senate-datarepeal (already 119-75 H 105), rather than silently adding a new removal or sanctions policy. The parallel 7744/8029 bodies were independently compared: distinct exact bills/dates/short titles, with otherwise matching operative annual/lapse-pay bodies. Each remains its own bill episode; no cross-bill analytical relation or unique-concept-breadth claim is invented. DivisionB 1001 covers the lapse ON OR ABOUT February 13, 2026 (not the February 14 date in the March 27 CRreplacement);1002 directs available 119-37 A/newdivision A personnel pay/allowance/benefit payments under existing 31 US 1341(c);1003 ratifies essential-life/property/orderly-shutdown/otherwise-authorized obligations only IF OTHERWISE IN ACCORD with the referenced Acts. Existing 1341(c) already supplies qualified furloughed/excepted standard-pay/leave compensation after a covered lapse ends subject to ending appropriations; this is not first-ever backpay or actual payment, and division B does not substitute a new 106(3)CRouterdate. The annual DHS titles would fund existing border processing/security, immigration enforcement, custody and removal, citizenship-services processing and verification, and associated oversight for FY 2026 within a wider DHS package. CBP Operations and Support is $17.727974 billion, with $550 million available through September 30, 2027, mixed customs/trade/travel, UAC transport, air/marine and law-enforcement functions, Harbor Maintenance and user-fee components, and qualified informant, preclearance and Tribal-road uses. CBP procurement/construction is $222.886 million with distinct September 2028 asset and September 2030 construction availability. The final table allocates CBP Ops across Border Security $6.644912 billion, Trade/Travel $6.610801 billion, Integrated Operations $1.730551 billion and Mission Support $2.741710 billion; these are not four independently voted immigration policies or all-person-removal spending. The earlier $650 million CBP-to-FEMA shelter-transfer row has no new Final Bill amount. ICE Ops is $10.036362 billion, including $46.696 million through September 2027, no-year forced-labor funds, qualified HERO/IP-rights/informant/special-operations uses and up to $11.216 million for care, maintenance and repatriation of smuggled aliens UNLAWFULLY PRESENT. The final allocations are HSI $2.591251 billion, ERO $5.453706 billion, Mission Support $1.543711 billion and OPLA $447.694 million. ERO includes Custody $3.838340 billion, Fugitive $165.016 million, Criminal Alien Program $312.835 million, ATD $393.647 million and Transport/Removal $743.868 million. HSI includes many non-immigration investigations; detention and ATD are different uses. These table amounts do not themselves establish actual beds, removals or expenditure. ICE procurement is $5 million through September 2028. USCIS Ops is $122.941 million: $112.566 million Employment Status Verification and $10.375 million Application Processing/backlog reduction in the Final Bill table, not exclusively E-Verify. USCIS has no new Federal Assistance/Citizenship and Integration Grant amount in the final table; previously funded grants and termination-justification reporting are distinct. Existing adjudication-fee authority 1356(m)/(n) and the bill no-required-fee-reduction proviso remain; the separate fee-funded-program table is not an extra new discretionary appropriation. OSEM Ops $316.295 million includes $10 million CRCL, $5 million Citizenship/Immigration Services Ombudsman, no new Immigration Detention Ombudsman allocation, and no new $15 million ATD Case Management Grant allocation; the last two do not abolish their statutory offices or all ATD. OBIM receives $271 million and IDENT/HART procurement $25 million. OIG Ops $257.599 million includes $20 million additional detention inspections through September 2027 and $12.814 million reconciliation-fund oversight. Section 109 adds $20 million for body-worn cameras for agents/officers enforcing INA authorities plus a 30 day spending plan. FEMA includes $85.5 million Operation Stonegarden within $494 million State Homeland grants. The wider TSA, Coast Guard, Secret Service, disaster, cyber, training, research, Supreme Court-security and air-traffic provisions remain whole-package context; membership in DHS does not make all their spending Immigration evidence.

The statutory restrictions preserve their exact funding and trigger scopes. Section 207 bars a NEW defined land-border crossing fee and a related study, beginning enactment, for pedestrians/cyclists/private-vehicle drivers/passengers at northern/southern LPOEs; it does not abolish all existing immigration or inspection fees.208 requires a 90 day CBP procurement plan before this Act's funds are obligated;209 permits altering National Targeting Center operations but protects planned vetting at existing locations across specified current/prior/fee funds unless later statute authorizes a reduction.210 bars funds for Border Security Assets/Infrastructure in this or prior Acts from procuring/deploying NONAUTONOMOUS surveillance SYSTEMS, using 119-21 section 90004(c)'s definition; the older 90004(b) restriction separately concerns tested/accepted autonomous TOWERS using that section's funds.211 requires the November 30, 2021 CBP pregnant/postpartum/nursing/infant custody policy OR substantively similar standards developed with maternal/pediatric experts to be in effect and fully implemented. The original covered populations include pregnancy with medical concerns OR third trimester/active labor, nursing individuals, postpartum within six months or recent pregnancy loss, and infants under one year. Health interviews/assessment/referral retain resource/operational and offered-assessment/acceptance qualifications; documented fifteen-minute welfare checks, nutrition/breastfeeding/infant supplies, facility/operational qualifications and incident records remain; it is not first-ever care, an automatic 72 hour release rule, or identical unqualified entitlements for every person.212 prohibits using ICE Ops to CONTINUE 287(g) delegations when the DHS IG determines a MATERIAL agreement violation.213 prohibits continuing a detention-services contract if its TWO most recent OVERALL performance evaluations are BELOW adequate/equivalent median, with ICE OPR conducting the evaluations. Neither trigger is every complaint or one failed component score.214 permits necessary ICE Ops reprogramming/transfers for detention of aliens prioritized for removal without 503(d)'s time/condition limit; it is not an unrestricted waiver of every appropriation or statutory restriction.

215 continues semimonthly 2021 detention-data reporting, including the original 2020 operational/ATD/facility/detention/release/removal data and 2021 additions such as solitary-confinement use/duration and length-of-stay bins.216 reapplies complete 2020 sections 216/217: no covered detention/removal/referral/initiation-of-proceeding of a UAC sponsor, potential sponsor or household member BASED ON HHS-shared information, EXCEPT the specified background-check findings of an aggravated-felony/child-abuse/sexual-violence/child-porn felony conviction OR pending related FELONY charge, business association involving unrelated minors below legal wage or denied school, or prostitution participation/implementation. It is neither an absolute sponsor exemption nor an exception for every conviction or illegal-entry suspicion. The accompanying IG 287(g) report covers participation, training, criminality/nationality, removals, outreach and future plans.217 replaces the earlier 45 day current-Act plan with a 30 day Director briefing/written plan covering ALL available current/prior/carryover/fee funds, monthly PPA/pay/nonpay projections and unchanged initial comparison; monthly updates are due within 15 days after the following month begins. Conditional $100,000 Executive Leadership/Oversight amounts become available on the 16 th of each month, at most $700,000 for the fiscal year, subject to timely reporting beginning 30 days after enactment.218 requires a 90 day plan for 119-21 detention-facility funding, locations/beds/cost/transport/removal-flight/end-state capacity, with quarterly updates within 30 days; reporting projections are not observed immigration outcomes.219 protects ICE attaché/liaison presence at foreign embassies/consulates using this or other Act funds, except the joint DHS/State foreign-policy explanation or a host-country cessation request.238 reapplies the 2021 fencing restriction WITH RESPECT TO THIS ACT's funds in the same manner: Santa Ana, Bentsen-Rio Grande Valley State Park, La Lomita, National Butterfly Center, within OR EAST of Vista del Mar Ranch, and historic cemeteries. Do not infer an unrestricted prohibition on every separate reconciliation-fund use.

USCIS 401 permits only five replacement vehicles where GSA does not lease, with authorized home/work use;402 restricts A-76 competition for five named USCIS employee classes, including temporary/term staff;403 permits collection/use of biometrics at Application Support Centers overseen VIRTUALLY by USCIS personnel using appropriate technology. This repeats existing 2024 authority, rather than first authorizing biometrics, universal remote adjudication or unrestricted searches.512 continues the THIS ACT funding restriction on amending the INA 337 naturalization oath, preserving 1448's existing qualifying modified oaths and disability/qualifying-child waivers;517 uses 1324 a(h)(3)'s employment-at-the-particular-time definition, excluding LPRs and law-authorized workers from unauthorized alien, not all noncitizens.514 restricts this Act's funds for national-ID planning/testing/piloting/development, not every immigration identity document.527 continues the funding restriction on restraints for pregnant or post-delivery women in DHS custody/transport/outside treatment, with individualized unavoidable serious flight risk/immediate harm or therapeutic-medical exceptions for a pregnant woman, safest/least-restrictive provider-determined restraints, an ABSOLUTE active-labor/delivery ban, barred pregnant positions/belts and feasible left-side positioning.528 protects covered death/possible-sexual-assault/abuse records and allegations of abuse/crime/disruption BY detainees from destruction, with disclosure on an affected punished individual's request under applicable law/litigation rules. It is not unrestricted public access to all detainee or staff records.536 repeats a this/other-Act funding bar on transferring/releasing/assisting transfer to or within the United States/territories/possessions of the specified Guantanamo DOD-held-on-or-after-June 24, 2009 NONcitizen/NONmilitary detainees, not a general new INA inadmissibility ground for all people held elsewhere.547 bars THIS ACT DHS funds from blocking Members or designated House/Senate employees conducting oversight of DHS-operated/contracted ALIEN detention/housing facilities or restaging conditions: Members need no prior notice; staff may be required 24 hours. It is not an unrestricted public-visitor right or a blanket rule for all HHS facilities/funding sources.

General appropriation controls remain:501 current-fiscal-year obligation limit unless express longer/no-year availability;502 merges prior balances for the original purposes/availability;503 advance reprogramming notices and 5 percent transfers/no more than 10 percent augmentation, June 15 initial-notification limit with imminent-life/property exception, grant/new-unapproved-PPA restrictions and deobligated-balance procedures.503(f) permits UP TO $20 million transferred into the EXISTING Immigration Emergency Fund with five-day notice. The old 404 note separately authorizes a $35 million BALANCE and qualified immigration-emergency withdrawals needing Presidential determination/certification, plus capped State/local reimbursements under 404(b)(2) for which that emergency determination is not needed. A transfer here is not a new emergency declaration, unrestricted withdrawal or actual reimbursement.505 carries up to 50 percent unobligated FY 2026 Ops balances through September 2027 with the printed June 15, 2027 recording deadline and 503 notification.524's qualified report publication retains national-interest determination, security/proprietary exceptions and 45 day committee availability unless otherwise specified, now with 503 suspension for failure;525 permits minor Ops procurement/construction with unit caps $250,000 personal/$4 million real property.537/538 require monthly independently validated arrival and detention/removal estimates, demographic separation, common planning/budget assumptions and agency/committee sharing; failure suspends 503 authority.539 requires alternatives/cost-benefit analysis BEFORE requesting DoD border support and post-request/grant/quarterly reports.541 transfers AT LEAST $5 million to ICE Blue Campaign with pre-obligation notice.546 requires seven-day and quarterly 119-21 obligations/fee-retention/remittance/planned-use reports.551-553 rescind only identified UNOBLIGATED account balances, with the printed emergency-designation exception in 551 and defined 2024 carryover balances in 552; this is not cancellation of every outstanding obligation or all reconciliation funds.107's I&A covered-activity funding restriction incorporates 6303: specified charged/custodial unadjudicated criminal interviews need consent AFTER counsel consultation, targeting journalists in their functions is covered, and U. S.-person interviews require factual reasonable belief in significant foreign intelligence; the definition includes known LPRs and qualified associations/corporations, with foreign-controlled-corporation exception. Legal/privacy/civic oversight and specified lawful information sharing are expressly preserved. It is not a general no-intelligence rule or new immigration status ground.

The January 22 explanatory narrative and visually checked FINAL BILL tables govern the named allocations; earlier House Report 119-173 PROPOSAL amounts and numbered proposed riders are not substituted for this actual text. The narrative says House report LANGUAGE has equal weight unless noted or addressed to the contrary, and repetition does not negate it unless expressly provided. Its operative directions include 287(g) cost-benefit/training/agreement evaluations and reports; border/credible-fear/parole/UAC/parent/veteran/tribal/arrest/removal/wrongful-return data; warrants/probable-cause/flight-risk reports; HART/IDENT oversight and qualified child-separation notifications; medical/water/food/shelter/TEDS and continued migrant-care requirements; free confidential ICE counsel communication/document/VAV access and legal-orientation continuation TO THE MAXIMUM EXTENT POSSIBLE; qualified family-unity/separation, pregnant-custody redeterminations and sensitive-location directions; facilities/segregation/inspections/PREA oversight; ATD metrics/consequence reporting, monitoring-feasibility and procurement directions; and USCIS processing dashboards/backlogs, fees/waivers, asylum/refugee/EAD/SIJ/H-2 A/H-2 B/R-1 processing/abuse and policy-change reporting. The separately incorporated 118-85,116-458 and 118-553 directions are source-bound, retaining their population/exception/scheduling/privacy/feasibility wording and distinguishing requested reports, encouraged actions, directives and statutory rights. For example, the port-of-entry counsel paragraph requests a 90 day briefing on requirements for a meaningful one-hour consultation for U. S. nationals, LPRs returning from a temporary foreign visit, valid unexpired immigrant/nonimmigrant visa holders, refugees, returning asylees or approved parole applicants, with greatest-practicable in-person advocacy, not an unconditional new lawyer entitlement for every border entrant. The related ICE counsel direction concerns free confidential unmonitored 60 minute calls/video with 24 hour scheduling, document exchange/delivery and facility access, not government-paid representation. Continued family reunification is qualified by best interests/possibility; the pregnancy-custody direction preserves required-law/exceptional-circumstance grounds and monthly review. The House TPS-Venezuela direction calls for reconsideration/analysis and a 30 day briefing, while the Ukraine program language urges continuation; neither itself grants a named person TPS/parole or first changes individual eligibility. The final fee-waiver language supersedes the House cost-recovery restriction while mandatory statutory fees and their own waiver limits are not silently repealed. The Housereport 50,000-bed proposal, earlier PPA figures and former numbered proposed sanctuary/rhetoric riders are not treated as actual present statutory conditions merely because the report is referenced. Conflicting or uncertain application of retained report language versus the final allocation/statutory scope remains a candidate-review question, not an accepted adjudication.

Baseline: 119-4 incorporated FY 2024 DHS 118-47 division C with specified exceptions/anomalies, including ICE's $9.986542 billion FY 2025 Ops level;119-37 division A carried relevant FY 2025 rates/conditions with its own exceptions, and 119-75 division H changed the residualCR date to February 13. The annual proposal replaces the relevant continuation with full FY 2026 DHS appropriations; many sponsor/contract/287(g)/fencing/oath/employment/restraint/oversight/biometric controls already existed and are not first-ever rights or powers. The separate 119-21 reconciliation appropriations and fees are not all repealed/replaced by these annual totals. Whole passage includes enforcement funds, services, protective limits, oversight and other DHS/non-DHS provisions together. No component-only preference, motive, actual detention/deportation/care improvement, pay/spending, later enactment or individual legal outcome is inferred.
The Clerk recorded the House result as 'Passed' on 2026-03-05. This does not establish enactment.
qualifications_on_both_levels: This is the whole exact annual DHS package, mixing enforcement, processing, custody protections, oversight and other spending. No component-only preference or actual removal/bed/care/spending outcome is inferred.

The FINAL BILL allocation columns control: CBP/ICE contain non-immigration uses; USCIS includes verification AND application processing. Fee-funded figures and separate reconciliation appropriations are not added as new discretionary funding here.

Existing sponsor restrictions retain specified background exceptions;287(g) and detention-contract bars require material IG findings or two below-adequate overall OPR evaluations. They are not absolute sponsor immunity or a bar triggered by any complaint.

Pregnant/postpartum custody policy may be replaced by substantively similar expert-developed standards. Restraint exceptions, absolute labor/delivery protections and retained law/exceptional-circumstance custody boundaries are not flattened into universal release or no-restraint claims.

Counsel/family/medical/report directions retain population, timing, privacy, legal and feasibility qualifications. POE counsel assessment is distinct from ICE confidential-access directives and government-paid representation; proposed report riders/amounts do not silently become actual statute.

Congressional oversight access applies to named Members/designated staff at DHS alien facilities with the printed notice and funding scopes; record disclosure, fee, fence and intelligence limits retain their own exceptions and scopes.

Some controls are continued; others add reporting, camera, surveillance or budget conditions. No new general INA admission/removal power, wholesale fee abolition, every visa-program sunset extension or unqualified expenditure authority is established.

The exact legislative version and bill episode control. Later engrossment corrections, the March continuing-resolution replacement and parallel bills do not retrospectively change this member choice. Ambiguous report/incorporation application remains candidate review, with no acceptance or public authorization.
