claim_source_map.passage: United States Policy With Respect to Involuntary Return of Persons in Danger of Subjection to Torture Pub. L. 105–277, div. G, subdiv. B, title XXII, §2242, Oct. 21, 1998, 112 Stat. 2681–822, provided that: "(a) Policy .—It shall be the policy of the United States not to expel, extradite, or otherwise effect the involuntary return of any person to a country in which there are substantial grounds for believing the person would be in danger of being subjected to torture, regardless of whether the person is physically present in the United States. "(b) Regulations .—Not later than 120 days after the date of enactment of this Act [Oct. 21, 1998], the heads of the appropriate agencies shall prescribe regulations to implement the obligations of the United States under Article 3 of the United Nations Convention Against Torture and Other Forms of Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment, subject to any reservations, understandings, declarations, and provisos contained in the United States Senate resolution of ratification of the Convention. "(c) Exclusion of Certain Aliens .—To the maximum extent consistent with the obligations of the United States under the Convention, subject to any reservations, understandings, declarations, and provisos contained in the United States Senate resolution of ratification of the Convention, the regulations described in subsection (b) shall exclude from the protection of such regulations aliens described in section 241(b)(3)(B) of the Immigration and Nationality Act (8 U.S.C. 1231(b)(3)(B)). "(d) Review and Construction .—Notwithstanding any other provision of law, and except as provided in the regulations described in subsection (b), no court shall have jurisdiction to review the regulations adopted to implement this section, and nothing in this section shall be construed as providing any court jurisdiction to consider or review claims raised under the Convention or this section, or any other determination made with respect to the application of the policy set forth in subsection (a), except as part of the review of a final order of removal pursuant to section 242 of the Immigration and Nationality Act (8 U.S.C. 1252). "(e) Authority To Detain .—Nothing in this section shall be construed as limiting the authority of the Attorney General to detain any person under any provision of law, including, but not limited to, any provision of the Immigration and Nationality Act [8 U.S.C. 1101 et seq.]. "(f) Definitions.— "(1) Convention defined .—In this section, the term 'Convention' means the United Nations Convention Against Torture and Other Forms of Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment, done at New York on December 10, 1984. "(2) Same terms as in the convention .—Except as otherwise provided, the terms used in this section have the meanings given those terms in the Convention, subject to any reservations, understandings, declarations, and provisos contained in the United States Senate resolution of ratification of the Convention."

§1341. Frauds and swindles Whoever, having devised or intending to devise any scheme or artifice to defraud, or for obtaining money or property by means of false or fraudulent pretenses, representations, or promises, or to sell, dispose of, loan, exchange, alter, give away, distribute, supply, or furnish or procure for unlawful use any counterfeit or spurious coin, obligation, security, or other article, or anything represented to be or intimated or held out to be such counterfeit or spurious article, for the purpose of executing such scheme or artifice or attempting so to do, places in any post office or authorized depository for mail matter, any matter or thing whatever to be sent or delivered by the Postal Service, or deposits or causes to be deposited any matter or thing whatever to be sent or delivered by any private or commercial interstate carrier, or takes or receives therefrom, any such matter or thing, or knowingly causes to be delivered by mail or such carrier according to the direction thereon, or at the place at which it is directed to be delivered by the person to whom it is addressed, any such matter or thing, shall be fined under this title or imprisoned not more than 20 years, or both. If the violation occurs in relation to, or involving any benefit authorized, transported, transmitted, transferred, disbursed, or paid in connection with, a presidentially declared major disaster or emergency (as those terms are defined in section 102 of the Robert T. Stafford Disaster Relief and Emergency Assistance Act (42 U.S.C. 5122)), or affects a financial institution, such person shall be fined not more than $1,000,000 or imprisoned not more than 30 years, or both. 

§1342. Fictitious name or address Whoever, for the purpose of conducting, promoting, or carrying on by means of the Postal Service, any scheme or device mentioned in section 1341 of this title or any other unlawful business, uses or assumes, or requests to be addressed by, any fictitious, false, or assumed title, name, or address or name other than his own proper name, or takes or receives from any post office or authorized depository of mail matter, any letter, postal card, package, or other mail matter addressed to any such fictitious, false, or assumed title, name, or address, or name other than his own proper name, shall be fined under this title or imprisoned not more than five years, or both. 

§1343. Fraud by wire, radio, or television Whoever, having devised or intending to devise any scheme or artifice to defraud, or for obtaining money or property by means of false or fraudulent pretenses, representations, or promises, transmits or causes to be transmitted by means of wire, radio, or television communication in interstate or foreign commerce, any writings, signs, signals, pictures, or sounds for the purpose of executing such scheme or artifice, shall be fined under this title or imprisoned not more than 20 years, or both. If the violation occurs in relation to, or involving any benefit authorized, transported, transmitted, transferred, disbursed, or paid in connection with, a presidentially declared major disaster or emergency (as those terms are defined in section 102 of the Robert T. Stafford Disaster Relief and Emergency Assistance Act (42 U.S.C. 5122)), or affects a financial institution, such person shall be fined not more than $1,000,000 or imprisoned not more than 30 years, or both. 

§1344. Bank fraud Whoever knowingly executes, or attempts to execute, a scheme or artifice— (1) to defraud a financial institution; or (2) to obtain any of the moneys, funds, credits, assets, securities, or other property owned by, or under the custody or control of, a financial institution, by means of false or fraudulent pretenses, representations, or promises; shall be fined not more than $1,000,000 or imprisoned not more than 30 years, or both. 

§1345. Injunctions against fraud (a)(1) If a person is— (A) violating or about to violate this chapter or section 287, 371 (insofar as such violation involves a conspiracy to defraud the United States or any agency thereof), or 1001 of this title; (B) committing or about to commit a banking law violation (as defined in section 3322(d) of this title); or (C) committing or about to commit a Federal health care offense; the Attorney General may commence a civil action in any Federal court to enjoin such violation. (2) If a person is alienating or disposing of property, or intends to alienate or dispose of property, obtained as a result of a banking law violation (as defined in section 3322(d) of this title) or a Federal health care offense or property which is traceable to such violation, the Attorney General may commence a civil action in any Federal court— (A) to enjoin such alienation or disposition of property; or (B) for a restraining order to— (i) prohibit any person from withdrawing, transferring, removing, dissipating, or disposing of any such property or property of equivalent value; and (ii) appoint a temporary receiver to administer such restraining order. (3) A permanent or temporary injunction or restraining order shall be granted without bond. (b) The court shall proceed as soon as practicable to the hearing and determination of such an action, and may, at any time before final determination, enter such a restraining order or prohibition, or take such other action, as is warranted to prevent a continuing and substantial injury to the United States or to any person or class of persons for whose protection the action is brought. A proceeding under this section is governed by the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, except that, if an indictment has been returned against the respondent, discovery is governed by the Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure. 

§1346. Definition of "scheme or artifice to defraud" For the purposes of this chapter, the term "scheme or artifice to defraud" includes a scheme or artifice to deprive another of the intangible right of honest services. 

§1347. Health care fraud (a) Whoever knowingly and willfully executes, or attempts to execute, a scheme or artifice— (1) to defraud any health care benefit program; or (2) to obtain, by means of false or fraudulent pretenses, representations, or promises, any of the money or property owned by, or under the custody or control of, any health care benefit program, in connection with the delivery of or payment for health care benefits, items, or services, shall be fined under this title or imprisoned not more than 10 years, or both. If the violation results in serious bodily injury (as defined in section 1365 of this title), such person shall be fined under this title or imprisoned not more than 20 years, or both; and if the violation results in death, such person shall be fined under this title, or imprisoned for any term of years or for life, or both. (b) With respect to violations of this section, a person need not have actual knowledge of this section or specific intent to commit a violation of this section. 

§1348. Securities and commodities fraud Whoever knowingly executes, or attempts to execute, a scheme or artifice— (1) to defraud any person in connection with any commodity for future delivery, or any option on a commodity for future delivery, or any security of an issuer with a class of securities registered under section 12 of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (15 U.S.C. 78l) or that is required to file reports under section 15(d) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (15 U.S.C. 78o(d)); or (2) to obtain, by means of false or fraudulent pretenses, representations, or promises, any money or property in connection with the purchase or sale of any commodity for future delivery, or any option on a commodity for future delivery, or any security of an issuer with a class of securities registered under section 12 of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (15 U.S.C. 78l) or that is required to file reports under section 15(d) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (15 U.S.C. 78o(d)); shall be fined under this title, or imprisoned not more than 25 years, or both. 

§1349. Attempt and conspiracy Any person who attempts or conspires to commit any offense under this chapter shall be subject to the same penalties as those prescribed for the offense, the commission of which was the object of the attempt or conspiracy. 

§1350. Failure of corporate officers to certify financial reports (a) Certification of Periodic Financial Reports .—Each periodic report containing financial statements filed by an issuer with the Securities Exchange Commission pursuant to section 13(a) or 15(d) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (15 U.S.C. 78m(a) or 78o(d)) shall be accompanied by a written statement by the chief executive officer and chief financial officer (or equivalent thereof) of the issuer. (b) Content .—The statement required under subsection (a) shall certify that the periodic report containing the financial statements fully complies with the requirements of section 13(a) or 15(d) of the Securities Exchange Act pf 1 1934 (15 U.S.C. 78m or 78o(d)) and that information contained in the periodic report fairly presents, in all material respects, the financial condition and results of operations of the issuer. (c) Criminal Penalties .—Whoever— (1) certifies any statement as set forth in subsections (a) and (b) of this section knowing that the periodic report accompanying the statement does not comport with all the requirements set forth in this section shall be fined not more than $1,000,000 or imprisoned not more than 10 years, or both; or (2) willfully certifies any statement as set forth in subsections (a) and (b) of this section knowing that the periodic report accompanying the statement does not comport with all the requirements set forth in this section shall be fined not more than $5,000,000, or imprisoned not more than 20 years, or both. 

§1351. Fraud in foreign labor contracting (a) Work Inside the United States .—Whoever knowingly and with intent to defraud recruits, solicits, or hires a person outside the United States or causes another person to recruit, solicit, or hire a person outside the United States, or attempts to do so, for purposes of employment in the United States by means of materially false or fraudulent pretenses, representations or promises regarding that employment shall be fined under this title or imprisoned for not more than 5 years, or both. (b) Work Outside the United States .—Whoever knowingly and with intent to defraud recruits, solicits, or hires a person outside the United States or causes another person to recruit, solicit, or hire a person outside the United States, or attempts to do so, for purposes of employment performed on a United States Government contract performed outside the United States, or on a United States military installation or mission outside the United States or other property or premises outside the United States owned or controlled by the United States Government, by means of materially false or fraudulent pretenses, representations, or promises regarding that employment, shall be fined under this title or imprisoned for not more than 5 years, or both. 

§1352. Demands by foreign officials for bribes (a) Definitions .—In this section: (1) Foreign official .—The term "foreign official" means— (A)(i) any official or employee of a foreign government or any department, agency, or instrumentality thereof; or (ii) any senior foreign political figure, as defined in section 1010.605 of title 31, Code of Federal Regulations, or any successor regulation; (B) any official or employee of a public international organization; (C) any person acting in an official capacity for or on behalf of— (i) a government, department, agency, or instrumentality described in subparagraph (A)(i); or (ii) a public international organization. (2) Public international organization .—The term "public international organization" means— (A) an organization that is designated by Executive order pursuant to section 1 of the International Organizations Immunities Act (22 U.S.C. 288); or (B) any other international organization that is designated by the President by Executive order for the purposes of this section, effective as of the date of publication of the order in the Federal Register. (b) Prohibition of Demand for a Bribe.— (1) Offense .—It shall be unlawful for any foreign official or person selected to be a foreign official to corruptly demand, seek, receive, accept, or agree to receive or accept, directly or indirectly, anything of value personally or for any other person or nongovernmental entity, by making use of the mails or any means or instrumentality of interstate commerce— (A) from— (i) any person (as defined in section 104A of the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act of 1977 (15 U.S.C. 78dd–3), except that that definition shall be applied without regard to whether the person is an offender) while the foreign official or person selected to be a foreign official, or a person acting on behalf of the foreign official or person selected to be a foreign official, is in the territory of the United States; (ii) an issuer (as defined in section 3(a) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (15 U.S.C. 78c(a))), or any officer, director, employee, or agent of an issuer or any stockholder thereof acting on behalf of the issuer; or (iii) a domestic concern (as defined in section 104 of the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act of 1977 (15 U.S.C. 78dd–2)), or any officer, director, employee, or agent of a domestic concern or any stockholder thereof acting on behalf of the domestic concern; and (B) in return for— (i) being influenced in the performance of any act or decision of the foreign official or person selected to be a foreign official in the official capacity of the foreign official or person selected to be a foreign official; (ii) being induced to do or omit to do any act in violation of the lawful duty of the foreign official or person selected to be a foreign official; (iii) conferring any improper advantage; or (iv) using the influence of the foreign official or person selected to be a foreign official with a foreign government or instrumentality thereof to affect or influence any act or decision of that government or instrumentality, in connection with obtaining or retaining business for or with, or directing business to, any person. (2) Penalties .—Any person who violates paragraph (1) shall be fined not more than $250,000 or 3 times the monetary equivalent of the thing of value, imprisoned for not more than 15 years, or both. (3) Jurisdiction .—An offense under paragraph (1) shall be subject to extraterritorial Federal jurisdiction. (4) Report .—Not later than 1 year after the date of enactment of this section, and annually thereafter, the Attorney General, in consultation with the Secretary of State as relevant, shall submit to the Committee on the Judiciary and the Committee on Foreign Relations of the Senate and the Committee on the Judiciary and the Committee on Foreign Affairs of the House of Representatives, and post on the publicly available website of the Department of Justice, a report— (A) focusing, in part, on demands by foreign officials for bribes from entities domiciled or incorporated in the United States, and the efforts of foreign governments to prosecute such cases; (B) addressing United States diplomatic efforts to protect entities domiciled or incorporated in the United States from foreign bribery, and the effectiveness of those efforts in protecting such entities; (C) summarizing major actions taken under this section in the previous year, including enforcement actions taken and penalties imposed; (D) evaluating the effectiveness of the Department of Justice in enforcing this section; and (E) detailing what resources or legislative action the Department of Justice needs to ensure adequate enforcement of this section. (5) Rule of construction .—This subsection shall not be construed as encompassing conduct that would violate section 30A of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (15 U.S.C. 78dd–1) or section 104 or 104A of the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act of 1977 (15 U.S.C. 78dd–2; 15 U.S.C. 78dd–3) whether pursuant to a theory of direct liability, conspiracy, complicity, or otherwise.

findings.headline: H.R.4638 federal police-animal immigration grounds
findings.compact: Foushee opposed passage of H.R.4638 with those grounds; no preferred alternative is established. H.R.4638 would add an inadmissibility ground for the specified federal police-animal offense and a matching deportability ground within the admitted-person framework; both permit conviction or specified admissions of conduct.
detail: Foushee opposed passage of H.R.4638 with those grounds; no preferred alternative is established.

The exact H.R.4638 EH proposal adds INA 212(a)(2)(J) inadmissibility and 237(a)(2)(G) deportability for an alien convicted of, admitting commission of, or admitting acts constituting the essential elements of an offense under 18 USC 1368. Both new clauses allow those specified admissions, despite the conviction-only phrasing in the bill title. Arrest alone is not the printed predicate. The incorporated 1368 offense already criminalizes willfully and maliciously harming a police animal, including attempts and conspiracies. Police animal means a dog or horse employed by a Federal agency in any branch primarily to aid criminal detection, law enforcement or apprehension. It is not every working animal or every State/local police animal, and the bill is not limited to CBP animals. The existing offense carries fine and up-to 1year imprisonment, with up-to 10 years for permanent disability/disfigurement, serious bodily injury or death; the immigration clauses do not add an injury/penalty-length threshold. The bill adds INA consequences to that existing crime, not a new animal-harm offense or a claim that all covered conduct previously had no immigration consequences. Existing INA conviction rules/other criminal grounds remain. Their enumerated petty-offense,212(h) and pardon exceptions are not written as exceptions to newJ/G; discretionary temporary-admission/T/U waiver authorities remain within their own scope. No blanket relief or automatic deportation is inferred. The new 237(a)(2) deportability ground sits within the existing 237(a) framework for an alien (including a crewman) in and admitted to the United States, with removal upon the specified government order. It is not a universal new deportability ground for every unadmitted alien. INA 101 distinguishes immigration admission (lawful entry after inspection/authorization) from admitting criminal conduct; parole alone is not admission. This governing status scope is separate from any offense's after-admission timing element. No individual admission status or actual removal order is inferred.
The Clerk recorded the House result as 'Passed' on 2026-03-19. This does not establish enactment.
qualifications_on_both_levels: INA 237(a) deportability concerns an alien in and admitted to the United States, subject to the governing order framework. Immigration admission and admissions of criminal conduct are different conditions; parole alone is not immigration admission. The new numbered ground does not discard this governing chapeau or necessarily add an after-admission-crime timing element.

Both new INA grounds allow conviction or specified admissions; neither requires conviction exclusively or follows from arrest alone. The incorporated offense requires willful and malicious harm, attempt or conspiracy.

The animal is a federally employed dog or horse with the specified principal criminal/law-enforcement purpose, regardless of Federal branch. All animals, all State/local police animals and only-CBP animals are unsupported expansions/narrowings.

18 USC 1368 is pre-existing. Its aggravated-harm prison ceiling is not an eligibility threshold in these new INA clauses; existing INA exceptions/waivers keep their own scope rather than universally attaching to newJ/G.
This complete bill passage choice establishes no component preference, animal injury, guilt, visa/admission denial, removal or enactment.

H.R.4638 would add an inadmissibility ground for the specified federal police-animal offense and a matching deportability ground within the admitted-person framework; both permit conviction or specified admissions of conduct.
detail: Foushee opposed passage of H.R.4638 with those grounds; no preferred alternative is established.

The exact H.R.4638 EH proposal adds INA 212(a)(2)(J) inadmissibility and 237(a)(2)(G) deportability for an alien convicted of, admitting commission of, or admitting acts constituting the essential elements of an offense under 18 USC 1368. Both new clauses allow those specified admissions, despite the conviction-only phrasing in the bill title. Arrest alone is not the printed predicate. The incorporated 1368 offense already criminalizes willfully and maliciously harming a police animal, including attempts and conspiracies. Police animal means a dog or horse employed by a Federal agency in any branch primarily to aid criminal detection, law enforcement or apprehension. It is not every working animal or every State/local police animal, and the bill is not limited to CBP animals. The existing offense carries fine and up-to 1year imprisonment, with up-to 10 years for permanent disability/disfigurement, serious bodily injury or death; the immigration clauses do not add an injury/penalty-length threshold. The bill adds INA consequences to that existing crime, not a new animal-harm offense or a claim that all covered conduct previously had no immigration consequences. Existing INA conviction rules/other criminal grounds remain. Their enumerated petty-offense,212(h) and pardon exceptions are not written as exceptions to newJ/G; discretionary temporary-admission/T/U waiver authorities remain within their own scope. No blanket relief or automatic deportation is inferred. The new 237(a)(2) deportability ground sits within the existing 237(a) framework for an alien (including a crewman) in and admitted to the United States, with removal upon the specified government order. It is not a universal new deportability ground for every unadmitted alien. INA 101 distinguishes immigration admission (lawful entry after inspection/authorization) from admitting criminal conduct; parole alone is not admission. This governing status scope is separate from any offense's after-admission timing element. No individual admission status or actual removal order is inferred.
The Clerk recorded the House result as 'Passed' on 2026-03-19. This does not establish enactment.
qualifications: INA 237(a) deportability concerns an alien in and admitted to the United States, subject to the governing order framework. Immigration admission and admissions of criminal conduct are different conditions; parole alone is not immigration admission. The new numbered ground does not discard this governing chapeau or necessarily add an after-admission-crime timing element.

Both new INA grounds allow conviction or specified admissions; neither requires conviction exclusively or follows from arrest alone. The incorporated offense requires willful and malicious harm, attempt or conspiracy.

The animal is a federally employed dog or horse with the specified principal criminal/law-enforcement purpose, regardless of Federal branch. All animals, all State/local police animals and only-CBP animals are unsupported expansions/narrowings.

18 USC 1368 is pre-existing. Its aggravated-harm prison ceiling is not an eligibility threshold in these new INA clauses; existing INA exceptions/waivers keep their own scope rather than universally attaching to newJ/G.
This complete bill passage choice establishes no component preference, animal injury, guilt, visa/admission denial, removal or enactment.

R. 4638 _______________________________________________________________________ AN ACT To amend the Immigration and Nationality Act to provide that an alien who has been convicted of harming animals used in law enforcement is inadmissible and deportable, and for other purposes. Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the United States of America in Congress assembled, SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE. This Act may be cited as the ``Federal Working Animal Protection Act''. SEC. 2. INADMISSIBILITY AND DEPORTABILITY RELATED TO HARMING ANIMALS USED IN LAW ENFORCEMENT. (a) Inadmissibility.--Section 212(a)(2) of the Immigration and Nationality Act (8 U.S.C. 1182(a)(2)) is amended by adding at the end the following: ``(J) Harming animals used in law enforcement.--Any alien who has been convicted of, who admits having committed, or who admits committing acts which constitute the essential elements of an offense under section 1368 of title 18, United States Code (relating to harming animals used in law enforcement), is inadmissible.''. (b) Deportability.--Section 237(a)(2) of the Immigration and Nationality Act (8 U.S.C. 1227(a)(2)) is amended by adding at the end the following: ``(G) Harming animals used in law enforcement.--Any alien who has been convicted of, who admits having committed, or who admits committing acts which constitute the essential elements of an offense under section 1368 of title 18, United States Code (relating to harming animals used in law enforcement), is deportable.''. Passed the House of Representatives March 19, 2026. Attest: Clerk. 119th CONGRESS 2d Session H. This is a whole-package passage choice, with qualifications. Massie opposed concurrence in that complete Senate replacement; no preferred alternative or separate component position is established. This May22 House passage is the whole H.R.1 reconciliation package, not a separate immigration-only vote. The controlling House choice uses H.Res.436: Rules Committee Print119-3 modified by the amendment printed in H.Rept.119-113 was considered adopted. The retained Immigration clauses are reconstructed against that chain and the contemporaneous as-amended floor Record. The currently served EH incorporates later corrections and renumbering and is a comparison witness for these unchanged selected clauses, not the controlling entire vote-time text. Later engrossment corrections and the July Senate replacement are not silently substituted for this choice. The description selects border infrastructure, detention, State reimbursement and asylum-fee mechanisms; it does not inventory every immigration-related tax, benefit, employment-authorization, child-sponsor or removal provision in this multi-domain package. Section60001 would make additional fiscal2025 CBP appropriations available until September30,2029: $46.5billion for primary/waterborne/secondary barriers, access roads and associated detection attributes; a separate $50million for specified invasive plants impeding RioGrande border operations; and $5billion for CBP facilities/checkpoints near the southwest, northern and maritime borders. These are different purposes, not one immigration-enforcement account or actual expenditures. The adopted manager amendment adds section60004: $12billion in additional fiscal2025 DHS funds, available until September30,2029, for grants reimbursing States for costs of actions on or after January21,2021 assisting federal border/immigration enforcement, including detention/removal and combating unlawful entry of persons/contraband. Applications need satisfactory cost evidence, and DHS cannot reimburse a State already reimbursed under another DHS grant program. This is funding subject to a process and conditions, not proof of State awards or a newly conferred State removal power. Section70101 would appropriate an additional $45billion for fiscal2025 to ICE, available until September30,2029, solely for single-adult alien detention and family residential-center capacity. DHS MAY detain family units pending a removal decision and, if ordered removed, until removal. Its family-center definition includes accompanied alien children, excludes unaccompanied alien children, and expressly applies regardless of State/local facility licensing. Its single-adult detention standards clause says they shall be set in the Secretary's SOLE discretion. Preserve that printed language without importing the Senate's express consistent-with-applicable-law qualification or deciding its interaction with judicial/other legal constraints. The existing unaccompanied-child definition in6USC279(g)(2) requires no lawful immigration status, age under18, and no US parent/legal guardian or none available for care/physical custody; childhood alone does not establish that category. Capacity funding and permission are not a universal detention mandate, removal order or actual detention outcome. Section70002 would require an additional fee at the time an alien files an asylum application: the fiscal2025 amount may be set by rule but cannot be less than $1,000. It cannot be waived/reduced. From fiscal2026 its amount increases using the prior fiscal-year fee and the printed July-to-July CPI-U increase, with the increment rounded down to a multiple of $10. Half of the Attorney-General-filed receipts go to EOIR; half of DHS-filed receipts go to USCIS's existing Immigration Examinations Fee Account; those credited amounts may be retained/spent without further appropriation, and the remainder goes to Treasury. Section70010 separately requires a fee for EACH CALENDAR YEAR an application remains pending, initially at least $100 for fiscal2025, with later CPI-U adjustment, Treasury disposition and no waiver/reduction. Its printed adjustment has no express rounding term; the filing-fee rounding rule is not copied into it. These are separate filing and pending-application charges, not fixed lifetime amounts or a claim that every asylum applicant actually paid. Section70023 changes existing INA208(d)(3)/8USC1158(d)(3) from MAY impose fees to SHALL, strikes the following cost-cap/installment/nonmandatory-fee language and preserves authority to set additional adjudication/naturalization fees under286(m). The existing paragraph already allowed fees for asylum consideration, employment authorization and asylum-based adjustment and capped them at adjudication costs; the bill does not create first-ever fee authority or establish a new substantive asylum eligibility test through that edit. Existing1356(m)/(n) supply the account/cost-recovery context. Employment-authorization provisions are separate from asylum filing and annual pending-application fees. House70003 would charge an additional fee on initial employment-authorization applications for asylum applicants underINA208(d)(2), paroled aliens and applicants underTPS244(a)(1)(B). Each initial fee has a fiscal2025 floor of$550, may be higher by DHS rule, cannot be waived/reduced and has the printed fiscal2026-onward July-to-July CPI-U increment rounded down to$10. All three initial authorizations would last no more than six months. In70003(a)(4), the House allocation sentence says25percent of fees received UNDER THIS SECTION goes to USCIS's existing fee account to retain/spend without further appropriation, with50percent of that credited amount for benefit-fraud detection/prevention; uncredited amounts go to Treasury. The separately printed parole/TPS subsections direct their fees to Treasury. Preserve those exact scope words rather than silently deciding their interaction. House70012 and70014 separately impose additional parole/TPS employment-authorization renewal or extension fees with fiscal2025$550floors, possible higher rule amounts, subsequent CPI increments rounded down to$10, Treasury disposition and no waiver/reduction. Both initial and renewed/extended authorizations in those sections last no more than six months. House70013 imposes at least$550 for each asylum-based renewal/extension, Treasury disposition and no waiver/reduction; that section prints no annual inflation formula. DHS MAY provide asylum-applicant employment authorization for at most six months, and each renewal/extension also has that limit. Authorization terminates immediately after an asylum-officer denial unless referred to an immigration judge;30days after an immigration-judge denial unless timely appealed to BIA; or immediately after BIA denies an appeal of asylum denial. After such termination DHS cannot grant, renew or extend it unless a FederalCourtOfAppeals remands to BIA. This restriction concerns employment authorization, not an automatic asylum denial, immediate removal or a bar on all judicial review. The pre-vote1158(d)(2) already says asylum applicants are not entitled to employment authorization but it may be provided by regulation; applicants not otherwise eligible cannot receive it before180days after asylum filing. Existing1254a(a)(1)(B)/(a)(2) authorizes employment and makes work authorization effective throughout TPS. Fee/document-validity provisions do not themselves end TPS, create first work authority or establish everyone's eligibility. Both deem the remittance a financing transaction for the specified multiple-party anti-conduit authority; existing 7701(l) permits appropriate regulation/recharacterization, not an automatic finding of evasion or wrongdoing. Transfer amendments apply to TRANSFERS MADE AFTER DECEMBER 31, 2025, not the vote date or a substituted later enacted date. The bound remittance definitions concern an ELECTRONIC, PROVIDER-INITIATED funds transfer requested by a CONSUMER/NATURAL-PERSON SENDER LOCATED IN A DEFINED STATE to an AUTHORIZED DESIGNATED RECIPIENT LOCATED IN A FOREIGN COUNTRY. Consumer/State, electronic and normal-course provider definitions are independently bound, with account-independence and the statutory SMALL-VALUE EXCLUSION retained. This is not every domestic payment, every cross-border business transaction, every family expense or a recipient-citizenship test. Electronic transfer technology and the Senate physical FUNDING instrument are different predicates. No specific transaction, person, provider, regulatory threshold or actual tax outcome is classified. The Senate tax applies ONLY where the sender provides CASH, MONEY ORDER, CASHIER'S CHECK OR ANOTHER SIMILAR PHYSICAL INSTRUMENT AS THE SECRETARY DETERMINES to the provider, and remains subject to its SEPARATE NONAPPLICATION provisions. Nonapplication covers funds WITHDRAWN FROM AN ACCOUNT held in/by an institution BOTH DESCRIBED IN 31 USC 5312(a)(2)(A)-(H) AND SUBJECT TO SUBCHAPTER II OF CHAPTER 53 requirements, OR funds PROVIDED WITH A DEBIT OR CREDIT CARD ISSUED IN THE US. The listed-institution AND regulatory-subjection conditions are conjunctive; not every institution or any card regardless of issuance suffices. Cash-only language is not used to erase a separately applicable nonapplication or classify intermediate withdrawals/funding paths. Complete debit/card definitions retain network/asset-account and no-paper-check scope; the bill says WITHOUT REGARD TO debit-definition (B), rather than an automatic exclusion of every possible prepaid card. The inherited credit-device definition is separately bound, with the US-issuance condition additional. The Senate prints EFTA 919(g) for remittance and 920(c)(2)/(3) for card definitions, matching the bound source-credit crosswalk; it has no counterpart to the selected House verified citizen/national-provider exception, new 36C credit or 6050BB reporting scheme. Those missing counterparts do not establish a citizenship-based Senate tax exemption or a person's final cost. All own funding/exclusion and statutory-definition predicates must be retained; no universal 1% charge on all remittances or outcome for a particular immigrant is inferred. The selected Senate ACA comparison remains its own 71301/71302/71303 eligible-alien, income-floor and verification mechanisms described above, with their respective tax/plan-year dates. Their complete operative sections do not contain the House 44201(i) named-June-2012-DACA amendments. No House title-wide, cost-sharing-section or preceding-Federal-payment-sentence exclusion is imported into those Senate clauses, and their own eligible-alien restrictions remain. This selected-section comparison does not claim Senate eligibility for every DACA recipient or whole-package absence of every possible DACA effect; the original memo is not a current ACA eligibility decision. The selected description does not resolve legal challenges or every other package mechanism. Support/opposition applies to this complete Senate replacement. Its relationship to the earlier House choice is one underlying legislative episode; chronology alone does not establish comparability, a change of belief or a trajectory.

Medicare section 1899C requires ONE own listed category: US citizen OR US national; lawful permanent residence; version-specific category(3); OR lawful US residence under a referenced COFA. The new list has NO NEW COMMON RESIDENCE modifier across all alternatives. Separate existing entitlement/enrollment predicates remain; the existing five-year LPR residence rule retains its own enrollment path, not every citizen or insured-benefit path. Listed status alone is not sufficient. Senate category(3) retains HAS BEEN GRANTED defined Cuban/Haitian entrant status, with each definition modifier in its own category/alternative; no House petition/program substitution or nationality-only grant. For those entitled/enrolled AS OF ENACTMENT, the restriction begins EIGHTEEN MONTHS AFTER ENACTMENT, with review completed within ONE YEAR of enactment. EACH person identified as outside ALL four categories receives notice as soon as practicable AFTER IDENTIFICATION, designed for comprehension and naming the enactment-relative termination date. Review, notice and termination are distinct; the grace is not from notice, a guaranteed minimum notice period, every later applicant or perpetual grandfathering. No vote-date/later-law calendar substitution, actual review/termination, individual award or whole-package closure follows.

ACA status treatment concerns a LAWFULLY PRESENT ALIEN who IS AND IS REASONABLY EXPECTED FOR THE ENTIRE CREDIT-ENROLLMENT PERIOD to hold an own listed LPR, version-specific Cuban-related or COFA status; these conditions are common to each alternative. Citizens/US nationals retain the separate existing condition. Status alone does not satisfy all credit/program requirements. Senate prints IF and requires HAS BEEN GRANTED defined entrant status, with own definition branches and the whole-period expectation; no House conjunction or IF AND ONLY IF repair. Its selected attestation/payment extension concerns credits; it has no direct House counterpart for 1402(e)/1331 status amendments. No continuing award or resolved residual program effect is inferred. Both credit restrictions retain the named section 151 tax-family condition (including taxpayer/spouse), INDIVIDUAL premium attribution and family-size/household-income calculations, not automatic whole-household loss or an insurance-enrollment ban. Both delete the special rule requiring ALL income NOT GREATER THAN 100 percent, lawful presence and Medicaid ineligibility BY REASON OF ALIEN STATUS. This does not alone prove credit loss at EXACTLY 100 percent, where the ordinary floor begins. The repeal starts taxable years after December 31, 2025; the status changes use taxable years after December 31, 2026 versus conforming PLAN YEARS on/after January 1, 2027. Senate lacks those direct conforming deletions/renumbering; application of the retained reference to deleted 36B(c)(1)(B) remains RESERVED. The 5000A(d)(3) reference change does not amend the existing zero monetary penalty components. No actual award, revived penalty, whole-package closure or component preference follows.

Exchange verification concerns INDIVIDUAL CREDIT COVERAGE MONTHS, not an enrollment ban: failure of this paragraph ALONE does NOT make an individual ineligible to enroll. Applicant PROVIDED OR VERIFIED information applies TO THE EXTENT RELEVANT. Senate requires enrollment AND advance-credit verification, with NO House cost-sharing third prong, HOUSEHOLD INCOME AND FAMILY SIZE and WHETHER AN ELIGIBLE ALIEN. Past-month verification prints IF. Secretary MAY waive ONLY (A) for one or more tax-year months enrolled during an SEP BASED ON CHANGE IN OWN FAMILY SIZE. ANY available data AND RELIABLE third-party sources remain FOR VERIFICATION BY THE APPLICANT. Exact June 25, 2025 final-rule(iii), printed 2026 ONLY, is expressly applied as though to ALL PLAN YEARS AFTER 2025; no substitution of its separate two-year introductory baseline or House March proposal. Both filing-compliance references retain HHS notification, advances for filer OR married spouse, the relevant tax-data year and failure to file/reconcile, with direct filer failure notice OR protected indirect risk/education notice; not a test imposed without those predicates or guaranteed notice-to-loss interval. ANY APPLICANT MAY use an Exchange-provided process BEGINNING NOT LATER THAN AUGUST 1 for the SUBSEQUENT PLAN YEAR; not a universal applicant deadline. Senate process covers HOUSEHOLD INCOME AND ENROLLMENT. Sections 112201/71303 apply to TAXABLE YEARS BEGINNING AFTER DECEMBER 31, 2027, distinct from the House discrepancy PLAN YEARS ON/AFTER JANUARY 1, 2026 and the Senate incorporated-rule duration. No automatic credit/coverage outcome, whole-package closure or component preference is inferred.

Senate cost-sharing dependency is now source-complete for this bounded question; no House annual filing/extension amendment or notice-version substitution is imported. NO reduction for ANY MONTH UNLESS a COVERAGE MONTH FOR WHICH 36B CREDIT IS ALLOWED TO THE INSURED OR AN APPLICABLE TAXPAYER ON THE INSURED'S BEHALF: necessary, not sufficient, and not every insured personally filing. Definitions share 36B terms; data use ADVANCE-DETERMINATION TAX YEAR, not credit-allowed tax year. The undeleted cost-sharing sentence/basic-health branch alone does not establish continuing benefits. Question 34 remains RESERVED, without actual credit/reduction/basic-health award or loss, legal repair, full-package closure or acceptance.

Senate tax is 1 PERCENT and ONLY named physical funding, subject to SEPARATE nonapplication: institution described (A)-(H) AND subject to BSA chapter 53/subchapter II, OR US-ISSUED debit/credit funding. No any-bank/card exception or universal cash charge. WITHOUT REGARD TO debit (B) is not automatic exclusion of every prepaid card. No House citizen-verification/36C/6050BB mechanism is imported or a citizenship-based Senate exemption inferred. Both retain consumer/NATURAL-PERSON sender in a DEFINED STATE, provider-initiated ELECTRONIC transfer to FOREIGN designated recipient, account-independence, normal-course provider and SMALL-VALUE exclusion. Physical funding is distinct from electronic transfer technology. SENDER pays; provider COLLECTS FROM SENDER AND REMITS QUARTERLY; secondary liability ONLY unpaid-at-transfer AND uncollected extent. Transfers apply AFTER DECEMBER 31, 2025. Anti-conduit deeming/regulatory discretion is not observed avoidance, wrongdoing or an individual tax finding. No specific person, provider, transaction path, credit/refund or actual net-cost outcome is determined.

Selected Senate 71301/71302/71303 retain own eligible-alien/income/verification predicates and effective dates; these sections do not contain House named-memo amendments. No House title-wide/CSR-section/Federal-payment-sentence exclusion is imported, and no automatic DACA eligibility or whole-package absence of DACA effects is inferred. Original memo is historical context, not a current ACA eligibility decision.

action_observations.compact: Massie opposed passage of that complete House proposal; no preferred alternative or separate component position is established. Selected House H.R. 1 provisions would fund border infrastructure and detention, set fiscal 2025 asylum filing/pending fee floors of $1,000/$100 and specified asylum/parole/TPS employment-authorization initial/renewal fee floors of $550, and limit those documents to at most six months. This is a whole-package passage choice, with qualifications.
detail: Massie opposed passage of that complete House proposal; no preferred alternative or separate component position is established.

This May22 House passage is the whole H.R.1 reconciliation package, not a separate immigration-only vote. The controlling House choice uses H.Res.436: Rules Committee Print119-3 modified by the amendment printed in H.Rept.119-113 was considered adopted. The retained Immigration clauses are reconstructed against that chain and the contemporaneous as-amended floor Record. The currently served EH incorporates later corrections and renumbering and is a comparison witness for these unchanged selected clauses, not the controlling entire vote-time text. Later engrossment corrections and the July Senate replacement are not silently substituted for this choice. The description selects border infrastructure, detention, State reimbursement and asylum-fee mechanisms; it does not inventory every immigration-related tax, benefit, employment-authorization, child-sponsor or removal provision in this multi-domain package. Section60001 would make additional fiscal2025 CBP appropriations available until September30,2029: $46.5billion for primary/waterborne/secondary barriers, access roads and associated detection attributes; a separate $50million for specified invasive plants impeding RioGrande border operations; and $5billion for CBP facilities/checkpoints near the southwest, northern and maritime borders. These are different purposes, not one immigration-enforcement account or actual expenditures. The adopted manager amendment adds section60004: $12billion in additional fiscal2025 DHS funds, available until September30,2029, for grants reimbursing States for costs of actions on or after January21,2021 assisting federal border/immigration enforcement, including detention/removal and combating unlawful entry of persons/contraband. Applications need satisfactory cost evidence, and DHS cannot reimburse a State already reimbursed under another DHS grant program. This is funding subject to a process and conditions, not proof of State awards or a newly conferred State removal power. Section70101 would appropriate an additional $45billion for fiscal2025 to ICE, available until September30,2029, solely for single-adult alien detention and family residential-center capacity. DHS MAY detain family units pending a removal decision and, if ordered removed, until removal. Its family-center definition includes accompanied alien children, excludes unaccompanied alien children, and expressly applies regardless of State/local facility licensing. Its single-adult detention standards clause says they shall be set in the Secretary's SOLE discretion. Preserve that printed language without importing the Senate's express consistent-with-applicable-law qualification or deciding its interaction with judicial/other legal constraints. The existing unaccompanied-child definition in6USC279(g)(2) requires no lawful immigration status, age under18, and no US parent/legal guardian or none available for care/physical custody; childhood alone does not establish that category. Capacity funding and permission are not a universal detention mandate, removal order or actual detention outcome. Section70002 would require an additional fee at the time an alien files an asylum application: the fiscal2025 amount may be set by rule but cannot be less than $1,000. It cannot be waived/reduced. From fiscal2026 its amount increases using the prior fiscal-year fee and the printed July-to-July CPI-U increase, with the increment rounded down to a multiple of $10. Half of the Attorney-General-filed receipts go to EOIR; half of DHS-filed receipts go to USCIS's existing Immigration Examinations Fee Account; those credited amounts may be retained/spent without further appropriation, and the remainder goes to Treasury. Section70010 separately requires a fee for EACH CALENDAR YEAR an application remains pending, initially at least $100 for fiscal2025, with later CPI-U adjustment, Treasury disposition and no waiver/reduction. Its printed adjustment has no express rounding term; the filing-fee rounding rule is not copied into it. These are separate filing and pending-application charges, not fixed lifetime amounts or a claim that every asylum applicant actually paid. Section70023 changes existing INA208(d)(3)/8USC1158(d)(3) from MAY impose fees to SHALL, strikes the following cost-cap/installment/nonmandatory-fee language and preserves authority to set additional adjudication/naturalization fees under286(m). The existing paragraph already allowed fees for asylum consideration, employment authorization and asylum-based adjustment and capped them at adjudication costs; the bill does not create first-ever fee authority or establish a new substantive asylum eligibility test through that edit. Existing1356(m)/(n) supply the account/cost-recovery context. Employment-authorization provisions are separate from asylum filing and annual pending-application fees. House70003 would charge an additional fee on initial employment-authorization applications for asylum applicants underINA208(d)(2), paroled aliens and applicants underTPS244(a)(1)(B). Each initial fee has a fiscal2025 floor of$550, may be higher by DHS rule, cannot be waived/reduced and has the printed fiscal2026-onward July-to-July CPI-U increment rounded down to$10. All three initial authorizations would last no more than six months. In70003(a)(4), the House allocation sentence says25percent of fees received UNDER THIS SECTION goes to USCIS's existing fee account to retain/spend without further appropriation, with50percent of that credited amount for benefit-fraud detection/prevention; uncredited amounts go to Treasury. The separately printed parole/TPS subsections direct their fees to Treasury. Preserve those exact scope words rather than silently deciding their interaction. House70012 and70014 separately impose additional parole/TPS employment-authorization renewal or extension fees with fiscal2025$550floors, possible higher rule amounts, subsequent CPI increments rounded down to$10, Treasury disposition and no waiver/reduction. Both initial and renewed/extended authorizations in those sections last no more than six months. House70013 imposes at least$550 for each asylum-based renewal/extension, Treasury disposition and no waiver/reduction; that section prints no annual inflation formula. DHS MAY provide asylum-applicant employment authorization for at most six months, and each renewal/extension also has that limit. Authorization terminates immediately after an asylum-officer denial unless referred to an immigration judge;30days after an immigration-judge denial unless timely appealed to BIA; or immediately after BIA denies an appeal of asylum denial. After such termination DHS cannot grant, renew or extend it unless a FederalCourtOfAppeals remands to BIA. This restriction concerns employment authorization, not an automatic asylum denial, immediate removal or a bar on all judicial review. The pre-vote1158(d)(2) already says asylum applicants are not entitled to employment authorization but it may be provided by regulation; applicants not otherwise eligible cannot receive it before180days after asylum filing. Existing1254a(a)(1)(B)/(a)(2) authorizes employment and makes work authorization effective throughout TPS. Fee/document-validity provisions do not themselves end TPS, create first work authority or establish everyone's eligibility. The existing parole paragraph1182(d)(5)(A)/(B) is case-by-case urgent-humanitarian/significant-public-benefit authority subject to the printed statutory exceptions, including the refugee qualification and does not constitute admission. These fees do not supply a grant of parole or automatic employment permission. House70007 imposes a separate additional sponsor-placement fee, collected by HHS from the individual BEFORE placing an unaccompanied alien child underTVPRA235(c). Its fiscal2025 floor is$3,500 or a higher rule amount, with fiscal2026-onward July-to-July CPI-U increments rounded down to$10 and no waiver/reduction. The stated purpose is partial reimbursement for the child's prior federal-custody processing, housing, food, education, transport and other care.25percent goes to HHS to retain/spend without further appropriation for sponsor/adult-household background checks; the remainder goes to Treasury. The specified checks include names, SSNs, dates of birth, validated residence, immigration status and contact information for the sponsor and all adult household residents, and records checks including sex-offender registry, public-records background and fingerprint-based national criminal history. Existing1232(c) already requires protective/suitability assessments, identity/relationship verification, independent risk findings and home studies in specified cases. This is not first-ever sponsor vetting or a new assertion that any sponsor has criminal activity. House70020 imposes ANOTHER additional sponsor fee BEFORE the unaccompanied child's release to the sponsor. Its fiscal2025 floor is$5,000 or a higher rule amount with later CPI increments rounded down to$10, Treasury disposition and no waiver/reduction. Despite its failure-to-appear title, collection is not conditioned on a child already missing court or having an in-absentia order. At the end of the child's immigration proceedings as an unaccompanied child OR at the end of that sponsorship, HHS MAY reimburse if the sponsor demonstrates the child was not ordered removed in absentia. If such an order was rescinded underINA240(b)(5)(C), the sponsor MAY SEEK reimbursement. Neither reimbursement pathway is an automatic refund. The two sponsor fees remain distinct additional charges; there is no claim that every applicant actually paid them or that payment establishes suitability. Existing1232(c) placement protections and279(g)(2) UAC definition remain material context; their interaction with fee collection is not a finding of actual placement, detention or legal enforceability. House70021 requires a separate fiscal2025 fee of at least$5,000, possibly higher by rule, on an alien BOTH ordered removed in absentia under1229a(b)(5) AND subsequently arrested by ICE. It has later CPI increments rounded down to$10, Treasury disposition and no waiver/reduction, and does not apply if the underlying order was rescinded under1229a(b)(5)(C). House70022 separately charges any INADMISSIBLE alien at the time CBP apprehends the person BETWEEN PORTS OF ENTRY; its fiscal2025 floor is$5,000 or higher by rule, later CPI increments rounded down to$10, Treasury disposition and no waiver/reduction. Do not treat every arrest, port-of-entry encounter, unadmitted person or failure to attend court as satisfying these exact fee predicates. The complete pre-vote1229a(b)(5) and(e) retain the written-notice rule and failure-to-provide-address exception, clear/unequivocal/convincing evidence of notice and removability, and separate rescission routes: a motion within180days showing exceptional circumstances beyond the alien's control, or at any time for missing statutory notice or no-fault failure while in federal/state custody. Filing those motions stays removal pending the immigration judge's disposition. Exceptional circumstances include the specified battery/extreme cruelty or serious illness/death examples, excluding less compelling circumstances; removability distinguishes inadmissibility for an unadmitted alien from deportability for an admitted alien.1229(a) preserves notice/address/change-of-hearing context. The fee provisions do not themselves create an in-absentia order, repeal rescission, establish a new removal ground or prove an individual enforcement outcome. House70004 adds a parole-entry fee with fiscal2025floor$1,000 or a higher DHS rule amount, fiscal2026-onward July-to-July CPI-U increments rounded down to$10, Treasury disposition and no waiver/reduction for an applicable fee. It applies to each alien paroled into the US EXCEPT where the alien establishes one of the printed parole-reason exceptions; fee exceptions are not erased by the separate waiver bar. The fee exceptions retain their actual predicates: a medical emergency with necessary treatment unavailable in the foreign state where the alien resides OR a life-threatening emergency with insufficient normal-visa time; the parent/legal guardian of such a medical-emergency MINOR; the alien needed in the US to donate an organ or tissue for transplant, with insufficient normal-visa time; a close family member in the United States whose death is imminent, when normal visa processing would prevent arriving while that person is alive; or seeking to attend a close family member's funeral, when normal visa processing would prevent arriving in the United States in time for it; an adopted child's urgent treatment needed before expected final adoption-related visa issuance while in the petitioner's legal custody; a LAWFUL INA245 adjustment applicant returning after temporary travel abroad; and a person returned to a contiguous country under235(b)(2)(C) paroled to attend the person's immigration hearing. The law-enforcement significant-public-benefit exception requires a DHS determination that significant public benefit has resulted or will result from the parole, BOTH assistance to the USGovernment AND presence required in that matter, PLUS at least one of inadmissibility, failure to meet nonimmigrant-admission eligibility, or insufficient normal-visa time; it is not every asserted public benefit. House exception9 separately requires a Cuban national LIVING IN CUBA, an approvedINA203(a) petition, no immediately available immigrant visa, all immigrant-visa eligibility requirements, no other inadmissibility AND a parole grant furthering the printed US minimum-annual-legal-migration commitment under the1994/1995Cuba-USagreements. Existing1153(a) identifies family-preference visa classes; that eligibility context does not prove approval, visa availability or an actual grant. This is not an exemption for every Cuban national, every parolee or the differently printed Senate Cuban/Haitianentrant category. Existing1182(d)(5) parole authority remains subject to its printed humanitarian/public-benefit/case-by-case/statutory-exception terms and non-admission distinction; a fee or exception does not confer parole, adjustment, admission or hearing outcome. House70005 adds a separate SIJ application fee with fiscal2025floor$500 or a higher rule amount, later CPI increments rounded down to$10, Treasury disposition and no waiver/reduction. The fee predicate requires that reunification with ONEparent or legal guardian is viable despite abuse/neglect/abandonment or a similar State-law basis making reunification with the OTHERparent/legalguardian not viable. It is not stated as a fee on every SIJ applicant or an amendment creating SIJ status. Complete1101(a)(27)(J) already requires the specified USjuvenile-court dependency/custody determination and nonviable reunification with1ORboth parents on the listed State-law bases, a best-interest finding against return to the identified former country, and DHSconsent; HHS-specific custody-jurisdiction consent and no derived rights by virtue of parentage remain. Do not substitute nonimmigrantJexchange-visitor provisions, infer a UAC-under18 rule, grant status from a fee, or assume that paying changes parental rights. House70006 adds a separate TPS-consideration fee with fiscal2025floor$500 or a higher rule amount, later CPI increments rounded down to$10, Treasury disposition and no waiver/reduction. Its status predicate is an alien NOTADMITTED to the US OR an admitted NONIMMIGRANT who at TPSapplication time failed to maintain/extend the applicable nonimmigrant status (including authorized-stay compliance) OR comply with its conditions. It is not an undifferentiated fee on every TPSapplicant, an EADfee, or proof of inadmissibility/criminal conduct. The pre-vote1254a(c)(1)(B) already permits a reasonable registration fee capped$50 and a separate additional work-document fee for post-July17,1991designations, with appropriation-credit language. This House fee is ADDITIONAL to other authorized fees; the separately stated registration cap is not described as a newly created TPS application right or the House newfee's ceiling. Other TPSeligibility/work-authorization protections remain; fee liability does not establish status eligibility or an actual collection. House 70008 adds a visa-integrity fee on each alien issued a nonimmigrant visa, collected upon issuance in addition to other authorized fees. The fiscal 2025 minimum is $250 or a higher DHS rule amount; fiscal 2026 onward adds the July-to-July CPI-U increment rounded down to the next lowest multiple of $1. Unreimbursed fees go to Treasury; the applicable fee cannot be waived or reduced. DHS MAY reimburse after the visa period of validity expires if the alien demonstrates ONE of three printed alternatives: did not seek admission during that validity period; OR after admission complied with ALL visa conditions, including no unauthorized employment, AND departed no later than five days after the date authorized to remain in the US; OR FILED to extend, change or adjust status within the visa validity period. Filing is the printed third alternative, not a required grant; nonuse is its own first alternative. Reimbursement is discretionary and qualified, not an automatic refund or a new permission to stay or work. Visa validity and authorized stay are not interchangeable, and the reimbursement departure condition is not described as a general grace period. The pre-vote 1101(a)(26) definition identifies a visa properly issued to an eligible nonimmigrant by a competent officer; issuance does not itself prove admission, compliance or reimbursement. House 70009 separately adds a fee on ANY alien applying for Form I-94, with fiscal 2025 minimum $24 or a higher DHS rule amount, later July-to-July CPI-U increments, no expressly printed increment-rounding rule, and no waiver/reduction. Twenty percent of each collected application fee is deposited pursuant to existing 1356(q)(2) and available to CBP to retain and spend without further appropriation for Form I-94 processing; the remainder goes to Treasury. The existing Land Border Inspection Fee Account was already established, including I-94/I-94W/I-68 and similar land-port receipts. The new section says any alien applying for the form; the account name does not narrow that application predicate to land ports. Existing subsection (q)(3) refunds appropriations for inspection expenses, not the applicant, and is not described as a personal fee-refund entitlement. No fee amount proves an actual application, collection, admission or immigration-status outcome. House 70017 amends the existing ESTA fee, rather than creating the travel-authorization System or treating it as admission. Pre-vote 1187(h)(3) already specifies an initial fee comprising $17 per travel authorization plus an amount at least sufficient to recover full System provision/administration costs. The proposal adds a $10 MINIMUM to that cost-recovery component while retaining the full-cost condition, and adds another component of at least $13. These are components of the existing sum, not an undifferentiated $10 or $13 total fee. It limits annual deposits from the existing $17 component into the Travel Promotion Fund to not more than $20 million, sending that component's remainder to Treasury; it expressly sends the new $13 component to Treasury. The existing administration-cost component remains transferred to Treasury and available for administering the System. The sunset edit extends only the existing clause(i)(I) Travel Promotion Fund fee restriction from fiscal years beginning after October31,2028 to those beginning after October31,2034. Fiscal2026-onward CPI-U adjustment expressly names clause(i)(II), but its prior-year base literally says the amount imposed UNDER THIS SUBSECTION. The full-cost component/subsection-base relationship is preserved for application review, not silently rewritten as a CPI adjustment of an isolated $10 amount or the whole total; no increment-rounding rule is printed here. The complete pre-vote System/validity limits distinguish eligible travel from admissibility and distinguish denial of ESTA travel eligibility from denial of visa eligibility. The selected ESTA amendment prints no new express fee-waiver prohibition; none is imported from EVUS, and waiver availability is not inferred. House 70018 separately edits the existing immigration inspection/preinspection user fee in 1356(d). Its collection event remains inspection of each passenger arriving at a US port, or preinspection outside the US before arrival, aboard a COMMERCIAL aircraft or vessel. The existing $7 becomes a fiscal2025 MINIMUM of $10, with later July-to-July CPI-U increments rounded down to the next lowest $0.25 and a no-waiver/reduction clause. It expressly makes (d) subject to the retained (e) exceptions. The old non-aircraft geographical-origin exemption for Canada/Mexico/the US/adjacent islands is removed; the separate $3 commercial-vessel-origin charge is replaced with an exemption from (d) for IMMIGRATION INSPECTION AT DESIGNATED PORTS OF ENTRY of passengers arriving either by the separately defined ferry or by the specified Great Lakes vessels. A passenger in transit to an outside-US destination AND receiving no immigration inspection remains exempt. The printed ferry definition remains: a vessel outside ocean/coastwise service, providing only deck-passenger and/or vehicle capacity, a short frequent run along the most direct water route, and a public bridge/tunnel-type service. The Great Lakes branch retains its Great Lakes/connecting-waterway and regular-schedule conditions. These own predicates are not transferred between exception branches, and the fee is not described as applying to every border crossing or every inadmissible person. The new clause directs $1 per inspected/preinspected individual to Treasury; unstruck 1356(h)(1)(A) separately says ALL (d) receipts enter the Immigration User Fee Account notwithstanding other provisions. Both printed provisions and the account's appropriations-refund framework remain visible for application review, without inventing a resolved residual distribution or personal refund right. House 70019 adds an EVUS fee at enrollment for an alien SUBJECT to that System, in addition to other authorized fees. Fiscal2025 minimum is $30 or a higher DHS rule amount; later CPI-U increments round down to $0.25 and the fee cannot be waived or reduced. It establishes a separate CBP EVUS Account; fees enter that account LESS $5 PER ENROLLMENT directed to Treasury. Account deposits are appropriated without further appropriation and available until expended for CBP costs administering EVUS. The collection event, quarter-dollar increment and fixed Treasury deduction are distinct from ESTA or the commercial-passenger inspection fee; no new System eligibility, admission, visa grant, compliance determination or actual collection follows from the fee. House 70011 adds a fee for EACH continuance that an alien BOTH REQUESTS and IS GRANTED by an immigration judge. The fiscal2025 minimum is $100 or a higher AttorneyGeneral rule amount, with fiscal2026-onward July-to-July CPI-U increments and no expressly printed increment-rounding rule. Fees go to Treasury. The no-waiver/reduction clause preserves a separate NO-FEE exception when the requested continuance is granted BASED ON the defined exceptional circumstances. Complete pre-vote1229a(e)(1), the section240 definition, requires circumstances BEYOND THE ALIEN'S CONTROL and excludes less compelling circumstances. Its examples are illustrative, not an exclusive list: battery/extreme cruelty to the alien or the alien's child/parent; serious illness of the alien; or serious illness/death of the alien's spouse/child/parent. Those own person/event predicates are not collapsed into any family illness/death, and ordinary good cause or a continuance request alone is not described as satisfying the statutory fee exception. The proposal does not charge a denied request merely because it was filed, turn the exception into a fee waiver, or establish an actual grant or exceptional-circumstances finding. House 70015 separately adds fees for two different diversity-visa events: filing a diversity immigrant-visa application ($400 fiscal2025 minimum or higher DHS rule amount, collected at filing) and registering for that program ($250 minimum or higher rule amount, collected at registration). Both have fiscal2026-onward July-to-July CPI-U increments; ONLY the application increment expressly rounds down to$10, while the registration formula prints no rounding rule. Both applicable fees cannot be waived or reduced. Across fees received under this SECTION, 10percent is directed to detecting/preventing program fraud and offsetting program costs, and a separate10percent is credited to ICE to retain/spend without further appropriation for detention, immigration enforcement and removal operations; amounts not used or credited go to Treasury. These are not percentages of only one fee or assumed actual expenditure. Complete pre-vote1153(c) already establishes diversity visa allocation, including its five-year admission/geographic formulas, high-admission-state exclusion, regional redistribution and seven-percent state limit, and the education OR qualified-work-experience requirement. The proposal adds fees to the identified program rather than creating it, changing those allocation/eligibility rules by payment, guaranteeing selection or issuing a visa. Registration, application, selection and actual grant remain distinct; no separate component preference follows from either member's whole-package vote. House 70016 adds ten EOIR court/application/appeal/motion fee provisions. In(a)-(c), an alien's court filing OR court adjudication of the identified adjustment, inadmissibility-waiver orTPS application triggers payment at filing OR, as applicable, before court adjudication; two automatic charges for the same application are not asserted. The(d)/(e) alien appeals, (f) practitioner appeal and(g) alien motion collect at filing. The(h)-(j) provisions collect when an alien files the identified suspension, permanent-resident cancellation or nonpermanent-resident cancellation/adjustment application WITH AN IMMIGRATION COURT. House(j) identifies the application for certain nonpermanent residents without copying Senate's distinct non-LPR-payer wording. The ten listed fiscal2025 floors are separate fee events, additional to other authorized fees, with a higher AttorneyGeneral rule amount permitted: adjustment to lawful permanent residence $1,500; waiver of grounds of inadmissibility $1,050; TPS $500; appeal from an immigration-judge decision $900; appeal from a DHS-officer decision $900; practitioner disciplinary appeal $1,325; motion to reopen or reconsider an immigration-judge or Board of Immigration Appeals decision $900; suspension of deportation application $600; cancellation of removal for the specified permanent-resident category $600; and cancellation/adjustment for the specified nonpermanent-resident category $1,500. Each subsection has fiscal2026-onward July-to-July CPI-U adjustment of its own prior-year fee, with the INCREMENT rounded down to $10, not an automatically exact future price or a sum charged to every alien. The disciplinary appeal payer is a PRACTITIONER filing an appeal of an adjudicating official's decision in a practitioner disciplinary case, not every alien or every attorney. The immigration-judge appeal provision separately excludes appeals of BOND decisions. The motion-fee exception identifies only motions to REOPEN an IN-ABSENTIA removal order under240(b)(5)(C)(ii) or an in-absentia deportation order under legacy242B(c)(3)(B), with the version's own printed temporal wording retained below. Complete pre-vote1229a(b)(5)(C)(ii) allows the identified motion at any time upon demonstrating either lack of notice in accordance with1229(a)(1) OR(a)(2), OR Federal/State custody AND nonappearance through no fault of the alien. Complete historical1252b(c)(3)(B) likewise allows the identified motion at any time upon demonstrating lack of notice in accordance with its(a)(2), OR Federal/State custody AND nonappearance through no fault of the alien. The surrounding notice/address requirements remain; these are not exemptions for every missed hearing, any custody, all reopening/reconsideration motions, or the separate180-day exceptional-circumstances grounds in240(b)(5)(C)(i)/242B(c)(3)(A). Visa-integrity reimbursement is discretionary and available only after the visa period of validity expires. House requires demonstration of one of three alternatives: no admission sought during that validity period; or compliance with all visa conditions after admission, including no unauthorized employment, together with departure no later than five days after the date authorized to remain; or filing to extend, change or adjust status within visa validity. Senate requires post-admission compliance with all visa conditions in BOTH alternatives, including no unauthorized employment, together with either (A) no request to extend the period of admission during the visa validity period AND departure no later than five days after the last day of "such period", or (B) a GRANTED nonimmigrant extension or adjustment to lawful permanent resident status during the visa validity period. Filing is not a grant; visa validity is not admission duration; the five-day reimbursement conditions do not establish general stay/work permission.
