(b) Eligible insured In this section, the term "eligible insured" means an individual— (1) who enrolls in a qualified health plan in the silver level of coverage in the individual market offered through an Exchange; and (2) whose household income exceeds 100 percent but does not exceed 400 percent of the poverty line for a family of the size involved. In the case of an individual described in section 36B(c)(1)(B) of title 26, the individual shall be treated as having household income equal to 100 percent for purposes of applying this section. 

(e) Rules for individuals not lawfully present (1) In general If an individual who is an eligible insured is not lawfully present— (A) no cost-sharing reduction under this section shall apply with respect to the individual; and (B) for purposes of applying this section, the determination as to what percentage a taxpayer's household income bears to the poverty level for a family of the size involved shall be made under one of the following methods: (i) A method under which— (I) the taxpayer's family size is determined by not taking such individuals into account, and (II) the taxpayer's household income is equal to the product of the taxpayer's household income (determined without regard to this subsection) and a fraction— (aa) the numerator of which is the poverty line for the taxpayer's family size determined after application of subclause (I), and (bb) the denominator of which is the poverty line for the taxpayer's family size determined without regard to subclause (I). (ii) A comparable method reaching the same result as the method under clause (i). (2) Lawfully present For purposes of this section, an individual shall be treated as lawfully present only if the individual is, and is reasonably expected to be for the entire period of enrollment for which the cost-sharing reduction under this section is being claimed, a citizen or national of the United States or an alien lawfully present in the United States. (3) Secretarial authority The Secretary, in consultation with the Secretary of the Treasury, shall prescribe rules setting forth the methods by which calculations of family size and household income are made for purposes of this subsection. Such rules shall be designed to ensure that the least burden is placed on individuals enrolling in qualified health plans through an Exchange and taxpayers eligible for the credit allowable under this section.

claim_source_map.passage: (a) In general The Secretary, in consultation with the Secretary of the Treasury, shall establish a program under which— (1) upon request of an Exchange, advance determinations are made under section 18081 of this title with respect to the income eligibility of individuals enrolling in a qualified health plan in the individual market through the Exchange for the premium tax credit allowable under section 36B of title 26 and the cost-sharing reductions under section 18071 of this title; (2) the Secretary notifies— (A) the Exchange and the Secretary of the Treasury of the advance determinations; and (B) the Secretary of the Treasury of the name and employer identification number of each employer with respect to whom 1 or more employee 1 of the employer were deter mined to be eligible for the premium tax credit under section 36B of title 26 and the cost-sharing reductions under section 18071 of this title because— (i) the employer did not provide minimum essential coverage; or (ii) the employer provided such minimum essential coverage but it was determined under section 36B(c)(2)(C) of title 26 to either be unaffordable to the employee or not provide the required minimum actuarial value; and (3) the Secretary of the Treasury makes advance payments of such credit or reductions to the issuers of the qualified health plans in order to reduce the premiums payable by individuals eligible for such credit. (b) Advance determinations (1) In general The Secretary shall provide under the program established under subsection (a) that advance determination of eligibility with respect to any individual shall be made— (A) during the annual open enrollment period applicable to the individual (or such other enrollment period as may be specified by the Secretary); and (B) on the basis of the individual's household income for the most recent taxable year for which the Secretary, after consultation with the Secretary of the Treasury, determines information is available. (2) Changes in circumstances The Secretary shall provide procedures for making advance determinations on the basis of information other than that described in paragraph (1)(B) in cases where information included with an application form demonstrates substantial changes in income, changes in family size or other household circumstances, change in filing status, the filing of an application for unemployment benefits, or other significant changes affecting eligibility, including— (A) allowing an individual claiming a decrease of 20 percent or more in income, or filing an application for unemployment benefits, to have eligibility for the credit determined on the basis of household income for a later period or on the basis of the individual's estimate of such income for the taxable year; and (B) the determination of household income in cases where the taxpayer was not required to file a return of tax imposed by this chapter for the second preceding taxable year. (c) Payment of premium tax credits and cost-sharing reductions (1) In general The Secretary shall notify the Secretary of the Treasury and the Exchange through which the individual is enrolling of the advance determination under section 18081 of this title. (2) Premium tax credit (A) In general The Secretary of the Treasury shall make the advance payment under this section of any premium tax credit allowed under section 36B of title 26 to the issuer of a qualified health plan on a monthly basis (or such other periodic basis as the Secretary may provide). (B) Issuer responsibilities An issuer of a qualified health plan receiving an advance payment with respect to an individual enrolled in the plan shall— (i) reduce the premium charged the insured for any period by the amount of the advance payment for the period; (ii) notify the Exchange and the Secretary of such reduction; (iii) include with each billing statement the amount by which the premium for the plan has been reduced by reason of the advance payment; and (iv) in the case of any nonpayment of premiums by the insured— (I) notify the Secretary of such nonpayment; and (II) allow a 3-month grace period for nonpayment of premiums before discontinuing coverage. (3) Cost-sharing reductions The Secretary shall also notify the Secretary of the Treasury and the Exchange under paragraph (1) if an advance payment of the cost-sharing reductions under section 18071 of this title is to be made to the issuer of any qualified health plan with respect to any individual enrolled in the plan. The Secretary of the Treasury shall make such advance payment at such time and in such amount as the Secretary specifies in the notice. (d) No Federal payments for individuals not lawfully present Nothing in this subtitle or the amendments made by this subtitle allows Federal payments, credits, or cost-sharing reductions for individuals who are not lawfully present in the United States. (e) State flexibility Nothing in this subtitle or the amendments made by this subtitle shall be construed to prohibit a State from making payments to or on behalf of an individual for coverage under a qualified health plan offered through an Exchange that are in addition to any credits or cost-sharing reductions allowable to the individual under this subtitle and such amendments.

findings.headline: Separate choices within one legislative episode
findings.compact: Massie supported passage of the complete H.R.4 EH rescission package. H.R.4 would permanently rescind $800 million of specified Migration and Refugee Assistance unobligated budget authority as part of a wider whole-bill rescission package. Massie supported the direct H.R.4 Senate-amendment concurrence and its complete rescission package. H.Res.590 would directly adopt concurrence in the H.R.4 Senate amendment, including an $800 million Migration and Refugee Assistance unobligated-balance rescission within the full package.
detail: Massie supported passage of the complete H.R.4 EH rescission package.

The complete H.R.4 EH final-passage proposal permanently rescinds the named State Migration and Refugee Assistance $800 million unobligated balance in2(b)(7). The House rule499provides a separate final passage and also adopts492engrossment corrections toH.R.1; those separate corrections are not transplanted into this H.R.4 meaning. The affected provision cancels $800 million of UNOBLIGATED budget authority in the Department of State Migration and Refugee Assistance account made available by DivisionA of enacted119-4, effective only on enactment of the proposed rescission package. It does not recover already obligated/executed payments, rescind every fiscal-year balance, eliminate the whole account or establish the actual balance/spending/refugee effect. Existing 119-4 section1101(a)(11)/(b)/(c) carries forward the identified2024State appropriations at their specified levels/authority/conditions;1102–1108preserve extent/manner, comparable multiple/no-year availability, prohibitions and applicable conditions, with enacted State-title anomalies. The complete 2024Migration and Refugee Assistance paragraph appropriates $3.928 billion to remain available until expended, including its $750 million emergency designation and $5 million Israel-resettling refugee allocation, for State to carry out2601(a)/(b), other refugee/migration needs and stated personnel/administrative expenses. Those baseline amounts identify the account framework, not a calculation of the unobligated balance at this vote. Existing 2601(a)/(b) authorizes IOM movement/contributions/participation costs, contributions for specified international refugee-assistance organizations, and presidentially designated assistance to refugees OUTSIDE the United States under the foreign-policy finding. Other refugee/migration needs are stated in the appropriation; the account is not solely an ICE/domestic-removal fund or solely refugee admission quotas.2601(c)Emergency Refugee and Migration Assistance Fund is a separately defined authority, not silently equated to this named account. This proposal rescinds the specified appropriation balance, not the underlying refugee/admission/status statutes, every resettlement benefit or all emergency-assistance authority. It does not alter individual visa, asylum, TPS or sponsor eligibility. The choice is the WHOLE multiaccount rescission package, not a separately recorded vote on the $800 million line, a preferred alternative or a factual judgment about refugees. The entire EH also rescinds listed international-organization/peacekeeping, two Global Health Programs paragraphs, other foreign-assistance/operating accounts and two public-broadcasting fiscal-year amounts. Those are acknowledged as other package choices, not independently interpreted Health/Security/Environment conclusions here. The later Senate replacement changes other account/proviso language and is not assumed part of this earlier June 12vote. No actual rescission, refugee harm/benefit, spending result or enactment is inferred.
The Clerk recorded the House result as 'Passed' on 2025-06-12. This does not establish enactment.

R. 4 _______________________________________________________________________ AN ACT To rescind certain budget authority proposed to be rescinded in special messages transmitted to the Congress by the President on June 3, 2025, in accordance with section 1012(a) of the Congressional Budget and Impoundment Control Act of 1974. Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the United States of America in Congress assembled, SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE. This Act may be cited as the ``Rescissions Act of 2025''. SEC. 2. RESCISSIONS OF BUDGET AUTHORITY. (a) In General.--Pursuant to the special message transmitted by the President on June 3, 2025, to the House of Representatives and the Senate proposing the rescission of budget authority under section 1012 of part B of title X of the Congressional Budget and Impoundment Control Act of 1974 (2 U.S.C. 682 et seq.), the rescissions described under subsection (b) shall take effect immediately upon the date of enactment of this Act. (b) Rescissions.--The rescissions described in this subsection are as follows: (1) Of the unobligated balances under the heading ``International Organizations--Contributions to International Organizations'' made available by the Department of State, Foreign Operations, and Related Programs Appropriations Act, 2024 (division F of Public Law 118-47), $33,008,764 are permanently rescinded. (2) Of the unobligated balances under the heading ``International Organizations--Contributions to International Organizations'' made available by the Full-Year Continuing Appropriations Act, 2025 (division A of Public Law 119-4), $168,837,230 are permanently rescinded. (3) Of the unobligated balances under the heading ``International Organizations--Contributions for International Peacekeeping Activities'' made available by the Department of State, Foreign Operations, and Related Programs Appropriations Act, 2024 (division F of Public Law 118-47), $203,328,007 are permanently rescinded. (4) Of the unobligated balances under the heading ``International Organizations--Contributions for International Peacekeeping Activities'' made available by the Full-Year Continuing Appropriations Act, 2025 (division A of Public Law 119-4), $157,906,000 are permanently rescinded. (5) Of the unobligated balances in the first paragraph under the heading ``Bilateral Economic Assistance--Funds Appropriated to the President--Global Health Programs'' made available by the Full-Year Continuing Appropriations Act, 2025 (division A of Public Law 119-4), $500,000,000 are permanently rescinded. (6) Of the unobligated balances in the second paragraph under the heading ``Bilateral Economic Assistance--Funds Appropriated to the President--Global Health Programs'' made available by the Full-Year Continuing Appropriations Act, 2025 (division A of Public Law 119-4), $400,000,000 are permanently rescinded. (7) Of the unobligated balances under the heading ``Department of State--Migration and Refugee Assistance'' made available by the Full-Year Continuing Appropriations Act, 2025 (division A of Public Law 119-4), $800,000,000 are permanently rescinded. (8) Of the unobligated balances under the heading ``Bilateral Economic Assistance--Funds Appropriated to the President--Complex Crises Fund'' made available by the Full- Year Continuing Appropriations Act, 2025 (division A of Public Law 119-4), $43,000,000 are permanently rescinded. (9) Of the unobligated balances under the heading ``Bilateral Economic Assistance--Funds Appropriated to the President--Democracy Fund'' made available by the Full-Year Continuing Appropriations Act, 2025 (division A of Public Law 119-4), $83,000,000 are permanently rescinded. (10) Of the unobligated balances under the heading ``Bilateral Economic Assistance--Funds Appropriated to the President--Economic Support Fund'' made available by the Full- Year Continuing Appropriations Act, 2025 (division A of Public Law 119-4), $1,650,000,000 are permanently rescinded. (11) Of the unobligated balances under the heading ``Multilateral Assistance--International Financial Institutions--Contribution to the Clean Technology Fund'' made available by the Full-Year Continuing Appropriations Act, 2025 (division A of Public Law 119-4), $125,000,000 are permanently rescinded. (12) Of the unobligated balances under the heading ``Multilateral Assistance--Funds Appropriated to the President--International Organizations and Programs'' made available by the Full-Year Continuing Appropriations Act, 2025 (division A of Public Law 119-4), $436,920,000 are permanently rescinded. (13) Of the unobligated balances under the heading ``Bilateral Economic Assistance--Funds Appropriated to the President--Development Assistance'' made available by the Full- Year Continuing Appropriations Act, 2025 (division A of Public Law 119-4), $2,500,000,000 are permanently rescinded. (14) Of the unobligated balances under the heading ``Bilateral Economic Assistance--Funds Appropriated to the President--Assistance for Europe, Eurasia and Central Asia'' made available by the Full-Year Continuing Appropriations Act, 2025 (division A of Public Law 119-4), $460,000,000 are permanently rescinded. (15) Of the unobligated balances under the heading ``Bilateral Economic Assistance--Funds Appropriated to the President--International Disaster Assistance'' made available by the Full-Year Continuing Appropriations Act, 2025 (division A of Public Law 119-4), $496,000,000 are permanently rescinded. (16) Of the unobligated balances under the heading ``United States Agency for International Development--Funds Appropriated to the President--Operating Expenses'' made available by the Full-Year Continuing Appropriations Act, 2025 (division A of Public Law 119-4), $125,000,000 are permanently rescinded. (17) Of the unobligated balances under the heading ``Bilateral Economic Assistance--Funds Appropriated to the President--Transition Initiatives'' made available by the Full- Year Continuing Appropriations Act, 2025 (division A of Public Law 119-4), $57,000,000 are permanently rescinded. (18) Of the unobligated balances under the heading ``Bilateral Economic Assistance--Independent Agencies--Inter- American Foundation'' made available by the Full-Year Continuing Appropriations Act, 2025 (division A of Public Law 119-4), $27,000,000 are permanently rescinded. (19) Of the unobligated balances under the heading ``Bilateral Economic Assistance--Independent Agencies--United States African Development Foundation'' made available by the Full-Year Continuing Appropriations Act, 2025 (division A of Public Law 119-4), $22,000,000 are permanently rescinded. (20) Of the unobligated balances under the heading ``Related Programs--United States Institute of Peace'' made available by the Full-Year Continuing Appropriations Act, 2025 (division A of Public Law 119-4), $15,000,000 are permanently rescinded. (21)(A) Amounts made available for ``Corporation for Public Broadcasting'' for fiscal year 2026 by Public Law 118-47 are hereby permanently rescinded. (B) Amounts made available for ``Corporation for Public Broadcasting'' for fiscal year 2027 by Public Law 119-4 are hereby permanently rescinded. Passed the House of Representatives June 12, 2025. United States Code, 2024 Edition Title 22 - FOREIGN RELATIONS AND INTERCOURSE CHAPTER 36 - MIGRATION AND REFUGEE ASSISTANCE Sec. 2601 - Refugees and migration From the U.S. Government Publishing Office, www.gpo.gov §2601. Refugees and migration (a) United States membership in International Organization for Migration; contributions to Organization (1) The President is authorized to continue membership for the United States in the International Organization for Migration in accordance with the constitution of such organization approved in Venice, Italy, on October 19, 1953, as amended in Geneva, Switzerland, on November 24, 1998, upon entry into force of such amendments. (2) For the purpose of assisting in the movement of refugees and migrants, there are authorized to be appropriated to the President such amounts as may be necessary from time to time for payment by the United States of its contributions to the International Organization for Migration and all necessary salaries and expenses incidental to United States participation in such organization. (b) Appropriations for assistance to refugees There are authorized to be appropriated such amounts as may be necessary from time to time— (1) for contributions to the activities of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees for assistance to refugees under his mandate or persons on behalf of whom he is exercising his good offices, and for contributions to the International Organization for Migration, the International Committee of the Red Cross, and to other relevant international organizations; and (2) for assistance to or on behalf of refugees who are outside the United States designated by the President (by class, group, or designation of their respective countries of origin or areas of residence) when the President determines that such assistance will contribute to the foreign policy interests of the United States. (c) United States Emergency Refugee and Migration Assistance Fund; appropriations (1) Whenever the President determines it to be important to the national interest he is authorized to furnish on such terms and conditions as he may determine assistance under this chapter for the purpose of meeting unexpected urgent refugee and migration needs. (2) There is established a United States Emergency Refugee and Migration Assistance Fund to carry out the purposes of this section. There is authorized to be appropriated to the President from time to time such amounts as may be necessary for the fund to carry out the purposes of this section, except that no amount of funds may be appropriated which, when added to amounts previously appropriated but not yet obligated, would cause such amounts to exceed $100,000,000. Amounts appropriated hereunder shall remain available until expended. (3) Whenever the President requests appropriations pursuant to this authorization he shall justify such requests to the Committee on Foreign Relations of the Senate and to the Speaker of the House of Representatives, as well as to the Committees on Appropriations. (d) Information to Congressional committees The President shall keep the appropriate committees of Congress currently informed of the use of funds and the exercise of functions authorized in this chapter. (e) Continued availability of certain funds Unexpended balances of funds made available under authority of the Mutual Security Act of 1954, as amended, and of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961, as amended, [22 U.S.C. 2151 et seq.], and allocated or transferred for the purposes of sections 405(a), 405(c), 405(d) and 451(c) 1 of the Mutual Security Act of 1954, as amended [22 U.S.C. 1925(a), (c), (d), 1951(c)], are authorized to be continued available for the purposes of this section and may be consolidated with appropriations authorized by this section. (f) Restrictions on foreign assistance not applicable to migration and refugee assistance The President may furnish assistance and make contributions under this chapter notwithstanding any provision of law which restricts assistance to foreign countries. action_observations.compact: Massie supported the direct H.R.4 Senate-amendment concurrence and its complete rescission package. H.Res.590 would directly adopt concurrence in the H.R.4 Senate amendment, including an $800 million Migration and Refugee Assistance unobligated-balance rescission within the full package.
detail: Massie supported the direct H.R.4 Senate-amendment concurrence and its complete rescission package.

The exact H.Res.590 EH resolved clause DEEMS the House to have taken H.R.4 with its Senate amendment from the Speaker table and to have concurred in that amendment. It does not merely permit a later concurrence motion; this recorded agreement directly decides the complete H.R.4 EAS replacement text, a distinct exact action in the same underlying bill episode. The complete EAS is independently bound with itsJuly 17Senate action before theJuly 18House choice. Its Migration and Refugee Assistance target is printed in2(b)(6), unchanged in dollar amount from the earlierEH2(b)(7). The EAS says rescinded, without the earlierEHword permanently; the candidate preserves that wording rather than inferring a temporary restoration or repeatedsecond $800 million cancellation. The affected provision cancels $800 million of UNOBLIGATED budget authority in the Department of State Migration and Refugee Assistance account made available by DivisionA of enacted119-4, effective only on enactment of the proposed rescission package. It does not recover already obligated/executed payments, rescind every fiscal-year balance, eliminate the whole account or establish the actual balance/spending/refugee effect. Existing 119-4 section1101(a)(11)/(b)/(c) carries forward the identified2024State appropriations at their specified levels/authority/conditions;1102–1108preserve extent/manner, comparable multiple/no-year availability, prohibitions and applicable conditions, with enacted State-title anomalies. The complete 2024Migration and Refugee Assistance paragraph appropriates $3.928 billion to remain available until expended, including its $750 million emergency designation and $5 million Israel-resettling refugee allocation, for State to carry out2601(a)/(b), other refugee/migration needs and stated personnel/administrative expenses. Those baseline amounts identify the account framework, not a calculation of the unobligated balance at this vote. Existing 2601(a)/(b) authorizes IOM movement/contributions/participation costs, contributions for specified international refugee-assistance organizations, and presidentially designated assistance to refugees OUTSIDE the United States under the foreign-policy finding. Other refugee/migration needs are stated in the appropriation; the account is not solely an ICE/domestic-removal fund or solely refugee admission quotas.2601(c)Emergency Refugee and Migration Assistance Fund is a separately defined authority, not silently equated to this named account. This proposal rescinds the specified appropriation balance, not the underlying refugee/admission/status statutes, every resettlement benefit or all emergency-assistance authority. It does not alter individual visa, asylum, TPS or sponsor eligibility. The choice is the WHOLE multiaccount rescission package, not a separately recorded vote on the $800 million line, a preferred alternative or a factual judgment about refugees. The Senate package removes the earlier $400 million second Global Health Programs paragraph, retains the first-paragraph $500 million with its printed protected-program provisos/family-planning exception, and qualifies specified Economic Support/Development/Disaster rescissions; other listed assistance, international-organization and public-broadcasting accounts remain part of the whole EAS choice. These actual version differences do not create a component vote or change this $800 million target. EarlierEHpassage is not a vote on these laterEASqualifiers. No actual rescission, refugee harm/benefit, spending result or enactment is inferred.
The Clerk recorded the House result as 'Passed' on 2025-07-18. This does not establish enactment.

United States Code, 2024 Edition Title 22 - FOREIGN RELATIONS AND INTERCOURSE CHAPTER 36 - MIGRATION AND REFUGEE ASSISTANCE Sec. 2601 - Refugees and migration From the U.S. Government Publishing Office, www.gpo.gov §2601. Refugees and migration (a) United States membership in International Organization for Migration; contributions to Organization (1) The President is authorized to continue membership for the United States in the International Organization for Migration in accordance with the constitution of such organization approved in Venice, Italy, on October 19, 1953, as amended in Geneva, Switzerland, on November 24, 1998, upon entry into force of such amendments. (2) For the purpose of assisting in the movement of refugees and migrants, there are authorized to be appropriated to the President such amounts as may be necessary from time to time for payment by the United States of its contributions to the International Organization for Migration and all necessary salaries and expenses incidental to United States participation in such organization. (b) Appropriations for assistance to refugees There are authorized to be appropriated such amounts as may be necessary from time to time— (1) for contributions to the activities of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees for assistance to refugees under his mandate or persons on behalf of whom he is exercising his good offices, and for contributions to the International Organization for Migration, the International Committee of the Red Cross, and to other relevant international organizations; and (2) for assistance to or on behalf of refugees who are outside the United States designated by the President (by class, group, or designation of their respective countries of origin or areas of residence) when the President determines that such assistance will contribute to the foreign policy interests of the United States. (c) United States Emergency Refugee and Migration Assistance Fund; appropriations (1) Whenever the President determines it to be important to the national interest he is authorized to furnish on such terms and conditions as he may determine assistance under this chapter for the purpose of meeting unexpected urgent refugee and migration needs. (2) There is established a United States Emergency Refugee and Migration Assistance Fund to carry out the purposes of this section. There is authorized to be appropriated to the President from time to time such amounts as may be necessary for the fund to carry out the purposes of this section, except that no amount of funds may be appropriated which, when added to amounts previously appropriated but not yet obligated, would cause such amounts to exceed $100,000,000. Amounts appropriated hereunder shall remain available until expended. (3) Whenever the President requests appropriations pursuant to this authorization he shall justify such requests to the Committee on Foreign Relations of the Senate and to the Speaker of the House of Representatives, as well as to the Committees on Appropriations. (d) Information to Congressional committees The President shall keep the appropriate committees of Congress currently informed of the use of funds and the exercise of functions authorized in this chapter. (e) Continued availability of certain funds Unexpended balances of funds made available under authority of the Mutual Security Act of 1954, as amended, and of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961, as amended, [22 U.S.C. 2151 et seq.], and allocated or transferred for the purposes of sections 405(a), 405(c), 405(d) and 451(c) 1 of the Mutual Security Act of 1954, as amended [22 U.S.C. 1925(a), (c), (d), 1951(c)], are authorized to be continued available for the purposes of this section and may be consolidated with appropriations authorized by this section. (f) Restrictions on foreign assistance not applicable to migration and refugee assistance The President may furnish assistance and make contributions under this chapter notwithstanding any provision of law which restricts assistance to foreign countries. global health programs For <<NOTE: Apportionment.>> necessary expenses to carry out the provisions of chapters 1 and 10 of part I of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961, for global health activities, in addition to funds otherwise available for such purposes, $3,985,450,000, to remain available until September 30, 2025, and which shall be apportioned directly to the United States Agency for International Development: Provided, That this amount shall be made available for training, equipment, and technical assistance to build the capacity of public health institutions and organizations in developing countries, and for such activities as: (1) child survival and maternal health programs; (2) immunization and oral rehydration programs; (3) other health, nutrition, water and sanitation programs which directly address the needs of mothers and children, and related education programs; (4) assistance for children displaced or orphaned by causes other than AIDS; (5) programs for the prevention, treatment, control of, and research on HIV/AIDS, tuberculosis, polio, malaria, and other infectious diseases including neglected tropical diseases, and for assistance to communities severely affected by HIV/ AIDS, including children infected or affected by AIDS; (6) disaster preparedness training for health crises; (7) programs to prevent, prepare for, and respond to unanticipated and emerging global health threats, including zoonotic diseases; and (8) family planning/ reproductive health: Provided further, That funds appropriated under this paragraph may be made available for United States contributions to The GAVI Alliance and to a multilateral vaccine development partnership to support epidemic preparedness: Provided further, <<NOTE: Determination. President. Abortion.>> That none of the funds made available in this Act nor any unobligated balances from prior appropriations Acts may be made available to any organization or program which, as determined by the President of the United States, supports or participates in the management of a program of coercive abortion or involuntary sterilization: Provided further, <<NOTE: Deadline.>> That any determination made under the previous proviso must be made not later than 6 months after the date of enactment of this Act, and must be accompanied by the evidence and criteria utilized to make the determination: Provided further, <<NOTE: Abortion.>> That none of the funds made available under this Act may be used to pay for the performance of abortion as a method of family planning or to motivate or coerce [[Page 138 STAT. 741]] any person to practice abortions: Provided further, That nothing in this paragraph shall be construed to alter any existing statutory prohibitions against abortion under section 104 of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961: Provided further, <<NOTE: Lobbying. Abortion.>> That none of the funds made available under this Act may be used to lobby for or against abortion: Provided further, <<NOTE: Family planning. Requirements. Determination. Reports.>> That in order to reduce reliance on abortion in developing nations, funds shall be available only to voluntary family planning projects which offer, either directly or through referral to, or information about access to, a broad range of family planning methods and services, and that any such voluntary family planning project shall meet the following requirements: (1) service providers or referral agents in the project shall not implement or be subject to quotas, or other numerical targets, of total number of births, number of family planning acceptors, or acceptors of a particular method of family planning (this provision shall not be construed to include the use of quantitative estimates or indicators for budgeting and planning purposes); (2) the project shall not include payment of incentives, bribes, gratuities, or financial reward to: (A) an individual in exchange for becoming a family planning acceptor; or (B) program personnel for achieving a numerical target or quota of total number of births, number of family planning acceptors, or acceptors of a particular method of family planning; (3) the project shall not deny any right or benefit, including the right of access to participate in any program of general welfare or the right of access to health care, as a consequence of any individual's decision not to accept family planning services; (4) the project shall provide family planning acceptors comprehensible information on the health benefits and risks of the method chosen, including those conditions that might render the use of the method inadvisable and those adverse side effects known to be consequent to the use of the method; and (5) the project shall ensure that experimental contraceptive drugs and devices and medical procedures are provided only in the context of a scientific study in which participants are advised of potential risks and benefits; and, not less than 60 days after the date on which the USAID Administrator determines that there has been a violation of the requirements contained in paragraph (1), (2), (3), or (5) of this proviso, or a pattern or practice of violations of the requirements contained in paragraph (4) of this proviso, the Administrator shall submit to the Committees on Appropriations a report containing a description of such violation and the corrective action taken by the Agency: Provided further, That <<NOTE: Grants. Discrimination. Compliance.>> in awarding grants for natural family planning under section 104 of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961 no applicant shall be discriminated against because of such applicant's religious or conscientious commitment to offer only natural family planning; and, additionally, all such applicants shall comply with the requirements of the previous proviso: Provided further, That <<NOTE: Definition.>> for purposes of this or any other Act authorizing or appropriating funds for the Department of State, foreign operations, and related programs, the term ``motivate'', as it relates to family planning assistance, shall not be construed to prohibit the provision, consistent with local law, of information or counseling about all pregnancy options: Provided further, <<NOTE: Condoms.>> That information provided about the use of condoms as part of projects or activities that are funded from amounts appropriated by this Act shall be medically accurate and shall include the public health benefits and failure rates of such use. findings.headline: Separate choices within one legislative episode
findings.compact: Massie opposed passage of the whole exact H.R. 7147 annual DHS funding proposal; no preferred funding or immigration alternative is established. H.R. 7147 would fund FY 2026 border, ICE and USCIS operations within the whole DHS package, retaining qualified sponsor, custody, contracting and oversight limits and adding surveillance, camera and budget-reporting provisions. Massie supported adoption of the complete H.R. 7147 House continuing-resolution replacement in Rules Committee Print 119-21. H.Res. 1142 would adopt the whole H.R. 7147 House replacement, continuing remaining appropriations including DHS immigration operations through May 22, 2026, subject to earlier applicable funding enactments and existing conditions, with qualified lapse-pay and obligation provisions.
detail: Massie opposed passage of the whole exact H.R. 7147 annual DHS funding proposal; no preferred funding or immigration alternative is established.

The January 22 H.R. 7147 PASSAGE choice uses the complete IH body AS AMENDED by adopted H.Res. 1014 section 7, which adds the Senate-data 213 repeal before passage. The rule permits explanatory material by January 23 and directs later incorporation into H.R. 7148; the annual appropriation clauses themselves name the Final Bill table. The LATER H.Res. 1016 engrossment correction must not be back-projected: as voted,230(b) bars procurement/equipping of long-range kinetic-capable unmanned aircraft using THIS ACT OR ANY OTHER ACT funds; the later EH instead limits that phrase to DHS funds in this/prior Acts. The House passage record and correction sequence are separately bound. The standalone printed reference to consolidated-Act section 4 and subsequent packaging/report implementation are preserved for independent candidate legal review rather than treated as an unprinted stand-alone section. This action shares the H.R. 7147 episode with the later whole House CR replacement, each with its own meaning and actual choice. The annual DHS titles would fund existing border processing/security, immigration enforcement, custody and removal, citizenship-services processing and verification, and associated oversight for FY 2026 within a wider DHS package. CBP Operations and Support is $17.727974 billion, with $550 million available through September 30, 2027, mixed customs/trade/travel, UAC transport, air/marine and law-enforcement functions, Harbor Maintenance and user-fee components, and qualified informant, preclearance and Tribal-road uses. CBP procurement/construction is $222.886 million with distinct September 2028 asset and September 2030 construction availability. The final table allocates CBP Ops across Border Security $6.644912 billion, Trade/Travel $6.610801 billion, Integrated Operations $1.730551 billion and Mission Support $2.741710 billion; these are not four independently voted immigration policies or all-person-removal spending. The earlier $650 million CBP-to-FEMA shelter-transfer row has no new Final Bill amount. ICE Ops is $10.036362 billion, including $46.696 million through September 2027, no-year forced-labor funds, qualified HERO/IP-rights/informant/special-operations uses and up to $11.216 million for care, maintenance and repatriation of smuggled aliens UNLAWFULLY PRESENT. The final allocations are HSI $2.591251 billion, ERO $5.453706 billion, Mission Support $1.543711 billion and OPLA $447.694 million. ERO includes Custody $3.838340 billion, Fugitive $165.016 million, Criminal Alien Program $312.835 million, ATD $393.647 million and Transport/Removal $743.868 million. HSI includes many non-immigration investigations; detention and ATD are different uses. These table amounts do not themselves establish actual beds, removals or expenditure. ICE procurement is $5 million through September 2028. USCIS Ops is $122.941 million: $112.566 million Employment Status Verification and $10.375 million Application Processing/backlog reduction in the Final Bill table, not exclusively E-Verify. USCIS has no new Federal Assistance/Citizenship and Integration Grant amount in the final table; previously funded grants and termination-justification reporting are distinct. Existing adjudication-fee authority 1356(m)/(n) and the bill no-required-fee-reduction proviso remain; the separate fee-funded-program table is not an extra new discretionary appropriation. OSEM Ops $316.295 million includes $10 million CRCL, $5 million Citizenship/Immigration Services Ombudsman, no new Immigration Detention Ombudsman allocation, and no new $15 million ATD Case Management Grant allocation; the last two do not abolish their statutory offices or all ATD. OBIM receives $271 million and IDENT/HART procurement $25 million. OIG Ops $257.599 million includes $20 million additional detention inspections through September 2027 and $12.814 million reconciliation-fund oversight. Section 109 adds $20 million for body-worn cameras for agents/officers enforcing INA authorities plus a 30 day spending plan. FEMA includes $85.5 million Operation Stonegarden within $494 million State Homeland grants. The wider TSA, Coast Guard, Secret Service, disaster, cyber, training, research, Supreme Court-security and air-traffic provisions remain whole-package context; membership in DHS does not make all their spending Immigration evidence.

The statutory restrictions preserve their exact funding and trigger scopes. Section 207 bars a NEW defined land-border crossing fee and a related study, beginning enactment, for pedestrians/cyclists/private-vehicle drivers/passengers at northern/southern LPOEs; it does not abolish all existing immigration or inspection fees.208 requires a 90 day CBP procurement plan before this Act's funds are obligated;209 permits altering National Targeting Center operations but protects planned vetting at existing locations across specified current/prior/fee funds unless later statute authorizes a reduction.210 bars funds for Border Security Assets/Infrastructure in this or prior Acts from procuring/deploying NONAUTONOMOUS surveillance SYSTEMS, using 119-21 section 90004(c)'s definition; the older 90004(b) restriction separately concerns tested/accepted autonomous TOWERS using that section's funds.211 requires the November 30, 2021 CBP pregnant/postpartum/nursing/infant custody policy OR substantively similar standards developed with maternal/pediatric experts to be in effect and fully implemented. The original covered populations include pregnancy with medical concerns OR third trimester/active labor, nursing individuals, postpartum within six months or recent pregnancy loss, and infants under one year. Health interviews/assessment/referral retain resource/operational and offered-assessment/acceptance qualifications; documented fifteen-minute welfare checks, nutrition/breastfeeding/infant supplies, facility/operational qualifications and incident records remain; it is not first-ever care, an automatic 72 hour release rule, or identical unqualified entitlements for every person.212 prohibits using ICE Ops to CONTINUE 287(g) delegations when the DHS IG determines a MATERIAL agreement violation.213 prohibits continuing a detention-services contract if its TWO most recent OVERALL performance evaluations are BELOW adequate/equivalent median, with ICE OPR conducting the evaluations. Neither trigger is every complaint or one failed component score.214 permits necessary ICE Ops reprogramming/transfers for detention of aliens prioritized for removal without 503(d)'s time/condition limit; it is not an unrestricted waiver of every appropriation or statutory restriction.

215 continues semimonthly 2021 detention-data reporting, including the original 2020 operational/ATD/facility/detention/release/removal data and 2021 additions such as solitary-confinement use/duration and length-of-stay bins.216 reapplies complete 2020 sections 216/217: no covered detention/removal/referral/initiation-of-proceeding of a UAC sponsor, potential sponsor or household member BASED ON HHS-shared information, EXCEPT the specified background-check findings of an aggravated-felony/child-abuse/sexual-violence/child-porn felony conviction OR pending related FELONY charge, business association involving unrelated minors below legal wage or denied school, or prostitution participation/implementation. It is neither an absolute sponsor exemption nor an exception for every conviction or illegal-entry suspicion. The accompanying IG 287(g) report covers participation, training, criminality/nationality, removals, outreach and future plans.217 replaces the earlier 45 day current-Act plan with a 30 day Director briefing/written plan covering ALL available current/prior/carryover/fee funds, monthly PPA/pay/nonpay projections and unchanged initial comparison; monthly updates are due within 15 days after the following month begins. Conditional $100,000 Executive Leadership/Oversight amounts become available on the 16 th of each month, at most $700,000 for the fiscal year, subject to timely reporting beginning 30 days after enactment.218 requires a 90 day plan for 119-21 detention-facility funding, locations/beds/cost/transport/removal-flight/end-state capacity, with quarterly updates within 30 days; reporting projections are not observed immigration outcomes.219 protects ICE attaché/liaison presence at foreign embassies/consulates using this or other Act funds, except the joint DHS/State foreign-policy explanation or a host-country cessation request.238 reapplies the 2021 fencing restriction WITH RESPECT TO THIS ACT's funds in the same manner: Santa Ana, Bentsen-Rio Grande Valley State Park, La Lomita, National Butterfly Center, within OR EAST of Vista del Mar Ranch, and historic cemeteries. Do not infer an unrestricted prohibition on every separate reconciliation-fund use.

USCIS 401 permits only five replacement vehicles where GSA does not lease, with authorized home/work use;402 restricts A-76 competition for five named USCIS employee classes, including temporary/term staff;403 permits collection/use of biometrics at Application Support Centers overseen VIRTUALLY by USCIS personnel using appropriate technology. This repeats existing 2024 authority, rather than first authorizing biometrics, universal remote adjudication or unrestricted searches.512 continues the THIS ACT funding restriction on amending the INA 337 naturalization oath, preserving 1448's existing qualifying modified oaths and disability/qualifying-child waivers;517 uses 1324 a(h)(3)'s employment-at-the-particular-time definition, excluding LPRs and law-authorized workers from unauthorized alien, not all noncitizens.514 restricts this Act's funds for national-ID planning/testing/piloting/development, not every immigration identity document.527 continues the funding restriction on restraints for pregnant or post-delivery women in DHS custody/transport/outside treatment, with individualized unavoidable serious flight risk/immediate harm or therapeutic-medical exceptions for a pregnant woman, safest/least-restrictive provider-determined restraints, an ABSOLUTE active-labor/delivery ban, barred pregnant positions/belts and feasible left-side positioning.528 protects covered death/possible-sexual-assault/abuse records and allegations of abuse/crime/disruption BY detainees from destruction, with disclosure on an affected punished individual's request under applicable law/litigation rules. It is not unrestricted public access to all detainee or staff records.536 repeats a this/other-Act funding bar on transferring/releasing/assisting transfer to or within the United States/territories/possessions of the specified Guantanamo DOD-held-on-or-after-June 24, 2009 NONcitizen/NONmilitary detainees, not a general new INA inadmissibility ground for all people held elsewhere.547 bars THIS ACT DHS funds from blocking Members or designated House/Senate employees conducting oversight of DHS-operated/contracted ALIEN detention/housing facilities or restaging conditions: Members need no prior notice; staff may be required 24 hours. It is not an unrestricted public-visitor right or a blanket rule for all HHS facilities/funding sources.

General appropriation controls remain:501 current-fiscal-year obligation limit unless express longer/no-year availability;502 merges prior balances for the original purposes/availability;503 advance reprogramming notices and 5 percent transfers/no more than 10 percent augmentation, June 15 initial-notification limit with imminent-life/property exception, grant/new-unapproved-PPA restrictions and deobligated-balance procedures.503(f) permits UP TO $20 million transferred into the EXISTING Immigration Emergency Fund with five-day notice. The old 404 note separately authorizes a $35 million BALANCE and qualified immigration-emergency withdrawals needing Presidential determination/certification, plus capped State/local reimbursements under 404(b)(2) for which that emergency determination is not needed. A transfer here is not a new emergency declaration, unrestricted withdrawal or actual reimbursement.505 carries up to 50 percent unobligated FY 2026 Ops balances through September 2027 with the printed June 15, 2027 recording deadline and 503 notification.524's qualified report publication retains national-interest determination, security/proprietary exceptions and 45 day committee availability unless otherwise specified, now with 503 suspension for failure;525 permits minor Ops procurement/construction with unit caps $250,000 personal/$4 million real property.537/538 require monthly independently validated arrival and detention/removal estimates, demographic separation, common planning/budget assumptions and agency/committee sharing; failure suspends 503 authority.539 requires alternatives/cost-benefit analysis BEFORE requesting DoD border support and post-request/grant/quarterly reports.541 transfers AT LEAST $5 million to ICE Blue Campaign with pre-obligation notice.546 requires seven-day and quarterly 119-21 obligations/fee-retention/remittance/planned-use reports.551-553 rescind only identified UNOBLIGATED account balances, with the printed emergency-designation exception in 551 and defined 2024 carryover balances in 552; this is not cancellation of every outstanding obligation or all reconciliation funds.107's I&A covered-activity funding restriction incorporates 6303: specified charged/custodial unadjudicated criminal interviews need consent AFTER counsel consultation, targeting journalists in their functions is covered, and U. S.-person interviews require factual reasonable belief in significant foreign intelligence; the definition includes known LPRs and qualified associations/corporations, with foreign-controlled-corporation exception. Legal/privacy/civic oversight and specified lawful information sharing are expressly preserved. It is not a general no-intelligence rule or new immigration status ground.

The January 22 explanatory narrative and visually checked FINAL BILL tables govern the named allocations; earlier House Report 119-173 PROPOSAL amounts and numbered proposed riders are not substituted for this actual text. The narrative says House report LANGUAGE has equal weight unless noted or addressed to the contrary, and repetition does not negate it unless expressly provided. Its operative directions include 287(g) cost-benefit/training/agreement evaluations and reports; border/credible-fear/parole/UAC/parent/veteran/tribal/arrest/removal/wrongful-return data; warrants/probable-cause/flight-risk reports; HART/IDENT oversight and qualified child-separation notifications; medical/water/food/shelter/TEDS and continued migrant-care requirements; free confidential ICE counsel communication/document/VAV access and legal-orientation continuation TO THE MAXIMUM EXTENT POSSIBLE; qualified family-unity/separation, pregnant-custody redeterminations and sensitive-location directions; facilities/segregation/inspections/PREA oversight; ATD metrics/consequence reporting, monitoring-feasibility and procurement directions; and USCIS processing dashboards/backlogs, fees/waivers, asylum/refugee/EAD/SIJ/H-2 A/H-2 B/R-1 processing/abuse and policy-change reporting. The separately incorporated 118-85,116-458 and 118-553 directions are source-bound, retaining their population/exception/scheduling/privacy/feasibility wording and distinguishing requested reports, encouraged actions, directives and statutory rights. For example, the port-of-entry counsel paragraph requests a 90 day briefing on requirements for a meaningful one-hour consultation for U. S. nationals, LPRs returning from a temporary foreign visit, valid unexpired immigrant/nonimmigrant visa holders, refugees, returning asylees or approved parole applicants, with greatest-practicable in-person advocacy, not an unconditional new lawyer entitlement for every border entrant. The related ICE counsel direction concerns free confidential unmonitored 60 minute calls/video with 24 hour scheduling, document exchange/delivery and facility access, not government-paid representation. Continued family reunification is qualified by best interests/possibility; the pregnancy-custody direction preserves required-law/exceptional-circumstance grounds and monthly review. The House TPS-Venezuela direction calls for reconsideration/analysis and a 30 day briefing, while the Ukraine program language urges continuation; neither itself grants a named person TPS/parole or first changes individual eligibility. The final fee-waiver language supersedes the House cost-recovery restriction while mandatory statutory fees and their own waiver limits are not silently repealed. The Housereport 50,000-bed proposal, earlier PPA figures and former numbered proposed sanctuary/rhetoric riders are not treated as actual present statutory conditions merely because the report is referenced. Conflicting or uncertain application of retained report language versus the final allocation/statutory scope remains a candidate-review question, not an accepted adjudication.

Baseline: 119-4 incorporated FY 2024 DHS 118-47 division C with specified exceptions/anomalies, including ICE's $9.986542 billion FY 2025 Ops level; at the January 22 vote, 119-37 division A carried relevant FY 2025 rates/conditions with its own exceptions and its printed January 30, 2026 outer date. Public Law 119-75 was enacted February 3, 2026, AFTER this exact House action; its February 13 continuing-resolution date is later chronology context only and must not govern the January choice. The annual proposal replaces the relevant continuation with full FY 2026 DHS appropriations; many sponsor/contract/287(g)/fencing/oath/employment/restraint/oversight/biometric controls already existed and are not first-ever rights or powers. The separate 119-21 reconciliation appropriations and fees are not all repealed/replaced by these annual totals. Whole passage includes enforcement funds, services, protective limits, oversight and other DHS/non-DHS provisions together. No component-only preference, motive, actual detention/deportation/care improvement, pay/spending, later enactment or individual legal outcome is inferred.
The Clerk recorded the House result as 'Passed' on 2026-01-22. This does not establish enactment.
Massie supported adoption of the complete H.R. 7147 House continuing-resolution replacement in Rules Committee Print 119-21.

The complete H.Res. 1142 EH directly deems the House to have taken H.R. 7147 from the Speaker's table and concurred in the Senate amendment WITH an amendment consisting of the whole Rules Committee Print 119-21. This is the final House replacement choice, not a rule merely permitting later consideration or a vote adopting the unamended Senate annual DHS text. The complete two-page print expressly replaces the entire matter proposed to be inserted by the Senate amendment. Its section 2 changes the date in 119-37 division A 106(3) to May 22, 2026. The existing 119-75 division H 101 date is February 13, 2026; the proposal continues the residual continuing-appropriations framework, including DHS border, immigration-enforcement and citizenship-services activities, under its existing rates, authority, conditions and exceptions. It does not supply the separate annual DHS funding totals or new riders from earlier H.R. 7147 annual versions, H.R. 7744 or H.R. 8029. Under 119-37 division A 101, FY 2025 rates and conditions derive from 119-4 division A subject to express exclusions and anomalies.119-4 incorporates FY 2024 DHS appropriations with identified exceptions and its own DHS 1701-1709 adjustments, including the 9.986542 b ICE Operations and Support annualized rate. That is an incorporated rate for continuation, not an assertion that this short extension newly appropriates or spends that full annual amount.119-37 section 106 still ends any project/activity appropriation or authority at the EARLIEST applicable project-specific appropriation, enactment of an applicable appropriations Act without that project, or the substituted date. It therefore does not extend already superseded appropriations for every agency indiscriminately. Sections 103-105 and 109-110 retain the pertinent manner, no-new-FY 2025-unfunded-activity, obligation-period and limited-continuation constraints. The date amendment does not expressly rewrite every separately fixed immigration-program sunset, change visa/admission/removal eligibility, grant a new enforcement power, abolish fees, or reproduce the separate FY 2025 reconciliation appropriations. The complete division A also retains its specific anomalies and linked-date extensions; only section 106(3) is expressly changed here. Section 3 includes the lapse beginning ON OR ABOUT February 14, 2026 in the covered period. Preserve that printed date rather than importing the February 13 wording of the separate March annual bills. Section 4 makes amounts already made available for personnel pay, allowances and benefits under 119-37 division A and 119-75 division H available for 31 US 1341(c) payments and directs that they SHALL be made. Existing 1341(c) already covers qualifying furloughed and excepted Government/DC employees, standard pay, earliest possible payment after a covered lapse ends, enactment of ending appropriations, and qualifying leave compensation; this proposal is not first-ever backpay authority or evidence anyone actually received pay. Section 5 ratifies anticipated obligations for essential life/property protection, orderly shutdown or otherwise legally authorized purposes ONLY if otherwise in accord with the referenced Acts. It does not validate any unlawful obligation without qualification. The whole adopted replacement also carries this personnel/obligation framework for the referenced Acts, beyond Immigration; no component-only immigration preference is attributed. Its legal vehicle remains H.R. 7147, one underlying bill episode, while this exact concurrence has a different operative proposal from the January annual funding choice. Do not substitute later enrolled/enacted text or infer enactment, May 22 actual operations, payments, removals or immigration outcomes from the House resolution result.
The Clerk recorded the House result as 'Passed' on 2026-03-27. This does not establish enactment.
qualifications_on_both_levels: This is the whole exact annual DHS package, mixing enforcement, processing, custody protections, oversight and other spending. No component-only preference or actual removal/bed/care/spending outcome is inferred.

The FINAL BILL allocation columns control: CBP/ICE contain non-immigration uses; USCIS includes verification AND application processing. Fee-funded figures and separate reconciliation appropriations are not added as new discretionary funding here.

Existing sponsor restrictions retain specified background exceptions;287(g) and detention-contract bars require material IG findings or two below-adequate overall OPR evaluations. They are not absolute sponsor immunity or a bar triggered by any complaint.

Pregnant/postpartum custody policy may be replaced by substantively similar expert-developed standards. Restraint exceptions, absolute labor/delivery protections and retained law/exceptional-circumstance custody boundaries are not flattened into universal release or no-restraint claims.

Counsel/family/medical/report directions retain population, timing, privacy, legal and feasibility qualifications. POE counsel assessment is distinct from ICE confidential-access directives and government-paid representation; proposed report riders/amounts do not silently become actual statute.

Congressional oversight access applies to named Members/designated staff at DHS alien facilities with the printed notice and funding scopes; record disclosure, fee, fence and intelligence limits retain their own exceptions and scopes.

Some controls are continued; others add reporting, camera, surveillance or budget conditions. No new general INA admission/removal power, wholesale fee abolition, every visa-program sunset extension or unqualified expenditure authority is established.

The exact legislative version and bill episode control. Later engrossment corrections, the March continuing-resolution replacement and parallel bills do not retrospectively change this member choice. Ambiguous report/incorporation application remains candidate review, with no acceptance or public authorization.
The adopted rule directly deems final concurrence WITH the complete House replacement. It does not adopt the annual DHS proposal or the unamended Senate text.

May 22, 2026 substitutes the continuing-resolution outer date. Earlier project-specific appropriation or applicable enactment endpoints, existing rates, conditions, anomalies and no-new-activity limits remain; no full annual ICE amount is newly counted as this extension.

The printed lapse date is on or about February 14. Personnel payments use existing 1341(c), and ratified obligations must otherwise accord with the referenced Acts; no first backpay entitlement, unconditional validation or actual payment is inferred.

No new admission/removal eligibility or agency power, blanket visa-program sunset extension, abolition of immigration fees or annual-DHS-rider adoption is established. This is the whole replacement within the underlying H.R. 7147 episode; implementation and enactment are not inferred.

S.-person interviews require factual reasonable belief in significant foreign intelligence; the definition includes known LPRs and qualified associations/corporations, with foreign-controlled-corporation exception. The January 22 explanatory narrative and visually checked FINAL BILL tables govern the named allocations; earlier House Report 119-173 PROPOSAL amounts and numbered proposed riders are not substituted for this actual text. The narrative says House report LANGUAGE has equal weight unless noted or addressed to the contrary, and repetition does not negate it unless expressly provided. Its operative directions include 287(g) cost-benefit/training/agreement evaluations and reports; border/credible-fear/parole/UAC/parent/veteran/tribal/arrest/removal/wrongful-return data; warrants/probable-cause/flight-risk reports; HART/IDENT oversight and qualified child-separation notifications; medical/water/food/shelter/TEDS and continued migrant-care requirements; free confidential ICE counsel communication/document/VAV access and legal-orientation continuation TO THE MAXIMUM EXTENT POSSIBLE; qualified family-unity/separation, pregnant-custody redeterminations and sensitive-location directions; facilities/segregation/inspections/PREA oversight; ATD metrics/consequence reporting, monitoring-feasibility and procurement directions; and USCIS processing dashboards/backlogs, fees/waivers, asylum/refugee/EAD/SIJ/H-2 A/H-2 B/R-1 processing/abuse and policy-change reporting. The separately incorporated 118-85,116-458 and 118-553 directions are source-bound, retaining their population/exception/scheduling/privacy/feasibility wording and distinguishing requested reports, encouraged actions, directives and statutory rights. For example, the port-of-entry counsel paragraph requests a 90 day briefing on requirements for a meaningful one-hour consultation for U. S. nationals, LPRs returning from a temporary foreign visit, valid unexpired immigrant/nonimmigrant visa holders, refugees, returning asylees or approved parole applicants, with greatest-practicable in-person advocacy, not an unconditional new lawyer entitlement for every border entrant. The related ICE counsel direction concerns free confidential unmonitored 60 minute calls/video with 24 hour scheduling, document exchange/delivery and facility access, not government-paid representation. Continued family reunification is qualified by best interests/possibility; the pregnancy-custody direction preserves required-law/exceptional-circumstance grounds and monthly review. The House TPS-Venezuela direction calls for reconsideration/analysis and a 30 day briefing, while the Ukraine program language urges continuation; neither itself grants a named person TPS/parole or first changes individual eligibility. The final fee-waiver language supersedes the House cost-recovery restriction while mandatory statutory fees and their own waiver limits are not silently repealed. The Housereport 50,000-bed proposal, earlier PPA figures and former numbered proposed sanctuary/rhetoric riders are not treated as actual present statutory conditions merely because the report is referenced. Conflicting or uncertain application of retained report language versus the final allocation/statutory scope remains a candidate-review question, not an accepted adjudication.

Baseline: 119-4 incorporated FY 2024 DHS 118-47 division C with specified exceptions/anomalies, including ICE's $9.986542 billion FY 2025 Ops level; at the January 22 vote, 119-37 division A carried relevant FY 2025 rates/conditions with its own exceptions and its printed January 30, 2026 outer date. Public Law 119-75 was enacted February 3, 2026, AFTER this exact House action; its February 13 continuing-resolution date is later chronology context only and must not govern the January choice. The annual proposal replaces the relevant continuation with full FY 2026 DHS appropriations; many sponsor/contract/287(g)/fencing/oath/employment/restraint/oversight/biometric controls already existed and are not first-ever rights or powers. The separate 119-21 reconciliation appropriations and fees are not all repealed/replaced by these annual totals. Whole passage includes enforcement funds, services, protective limits, oversight and other DHS/non-DHS provisions together. No component-only preference, motive, actual detention/deportation/care improvement, pay/spending, later enactment or individual legal outcome is inferred.

qualifications: This is the whole exact annual DHS package, mixing enforcement, processing, custody protections, oversight and other spending. No component-only preference or actual removal/bed/care/spending outcome is inferred.

The FINAL BILL allocation columns control: CBP/ICE contain non-immigration uses; USCIS includes verification AND application processing. Fee-funded figures and separate reconciliation appropriations are not added as new discretionary funding here.

Existing sponsor restrictions retain specified background exceptions;287(g) and detention-contract bars require material IG findings or two below-adequate overall OPR evaluations. They are not absolute sponsor immunity or a bar triggered by any complaint.

Pregnant/postpartum custody policy may be replaced by substantively similar expert-developed standards. Restraint exceptions, absolute labor/delivery protections and retained law/exceptional-circumstance custody boundaries are not flattened into universal release or no-restraint claims.

Counsel/family/medical/report directions retain population, timing, privacy, legal and feasibility qualifications. POE counsel assessment is distinct from ICE confidential-access directives and government-paid representation; proposed report riders/amounts do not silently become actual statute.

Congressional oversight access applies to named Members/designated staff at DHS alien facilities with the printed notice and funding scopes; record disclosure, fee, fence and intelligence limits retain their own exceptions and scopes.

Some controls are continued; others add reporting, camera, surveillance or budget conditions. No new general INA admission/removal power, wholesale fee abolition, every visa-program sunset extension or unqualified expenditure authority is established.
